title: Ravens Report Card, Week 9: More dreadful offensive play leading to a lopsided loss
summary: The Baltimore Ravens were defeated handedly by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night, 33-10. It marked the team’s fourth straight loss and third consecutive defeat by 20+ points, representing a rock-bottom moment for the Ravens. Here are report card grades for Ravens’ position groups from another merciless loss in Week 9. Quarterback: F Joe Fagnano […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 05: Derrick Henry #22 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball against Albert Regis #98 of the Jacksonville Jaguars during the third quarter of the game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 05, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Patrick Smith/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens were defeated handedly by the Jacksonville Jaguars on Thursday night, 33-10. It marked the team’s fourth straight loss and third consecutive defeat by 20+ points, representing a rock-bottom moment for the Ravens. Here are report card grades for Ravens’ position groups from another merciless loss in Week 9. Quarterback: F Joe Fagnano had a few factors working against him in this game: he was playing through an ankle injury, had only a few days of preparation, and was facing a talented Jaguars’ defense. Nevertheless, he struggled mightily in his first career NFL start. Fagnano completed 10-of-18 passes for just 60 yards and was intercepted twice. To what extent Fagnano was limited by his ankle is unknown, but the Ravens clearly did not trust him to attempt passes more than a few yards downfield. While Fagnano was great in the preseason, a high-stakes regular season contest is clearly a different ball game for an undrafted rookie quarterback. Running Back: C+ Derrick Henry had another inefficient rushing game, totaling 57 yards on 17 carries with a longest run of only eight yards. Henry ran hard and took on a number of wildcat snaps, but once again there was little running room to be found behind the offensive line. Justice Hill managed to break free for a long 65-yard rushing touchdown late in the game, giving the Ravens at least one notable offensive highlight. Hill finished with 92 scrimmage yards. Wide Receiver: C- It’s hard to knock the Ravens’ wide receivers too much given the dire state of the team’s passing attack. With Fagnano attempting few if any downfield throws, there was no chance of the wideouts doing significant damage in this game. Zay Flowers caught three passes and gained only six yards and rushed three times for 17 yards. His body language appeared deflated in the second half. Rashod Bateman and LaJohntay Wester each had once catch as well for minimal impact. Tight End: D Mark Andrews was the team’s leading receiver on the night with just two grabs for 19 yards. His costly miscues outweighed any impact as a pass-catcher or blocker, though. Andrews was flagged for another false start, which is a weekly occurrence now, and fumbled a snap on a fourth-and-one conversion attempt. Matthew Hibner was targeted twice and made one catch for five yards. He dropped a would-be long first down conversion, although the ball was tipped and appeared to alter the trajectory of the pass — but it still hit him in the hands. Josh Cuevas was not targeted but was flagged for a penalty. Offensive Line: D+ Aside from Hill’s one long 65-yard run in the second half, the Ravens were once again unable to open up many rushing lanes up front. Fagnano was only sacked once and hit four times, but he didn’t drop back in the pocket very often anyways. It was a positive to have Vega Ioane back in the lineup at right guard, which allowed the Ravens to finally play a full game with their ideal five-man group together. Unfortunately, the results were not notable. Ronnie Stanley was flagged for another pre-snap penalty, his fifth flag in the last two weeks. Defensive Line: C The Ravens did a great job defending the run up front. Jacksonville’s top two rushers, Byshaul Tuten and Chris Rodriguez Jr., combined for 22 carries and gained 48 yards. They each scored a touchdown, but their scores came on short yardage runs in the red zone. Unfortunately, the Ravens got very little pressure through the interior on Trevor Lawrence. On the bright side, Nnamdi Madubuike had two deflected passes (although he was flagged for a costly offside penalty on fourth down) and Broderick Washington had a pass breakup. Madubuike had the team’s only quarterback hit. Travis Jones played strong as well and recorded a tackle for loss. Edge Rusher: D+ The edge rushers were a positive factor against the run as well, setting the edge and preventing explosive outside rushes. However, they were almost a complete no show in the pass rushing department. Not a single edge defender recorded a sack, quarterback hit or tackle for loss. Trey Hendrickson is clearly bothered by his finger injury, but it would still be nice to see him start making impact plays more consistently. Mike Green had a nice run stop at the line of scrimmage, but the Ravens need him to get after the quarterback. Without Tavius Robinson, this group has left much to be desired over the last few weeks. Linebacker: B- Roquan Smith had a team-leading eight tackles and made a strong stop at the goal line on the Jaguars’ opening drive. In pass coverage, Smith appears out of place over the middle of the field too often. Trenton Simpson had six tackles, and Teddye Buchanan recovered a fumble in the second half along with a good play against the run too. Cornerback: D+ The hits keep on coming for Marlon Humphrey, who was beaten for a long 52-yard reception within the first few plays of the game. On that play, the Ravens had the Jaguars dead to rights, but Humphrey got lost and allowed a backup tight end to get behind him. He had two pass breakups later in the game. With Nate Wiggins sidelined, Chidobe Awuzie got the start and had one tackle. Awuzie was beaten at least once by Jakobi Meyers and appeared to whiff on a tackle in space. As a whole, the Ravens’ corners continue to be far too inconsistent and prone to coverage lapses. Safety: C – Kyle Hamilton exited the game in the second half with a hip injury and did not return. Prior to that, he was one of the team’s lone bright spots, blowing up a run that nearly resulted in a safety and recording a pass breakup that should have been picked off. Malaki Starks was beaten badly by Parker Washington in the slot for a long 50-yard touchdown reception. Starks should not have been in one-on-one coverage against Washington, but it was a reminder of his limitations as a coverage player. He did redeem himself with a forced fumble on Travis Hunter later in the game. Special Teams: C + Jake Moody made a good first impression as the Ravens’ new kicker, nailing a 53-yard attempt in the first quarter. Ryan Eckley had five punts with three inside the 20-yard line and a longest of 55 yards. In the punt return game, Wester returned only one try and gained 10 yards. Given their offensive limitations right now, the Ravens badly need some splash special teams plays to win and they aren’t getting them.

full_text: The Buffalo Bills are off to a great start, sitting at 6-1 atop the entire AFC. The Minnesota Vikings are also off to a great start, and they are second in the NFC with a a6-1 record, as they are currently tired with the San Francisco 49ers. The Vikings have the NFL’s best defense. The Bills have the NFL’s best offense. Something’s gotta give, as the move title suggests, and while I don’t expect to see Jack Nicholson in this one—or Diane Keaton, for that matter—I do expect to see a darn good football game. If the Bills are going to come out on top, they’ll need all of their top players to perform to their capability. Here are five Bills to watch on Monday night. _____________________________________________________________________________ QB Josh Allen In a game like this, Allen has to avoid trying to do too much. Just take the checkdown. Take the easy money. Take the thing the defense gives you so that you can sustain the drive. Don’t come out juiced up trying to be a hero from the jump. Just play within the system, hit your keys, focus on your reads, and throw it to the guys wearing white helmets. If you do that, you’re probably going to leave Minnesota with a win. If you hold the ball, force it downfield into double coverage, and try to make chicken salad out of a far less desireable byproduct of chicken feed? Well, this is a defense that will make you pay. Allen doesn’t need to be Superman for the Bills to win on Monday. He just needs to be Josh Allen. RB James Cook III IF this stellar Vikings defense has a weakness, it’s the running game. They’re currently allowing opposing teams to average 4.5 yards per carry. That doesn’t bode well for the Vikings against the NFL’s third-best rushing offense. Cook averages 5.1 yards per carry this season, and Buffalo’s second-leading rusher—Allen—averages 4.9 yards per rush. If those two can take off, look out. The Bills worked Ray Davis into the rotation a bit more last week, which was nice to see. I’d like to see them do that a little bit more on Monday, as well, as Davis offers a different build and different running style to Cook. If Buffalo’s top back can find his footing, though, it will go a long way towards keeping the Bills on schedule, which will lead to points. Injured Offensive Linemen Which Buffalo offensive linemen will play? Alec Anderson missed Thursday’s practice with an ankle injury—is Austin Corbett going to slot in and start? Dion Dawkins missed practice with a rib injury—is Tylan Grable going to play left tackle just one week after starting in place of Spencer Brown at right tackle? Speaking of Brown, he was limited in practice thanks to his back injury. What happens if both he and Dawkins can’t suit up? Rookie Jude Bowry was terrible in the preseason, so making his first career start against the NFL’s top defense isn’t exactly ideal. The Bills could move Anderson out to tackle in pinch, but again, if he’s hurt too…what do the Bills do? The offensive line, and who is able to play, is a huge area of concern this week. LB Terrel Bernard Minnesota’s second most frequently targets receiver is tight end T.J. Hockenson. Bernard has been playing much better of late, as he seems to be settling in a touch in new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard’s scheme. The Vikings have struggled this year on offense, averaging just 20 points and 279 yards per game. However, Buffalo’s defense has also struggled, allowing 26 points and 352 yards per game. If Bernard can combine with Buffalo’s other linebackers and slot players to limit Hockenson, it will go a long way towards stymying a mid-level Minnesota offense. If he can’t, well, it could lead to a scenario where the moveable force (Buffalo’s defense) is pushed around by the immoveable object (Minnesota’s offense). Hopefully, Bernard continues his upward trajectory this week. CB Christian Benford Minnesota’s top receiving target needs no introduction, as Justin Jefferson is one of the NFL’s elite receivers. After a poor start to the season, Benford has thrived the last two games as an eraser for the opposing team’s top target. He traveled with Raiders’ tight end Brock Bowers and largely eliminated him from the game in Buffalo’s 33-30 victory three weeks ago. Then, last week, he traveled with Baltimore Ravens’ wideout Zay Flowers and completely erased him from the game, as Flowers logged the first zero-catch game of his career. Benford is a legitimate stud corner, and Jefferson is a legitimate stud wideout. This is a premier matchup, and I expect it to be one of the biggest keys to the entire game for both teams. If Benford can limit Jefferson, it will give the Bills a huge boost in the game.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Report: Buffalo Bills are looking to trade for defensive back
summary: This is not exactly a shock, but now we have a report from a national insider about what the Buffalo Bills are looking for at the NFL trade deadline. That insider is Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer. I recently tweeted the lack of reports this season represents a stark contrast to recent years, when the Bills […]
full_text: This is not exactly a shock, but now we have a report from a national insider about what the Buffalo Bills are looking for at the NFL trade deadline. That insider is Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer. I recently tweeted the lack of reports this season represents a stark contrast to recent years, when the Bills were listed in essentially every trade-deadline insight article in the weeks leading up to the deadline. Now, there was one mention of the Bills’ intentions, from Breer, in late October. We wrote about here at Rumblings. It was one sentence and relatively vague compared to the rest of the mentions pertaining to other teams and trade chips. “ The Bills are looking for another piece or two on defense .” This time around, in a response to a tweet that highlighted the lack of a Bills mention in his latest trade-deadline article , Breer wrote this: I had it in my last trade column, and will add it here—The Bills are still looking in to adding a piece on the defensive side of the ball. And specifically at corner and safety. https://t.co/CkjvAiQRLa — Albert Breer (@AlbertBreer) November 7, 2026 The positions are the unexpected part. However, the Bills have recently added Tre’Davious White and Kader Kohou to the practice squad at cornerback. They just got a quality effort from Te’Cory Couch in the slot. At safety, Jordan Hancock is close to returning. Damar Hamlin is playing sound football. Geno Stone tied for the team lead in tackles with six against the Ravens on just 19 snaps, and he tipped a pass that led to Davison Igbinosun’s first career interception. According to Breer, the Bills are want to add a defensive back at the trade deadline. We’ll see if it happens.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills injury report: Dion Dawkins, Alec Anderson still out
summary: Not much changed on the Buffalo Bills’ injury report as they completed their second day of practice as they gear up to take on the NFC’s two-seeded Minnesota Vikings.   Here’s what changed:  There were a few minor changes that ensures us the Bills’ PR department didn’t just copy and paste yesterday’s report.   Here’s what […]
full_text: Not much changed on the Buffalo Bills’ injury report as they completed their second day of practice as they gear up to take on the NFC’s two-seeded Minnesota Vikings. Friday injury report pic.twitter.com/VhJtUBmzFt — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 6, 2026 Here’s what changed: There were a few minor changes that ensures us the Bills’ PR department didn’t just copy and paste yesterday’s report. Ty Johnson returned to practice, but now it’s Sam Franklin, Jr. who is out with an illness. No worries, like Johnson, it’s likely he will be back tomorrow. Dalton Kincaid was upgraded to a full participant. It’s a good sign for the fourth-year tight end who is still looking to finish a full season without missing any playing time. Khalil Shakir missed Friday’s practice for personal reasons. Nothing to worry about here. Deone Walker was listed with a thumb injury for the first time. Whatever the injury is, it didn’t keep him from participating fully on Friday. Here’s what we’re watching: Dion Dawkins missed a second straight day of practice with a rib injury. It’s an injury he says came in the first quarter of last week’s win over the Baltimore Ravens. The Bills’ left tackle said he plans to be ready to go Monday night. Alec Anderson not practicing for two days with an ankle injury is not a good sign. He was seen in a boot after Sunday’s game. I would bet he misses Monday. The question is will it be Tylan Grable or Austin Corbett in his slot. Spencer Brown has been limited both days this week. I would expect he gets a questionable designation Saturday, but suits up anyway. The question is how long can he go Monday night without his back seizing back up. The Buffalo Bills game plan likely has a lot of James Cook in it. That and some really quick slants. Will a patched up front line be able to hold? _________________ As for the Vikings, they only had a few changes of their own on Friday’s report. Running back Demond Claiborne was downgraded from limited with a knee injury to not practicing at all. Wide receiver Juan Jennings was also downgraded from limited with a calf injury to a did-not-participate. They had three players move from limited to full practice today: OT Christian Darrisaw, LB Jake Golday, and CB Isaiah Rodgers Today's #Vikings injury report pic.twitter.com/ow7cmRhFwT — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) November 6, 2026

title: NFL trade deadline: Buffalo Bills trade candidate – Nick Cross
summary: Another safety candidate for the Buffalo Bills before the NFL trade deadline… why not? Highlighted today is Commanders safety Nick Cross, a fifth-year explosive defensive back with 2,914 career snaps entering Week 9 who resides on an 2-4-1 Washington team that hosts the Los Angeles Rams in Week 9. This article is the eleventh in […]
full_text: Another safety candidate for the Buffalo Bills before the NFL trade deadline… why not? Highlighted today is Commanders safety Nick Cross, a fifth-year explosive defensive back with 2,914 career snaps entering Week 9 who resides on an 2-4-1 Washington team that hosts the Los Angeles Rams in Week 9. This article is the eleventh in the trade-candidate series I’ll continue to sprinkle onto the site until the actual trade deadline until November 10. Past installments in this series: Derwin James , Brian Thomas Jr. Jessie Bates , Tariq Woolen , Amani Hooker , Antoine Winfield Jr. , Cam Bynum , Zack Baun , Josh Downs , Budda Baker Age: 25 A third-round pick by the Colts in 2022 after a productive career at the University of Maryland and a combine performance in which he ran 4.34 with a 130-inch broad jump (92nd percentile) at over 6’0” and 212 pounds, Cross didn’t become a full-time contributor on Indianapolis’ defense until this third professional season. In that year, 2024, Cross made 146 tackles with six tackles for loss, five pass breakups, and three interceptions. A truly breakout season on an 8-9 Colts team. Last season, Cross had 120 tackles, five tackles for loss, a pick, five more pass breakups, and 2.5 sacks. He signed a tw0-year, $13 million deal with the Commanders in March, which felt low relative to his youthfulness and 2024 and 2025 productivity. 2026 snap splits Box: 31.3% Free safety: 33% Slot corner: 30% Defensive line: 4.2% Cross has been asked to assume a truly versatile role this season in Washington, which aligns with his ascendence in Indianapolis, where he played roughly the same percentage of snaps in the box as he did at free safety a season ago. After Week 2’s game against the Cowboys, Cross stayed at a local Dallas hospital for an undisclosed internal injury but returned to the field in Week 6. He’s played at least 54 snaps in all four games he’s been available for to date on the Commanders defense. In those contests, he has 22 tackles and four tackles for loss. He’s allowed 10 of 11 targets in his coverage area to be completed but only for 69 yards with one touchdown. How he’d fit with Bills I had a draft crush on Cross coming out of Maryland. He was an absolute missile to the football in coverage, both against the run and the pass. While not necessarily built to follow intricate separators underneath, he felt like a new-age safety who could lay the lumber on outside runs and screens as well as fly to the football downfield to make plays on it. Full disclosure here too — I built a predictive NFL Draft algorithm in the summer of 2022 called Reverse Engineered Scouting Index Number (RESIN). Within the RESIN system that spans from the 2018 to 2026 draft classes, Cross has the ninth-highest safety RESIN among 213 safeties. If he were to be traded to the Bills, I assume Jim Leonhard would allow him to mostly play free safety while Cole Bishop remained close to the line of scrimmage frequently… and that’d be ideal for Cross. Ideal for both of them, really. At free safety, Cross’ 4.34 speed in coverage would be accentuated. He could regularly watch the quarterback’s eyes and erupt to the football. Plus, he’s a quality tackler and has demonstrated the ability to be a high-volume tackling type in the secondary. His career missed tackle rate is a respectable 11.2% and just 8.3% entering Week 9 this season. Financial obligation for Bills to trade for him 2026 salary: $3.05M If the Bills trade for Cross after Week 9, they’d be on the hook for $1.525M in prorated 2026 base salary plus a grand total of $270,000 in possible per-game roster bonuses. Altogether $1.795M. Buffalo has roughly $4M in 2026 space currently, so they could add Cross to their books without any financial issues. In 2027, his base salary is $5.55M with an additional workout and per-game bonuses that would bring his cap hit to a very reasonable $6.25M. Projected cost to acquire Using Syndicate32.com’s trade machine , the projected cost to trade for Cross is a mid fourth-round pick in 2027 . I can’t imagine Cross, who only garnered a contract worth $6.5M in APY netting Washington a fourth-round pick after he played four games for them, yet his steady improvement in Indianapolis could keep his price in this range. Should the Bills trade for Nick Cross? The announcement of this trade would hardly move the needle from an optics perspective. But I really like the idea of it because of what Cross would bring this defense. He’s a super-fast, rangy, quality tackler who plays with an edge and is only 25 years old without a bloated cap hit next season. And on this Bills team, he likely wouldn’t be asked to split his snaps into thirds between managing the slot, playing free safety, and acting as a linebacker in the box… although he’s proven to be capable of carrying out all those duties reasonably well. Is Cross an All-Pro caliber player? Of course not. But at his age, with his athleticism, and given what he’s shown over the past two plus seasons, there’s still plenty of potential within Cross, probably about as much as a team could find at the trade deadline for a player in his fourth NFL season. If the Bills could get this done for a fourth or fifth-round pick, I’d be giddy about the move. He’d make the Bills better instantly, raising the floor of the other safety position, and he can act as a mentor for Jalon Kilgore and Jordan Hancock as they continue to develop early in their respective Bills careers.

title: Buffalo Bills vs. Minnesota Vikings: Time capsule
summary: The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings have been playing football against each other since 1971. But in more than five decades, they’ve met just 15 times.  Minnesota holds a 9-6 advantage in the all-time series, although Buffalo has won four of the past six meetings. And, while there aren’t a whole lot of games to […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings have been playing football against each other since 1971. But in more than five decades, they’ve met just 15 times. Minnesota holds a 9-6 advantage in the all-time series, although Buffalo has won four of the past six meetings. And, while there aren’t a whole lot of games to choose from, there are certainly a few worth remembering. There’s the afternoon Drew Bledsoe threw for more than 400 yards. The day a rookie Josh Allen introduced himself to the NFL by hurdling a linebacker. And, of course, there’s that game in 2022 that Bills fans would probably rather forget. So, before Allen heads back to Minnesota, we’re opening the Time Capsule to revisit five of the more memorable meetings between the Bills and Vikings, starting with a comeback in 1982. _____________________________________________________________________________ 1982 — A comeback worth remembering The Minnesota Vikings had a 19-0 lead over Buffalo on Sept. 16, 1982, and every reason to think they had the game under control. Joe Ferguson, however, had other plans. The Bills offense was a little late to the party, but it was about to make up for lost time. Ferguson threw for 330 yards and three touchdowns as Buffalo rallied for a 23-22 win. He got the Bills on the scoreboard with a 6-yard touchdown pass to Frank Lewis before halftime, then connected with Jerry Butler for a 4-yard score in the third quarter. Minnesota still held a 22-13 lead heading into the fourth, but a 21-yard field goal from Nick Mike-Mayer brought Buffalo within six. Ferguson and Butler connected again, this time from 11 yards out, and Mike-Mayer’s extra point gave the Bills the win. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2002 — An overtime shootout The Bills and Vikings combined for 78 points on Sept. 15, 2002, and somehow needed extra time and another six points to find a winner. Drew Bledsoe threw for a franchise-record 463 yards, but Buffalo needed a little last-second magic just to get the game into overtime. The Bills had taken a 36-32 lead on Bledsoe’s 3-yard touchdown pass to Peerless Price with 3:08 remaining, only for Minnesota to answer with a touchdown of its own and go ahead 39-36 with 26 seconds left. Bledsoe got Buffalo into position for a Mike Hollis 54-yard field goal as regulation expired. Then Bledsoe and Price delivered the finish. The two connected on a 48-yard touchdown pass to give Buffalo a 45-39 win. And those weren’t even the only fireworks. Charlie Rogers returned a kickoff 90 yards for a touchdown, and defensive tackle Ron Edwards recovered a fumble in the end zone for another Buffalo score. It was the kind of afternoon when just about everything seemed possible. And, not surprisingly, Bledsoe’s 463 passing yards remain the franchise’s single-game record – but maybe don’t tell Josh Allen. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2014 — A last-second escape Buffalo needed every last second of its Oct. 19, 2014, meeting with Minnesota, and Kyle Orton made sure none of them went to waste. Trailing 16-10 with less than three minutes remaining, Orton took over at his own 20-yard line and began an 80-yard drive that nearly ended before it could reach midfield. Facing fourth-and-20, Orton found tight end Scott Chandler for 24 yards to keep Buffalo’s hopes alive. An 18-yard completion to Sammy Watkins on third-and-12 kept the drive moving, and a 28-yard pass to Chris Hogan put the Bills at the Minnesota 2-yard line. With just one second remaining, Orton found Watkins in the end zone for the tying touchdown. Dan Carpenter’s extra point gave Buffalo a 17-16 win. It wasn’t the cleanest afternoon for the Bills, who committed four turnovers, but they managed to save their best drive for last. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2018 — The rookie nobody saw coming The Bills arrived in Minnesota on Sept. 23, 2018, as 16.5-point underdogs. They left with a 27-6 win, and the NFL had its first real glimpse of what Josh Allen could do. Making just his second career start, Allen scored three touchdowns in the first half, running for two and throwing a 26-yard touchdown pass to Jason Croom. Buffalo scored on its first five possessions, building a 27-0 halftime lead while holding Minnesota to just 46 yards of offense before the break. But the play everyone remembers wasn’t a touchdown. Facing third-and-9, Allen scrambled toward the sideline and, rather than going around Vikings linebacker Anthony Barr, decided to go over him. The rookie quarterback hurdled Barr, picked up the first down, and produced one of the earliest signature highlights of his career. It was Allen’s first NFL win, and that hurdle gave everyone a little preview of what was coming. Eight years later, jumping over defenders has become just another day at the office for Buffalo’s quarterback. _____________________________________________________________________________ 2022 — The one that got away The Bills and Vikings had a little extra history going into their Nov. 13, 2022, meeting. Buffalo had sent its 2020 first-round pick to Minnesota in the trade for Stefon Diggs, and the Vikings used that pick to select Justin Jefferson. Both receivers had become stars, and fans on both sides were still arguing over who won the trade. Jefferson certainly gave Buffalo fans something to talk about that afternoon. He finished with 193 receiving yards, including an unbelievable one-handed catch over Cam Lewis on fourth-and-18. Diggs wasn’t exactly quiet, either, hauling in 12 passes for 128 yards. But the receivers weren’t the only ones putting on a show. Buffalo led 27-10 late in the third quarter before Dalvin Cook brought a little sibling rivalry into the mix. With his younger brother on the opposite sideline, Cook broke loose for an 81-yard touchdown run that helped spark Minnesota’s comeback. And then things got weird. With less than a minute remaining, Buffalo stopped Minnesota on fourth-and-goal at the 1-yard line. The Bills had the lead, the ball, and what looked like a win. Instead, Allen fumbled the snap, and Eric Kendricks recovered in the end zone to put Minnesota ahead. Allen wasn’t finished, though. With just 41 seconds remaining, he moved Buffalo downfield to set up Tyler Bass for a 29-yard field goal that forced overtime. Minnesota took a 33-30 lead on a field goal in the extra frame, but the Bills still had one more chance to win it. Allen drove Buffalo into the red zone before Patrick Peterson intercepted his pass, bringing the wild afternoon to an end. The Bills had led by 17 points, survived Jefferson’s ridiculous catch, and made a goal-line stand that should have ended it. Somehow, they still lost. Four years later, this one probably hasn’t gotten any easier for Bills fans to watch. _____________________________________________________________________________ These two teams go years between meetings, so it’s no surprise they pack each one with as many memorable moments as possible. Monday night isn’t likely to be any different. There will probably be plenty to talk about afterward. Let’s just hope it’s more of the Allen-leaping-tall-buildings variety than the nightmare-before-Thanksgiving variety.
author: Rachel Auberger

title: Does Carson Wentz make the Minnesota Vikings a bigger threat to Buffalo Bills?
summary: I want to start with an apology this week as my full time and life convened to sap most of my time and energy. I wasn’t going to do nothing for this week’s opponent preview though and luckily the Minnesota Vikings handed me a softball with the decision to start Carson Wentz at quarterback over […]
full_text: I want to start with an apology this week as my full time and life convened to sap most of my time and energy. I wasn’t going to do nothing for this week’s opponent preview though and luckily the Minnesota Vikings handed me a softball with the decision to start Carson Wentz at quarterback over Kyler Murray. Even better, Wentz has played a couple game this season meaning we don’t have an empty data set on what to expect. So then… Was Wentz actually better than Kyler Murray? Splits and Charts Data Splits I can’t believe I’ve gotten this far into the season without a shoutout to pro-football-reference.com The chart below is courtesy of PFR with some columns removed that I don’t personally love for analysis purposes (and I needed to cut out some clutter as this is already a wiiiiiiiide image). Now, when it comes to the split, Murray started Week 1 against the Green Bay Packers for 11 snaps before Carson Wentz took over after a late hit led to an early exit for Murray. Wentz started the following week against the Chicago Bears. Wentz threw 19 times against Green Bay and 20 times against Chicago. Basically what I’m saying is treat this more like Murray has played five games and Wentz has played two. Yes that’s still a smaller sample size than I’d love to work from but it does give us a little window into things with both playing for the current team we’re looking to analyze. So let’s get to it; what might we expect to be different? First off, we see that Kyler Murray actually has the higher completion rate and it’s not an insignificant one. Making that even more wild is that of the two games Wentz played, the one he came in expecting to be the backup was the one where he had the higher rate. That suggests that the completion rate may not improve for Wentz despite getting starter’s reps this week. Now scan to the right and see that Wentz has the higher yards per attempt and completion. If you’re into math, you might know why I jumped to this stat next. For completion rate, a lower number means more incomplete passes. The yards per attempt on an incomplete pass are always 0. A low completion percentage then tends to drag down your yards per attempt metric. Wentz has not thrown enough passes for me to confirm this on next gen stats, but this should be a lock to mean that Wenz has a higher average intended air yards. That’s a fancy way of saying that he’s pushing the ball down the field more than Murray. There’s also a drastic difference in touchdown percentage with Wentz throwing touchdowns 7.7% of the time to Murray’s 3.2%. That’s a massive difference. It’s also a mirage. Wentz threw for three touchdowns in the season opener and zero in the next week. That Week 1 fluke was also the only time the Vikings scored more than 23 points. That Week 2 game was also their worst output of the season with Wentz under center, scoring only nine. For interceptions, Wentz has the edge there as well but with the small sample size and Murray also having a decent rate I would wager there’s not a huge gulf between the two. As a reference point, if Wentz had one interception this season he’d have a 2.6% interception rate. Last but not least is sack rate where the data (again, small sample size) suggests that Murray has the distinct advantage. For a defense looking to find its groove, that could be a very good sign indeed. If we take a look historically, there’s some validation for the above. Wentz’s 4.6% touchdown rate is a bit ahead of Murray at 4.1%. They both have an identical 2.0% interception rate for their careers. Interestingly, Murray has a slight edge on yards per attempt (opposite of above) but retains a significantly better completion rate. So it still means Wentz is more likely to throw it deep than Murray, but also more likely to let the ball hit the turf. And finally, Wentz is more likely to take a sack but it’s not a massive difference there over their careers. A couple of charts The NFL’s Next Gen Stats site has cool scatterplots of thrown passes if you’re not aware. For Kyler Murray, I think this one is pretty representative of his season in Minnesota so far. There’s a lot here near the line of scrimmage but a few shots down the field, mostly to the left side. Notice too all the white dots on the left hand side. They keep trying to hit there, but they’re struggling. Here’s the one chart so far this season for Carson Wentz. Yeah, in this game he looked a lot like that Kyler Murray chart, didn’t he? That leads me to… The Final Straw I’ll keep this short and sweet. There are some differences between the two quarterbacks for sure. It’s just that none of them are drastic differences. This comes across as a shakeup for the sake of a shakeup or to try to disrupt game planning for their opponent (which is us). I don’t see why the Bills would need to put a whole lot of extra effort in though to handle Wentz rather than Murray. If anything, the one big difference between the two means Wentz could be easier to plan for. Wentz has ran the ball eight times this year and is average 0.8 yards per carry. Murray isn’t known for running, but is averaging 5.8 yards per carry. The two quarterbacks have similar output, but Wentz is one-dimensional. On the surface, it sounds like the Vikings may have purposefully downgraded.

title: Bills Mafia takes over Minneapolis: Your guide to food, football, and fun before Monday Night Football
summary: Bills Mafia, pack your gear and get ready to take over another NFL city! The Buffalo Bills are headed to Minneapolis to face the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football, November 9, at U.S. Bank Stadium. But for those of us traveling in for the game, the fun starts long before kickoff. Whether you’re making […]
full_text: Bills Mafia, pack your gear and get ready to take over another NFL city! The Buffalo Bills are headed to Minneapolis to face the Minnesota Vikings on Monday Night Football, November 9, at U.S. Bank Stadium. But for those of us traveling in for the game, the fun starts long before kickoff. Whether you’re making your first trip to Minnesota or returning for another road-game adventure, there’s plenty to keep you entertained throughout the weekend. From gathering with fellow Bills fans and reliving one of Josh Allen’s earliest signature performances to sampling Minnesota’s famous cheese-stuffed burgers, here’s your guide to making the most of your time in the Twin Cities. Eat like a Minnesotan: Foods you absolutely have to try The Juicy Lucy: Minnesota’s famous inside-out cheeseburger If there’s one food you absolutely must try while visiting Minneapolis, it’s the Juicy Lucy, sometimes spelled Jucy Lucy. Unlike a traditional cheeseburger, the cheese is stuffed inside the beef patty, creating a pocket of melted goodness that comes pouring out when you bite into it. But consider yourself warned: That first bite can be dangerously hot! Every NFL city has its own personality, traditions, and local food favorites. Buffalo has its wings and beef on weck. Philadelphia has cheesesteaks. Kansas City has barbecue. And Minnesota? Well, they’ve figured out how to put the cheese inside the burger. Where to try one: Matt’s Bar: A Minneapolis institution dating back to 1954, famous for its original Jucy Lucy. 5-8 Club: Another legendary Minneapolis burger destination, offering several variations of the cheese-stuffed classic. Crooked Pint Ale House: A convenient option for visitors who want a stuffed burger in a sports-bar setting. Fun fact: Matt’s Bar and the 5-8 Club have been locked in a friendly rivalry for decades, with both claiming to have invented the famous burger. So here’s my challenge to Bills Mafia: Try a Juicy Lucy while you’re in Minneapolis and decide for yourself which version deserves the crown. Tater Tot Hotdish: Minnesota comfort food at its finest If you’ve never heard of hotdish, you’re not alone! But I got a little Midwestern education today so now you will too. Hotdish is Minnesota’s answer to a casserole, typically made with ground beef, vegetables, a creamy sauce, and a crispy layer of tater tots on top! Event List Saturday, November 7: Let the Bills Mafia festivities begin! Fans of Buffalo welcome gathering Time: 7 p.m. CT Location: Tom’s Watch Bar, 609 Hennepin Ave., Minneapolis, MN What better way to kick off a Bills road trip than spending Saturday night with fellow members of Bills Mafia Fans of Buffalo will be gathering at Tom’s Watch Bar in downtown Minneapolis, and all fans are welcome. With massive television screens, plenty of football atmosphere, and Bills fans arriving from across the country, it’s a great opportunity to reconnect with familiar faces, meet new friends, and start the weekend off right. Sunday, November 8: Football, hockey and a little basketball? Sunday offers plenty of options for Bills fans looking to fill the day before Monday night’s matchup. Buffalo Sabres watch party and NFL Sunday football Time: 2:30 p.m. CT Location: Buffalo Wild Wings, 2001 University Ave. SE, Minneapolis, MN Just because we’re on the road supporting the Bills doesn’t mean we have to forget about our other Buffalo teams! Join fellow fans at Buffalo Wild Wings for a Buffalo Sabres watch party, with NFL Sunday afternoon games also on the televisions.The location is a gathering spot for the Minneapolis/St. Paul Bills Backers, making it a natural destination for visiting fans looking for a little Buffalo atmosphere in Minnesota. Relive the 2018 Bills–Vikings upset at Tom’s Watch Bar Time: 6–10 p.m. CT Location: Tom’s Watch Bar, 609 Hennepin Ave., Minneapolis, MN Before Buffalo and Minnesota meet again on Monday night, why not revisit the game that introduced the Vikings to a young quarterback named Josh Allen? Tom’s Watch Bar will be replaying the Bills’ unforgettable 27–6 victory over Minnesota from 2018, along with Sunday afternoon games and Sunday Night Football. Want something different? Catch a live NBA game! Minnesota Timberwolves vs. Utah Jazz Time: 6 p.m. CT Location: Target Center, downtown Minneapolis Bills Mafia, if you’re looking to switch things up and experience another professional sporting event while you’re in town, the Minnesota Timberwolves are hosting the Utah Jazz on Sunday evening. Target Center is located in downtown Minneapolis, making it a convenient option for visitors staying in the city. It’s a chance to enjoy some live NBA basketball before turning your attention back to the football field Monday night. Monday, November 9: It’s game day! Fans of Buffalo Minnesota Tailgate The main event is finally here! Fans of Buffalo will be hosting its Minnesota tailgate ahead of Monday Night Football, bringing together Bills fans from near and far for a pregame celebration. Whether you’re traveling from Western New York, Florida, or somewhere in between, there’s nothing quite like walking into an opposing team’s city and finding yourself surrounded by red, white, and blue. Tickets and event information: Fans of Buffalo Minnesota Tailgate on TickPick Be sure to check the event listing for the latest tailgate details and ticket availability. Buffalo Bills vs. Minnesota Vikings Kickoff: 7:15 p.m. CT Location: U.S. Bank Stadium, Minneapolis, MN Monday Night Football. A primetime audience. Josh Allen. And Bills Mafia invading Minnesota. What more could we ask for? Well, besides a Bills victory, of course. More things to do while visiting Minneapolis Explore the Mall of America If you’ve never been to Minnesota, the Mall of America is one of those places worth seeing at least once. Located in Bloomington, just outside Minneapolis, it’s much more than a shopping mall. Inside, you’ll find hundreds of stores, restaurants, attractions, and even an indoor amusement park. Yes, an amusement park inside a mall. For fans arriving early or looking for something to do before game day, it’s a popular stop. Visit Minnehaha Falls Want to see a little of Minnesota beyond the stadiums and sports bars? Minnehaha Falls is one of Minneapolis’ most recognizable natural attractions, featuring a 53-foot waterfall surrounded by parkland and walking paths. It’s a beautiful place to explore if the November weather cooperates… and it looks like it will! Walk along the Mississippi River The Mississippi River runs directly through Minneapolis, and the city’s riverfront offers scenic views, walking paths, historic landmarks, and the iconic Stone Arch Bridge. It’s a great option for anyone wanting to get outside, stretch their legs, and see a different side of the city. Check out the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden Home to the famous Spoonbridge and Cherry sculpture, the Minneapolis Sculpture Garden is another recognizable local attraction. And yes, it’s exactly what it sounds like: an enormous spoon with a giant cherry balanced on top.Because apparently putting cheese inside hamburgers wasn’t enough creativity for one city. A few things to know before heading to Minnesota Dress for the weather. November in Minneapolis can be unpredictable. Check the forecast before packing, and bring layers for walking around downtown. Plan your transportation. Minneapolis has light rail service connecting Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport, downtown Minneapolis, and U.S. Bank Stadium. It’s worth considering if you don’t want to deal with game-day traffic. Remember the time difference. Minnesota operates on Central Time, one hour behind Buffalo and the rest of the Eastern Time Zone. All event times in this guide are listed in Central Time. One more road trip, one more chance to make memories For so many of us, following the Bills isn’t just about the three hours spent watching football. It’s about the people we meet, the places we visit, and the memories we collect…

title: Reacts Results: Settling expectations into the gutter
summary: Go back into the comments this week on almost any article and you’ll find a number of our readers referencing “shuffling the deck chairs on the titanic.” That’s the mood across the Carolina Panthers fandom after two consecutive, demoralizing losses that have highlighted both the weaknesses of the coaching staff and the limitations of this […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Luke Fortner #77 of the Carolina Panthers defends against the Philadelphia Eagles during an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Go back into the comments this week on almost any article and you’ll find a number of our readers referencing “shuffling the deck chairs on the titanic.” That’s the mood across the Carolina Panthers fandom after two consecutive, demoralizing losses that have highlighted both the weaknesses of the coaching staff and the limitations of this heavily injured roster. Fan confidence, which was riding in the 90s for a couple of week as the Panthers built themselves up to a 3-2 record after their early bye week, has cratered. The inability of the remains of Carolina’s offensive line to do anything with much success has hamstrung the high-flying offense that began the season with hopes of an NFL-leading passer and whispers of the MVP conversation. Now, instead of an award, the team views a first down as a lofty aspiration. Staff firings aren’t surprising with these kinds of confidence numbers. Many have been out on Evero for years as his “bend but don’t break” style of defense too often broke. What is telling, however, is that most Panthers fans don’t think his removal moves the needle much. Head coach Dave Canales has a battle ahead of him to not lose the fanbase entirely. From one perspective, it is simple: start winning again. From another, it is much harder. Just as fans are right not to expect major changes for a unit devastated by injury just because their much-maligned leader has been fired, fans also shouldn’t expect a massive change in the Panthers ability to compete. They are fielding what is, at many positions, a roster with less reliable or less heralded players than they had during the preseason. Cornerback and left guard have been particularly affected. Left tackle, center, and right guard have experienced much less turmoil and yet also been somehow more disappointing as the season has worn on. Some of that blame is rightly laid at Canales’ feet. Coaching plays a part in every players performance and the buck stops with him on that front. Some if it, however, comes down to luck and the players. Injuries, regressions, and mistakes are things that happen. It takes a team effort to overcome them and, for the moment, that effort seems lacking across the board. summary: The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Veteran offensive lineman Brady Christensen has been progressing and looks […]
full_text: The Carolina Panthers front office is busy throughout the season with transactions, roster moves, and injury updates. Here’s what’s happening at Mint Street this week. Injuries Carolina’s injury report is scarier than many of last week’s Halloween costumes. Let’s start with the good news first. Veteran offensive lineman Brady Christensen has been progressing and looks like he will be active this week. He is officially listed as questionable. Provided he’s healthy, it will be up to the coaching staff to determine if — and which position — he ends up playing this week. The Panthers offensive line is a shambles right now and Christensen has the versatility to play all five positions. Here’s to hoping he’s both healthy and productive against the Broncos. Defensive tackle Bobby Brown is also trending in the right direction after missing last week’s game with a hand injury. He was a full participant in practice this week and doesn’t have an injury designation as of Friday’s practice. Now, the bad part. Three important contributors to the Panthers defense are in bad shape including outside linebacker Jaelen Phillips, cornerback Will Lee, and linebacker Bobby Okereke. They are all listed as out this week. On the offensive side of the ball, guard Damien Lewis missed last week’s game with a knee injury and is also out against the Broncos. Transactions Signed CB Jakorian Bennett to the practice squad Jakorian Bennett could help provide reinforcements to the Panthers’ bruised and bloodied cornerbacks room. He was originally a 2023 fourth-round pick by the Las Vegas Raiders. In two seasons in Sin City he appeared in 24 games with 11 starts, registering 58 tackles and an impressive 11 passes defended. After two solid seasons Raiders traded him before the 2025 season to the Philadelphia Eagles. He appeared in 11 games for Philly last year with seven tackles before suffering an injury and getting waived just a few days ago with an injury designation. Signed OT Da’metrius Weatherspoon to the practice squad Speaking of battered and bruised units on the Panthers roster, the entire offensive line needs some reinforcement. This week the Panthers signed tackle Da’metrius Weatherspoon to the practice squad. He entered the league this year as an undrafted free agent out of Syracuse and has spent some time with the Bills and Patriots before coming to Charlotte. He has yet to appear in an NFL game. Signed LB Mohamoud Diabate to the practice squad If the name Mouhamoud Diabate sounds familiar it’s because he’s had a decent NFL career in what is now his fifth season. He spent his first three seasons with the Cleveland Browns from 2023 through 2025 appearing in 46 games with 127 tackles. He had a career-high 70 tackles back in 2024. But his previously promising young career hit a detour last year when he joined the Tennessee Titans and appeared in only one game while bouncing around the practice squad. He now joins the Panthers practice squad with a decent amount of on-field experience. Releases: This week the Panthers also released CB Zion Childress LB Maema Njongmeta from the practice squad.

title: Chicago Bears vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Week 9 Players to Watch
summary: Two straight prime-time victories against the two Super Bowl representatives from a year ago lead us to one last prime-time matchup before Chicago’s BYE in Week 10. This time around, Chicago plays a feisty Buccaneers squad who just shut out a divisional rival last week without passing for a single yard. Clearly, the run game […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - SEPTEMBER 13: Tampa Bay Buccaneers linebacker Josiah Trotter (45) intercepts the ball for a touchdown during the game between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Two straight prime-time victories against the two Super Bowl representatives from a year ago lead us to one last prime-time matchup before Chicago’s BYE in Week 10. This time around, Chicago plays a feisty Buccaneers squad who just shut out a divisional rival last week without passing for a single yard. Clearly, the run game in Tampa is rolling, but don’t overlook the defense. Let’s get to the players for the Bucs that have my attention, starting with that defense. Defense: Josiah Trotter, #45 – LB The son of former Philadelphia Eagles great Jeremiah Trotter and brother of current Eagles LB Jeremiah Trotter Jr., Jeremiah is making a name for himself down in Tampa. After being drafted in the 2nd round of the 2026 NFL draft out of Missouri, Trotter wasted zero time doing just that as a pro. Against the Bengals in Week 1, the rookie notched 11 tackles with 1 sack and 1 stuff, along with 1 INT that he returned for a TD and another pass deflection. Despite having missed a game, he is currently leading all Tampa defenders in tackles by 25! At 6’2”, 237lbs, Josiah isn’t quite as stout as his dad, but he is a beast in his own right having done 27 reps of 225lb at the NFL combine and he could be the most athletically gifted of the whole crew. Caleb and Co. will have to know where #45 is so they don’t get blasted like Michael Penix Jr. did in the picture above. If Trotter can make his presence felt in the run and passing games, watch for Tampa to keep this one close. If Chicago’s offensive line can keep Caleb and the RBs clean, Tampa will need to pray that some more turnover treasure is looted to give them a chance. Offense: Tez Johnson, #15 – WR After the Jeffery Simmons trade, it would appear that Cornerback is Chicago’s last remaining weakness. Particularly against the deep ball. A few weeks ago I highlighted Falcons receiver Jahan Dotson in this piece for similar reasons and Dotson went on to post 87 yards on three catches. Three. That is a 29 yard average per catch. Tez Johnson is the deep threat for Tampa and averages 19.8 yards per catch himself. With Emeka Egbuka hobbled and Chris Godwin aging, Tez has stepped into a larger role in the offense and has played in all 8 games so far this season – though he has only been targeted 15 times. If Tampa once again is committed to run the football behind one of the most underrated offensive lines in the entire league, watch for the play-action to #15. If Tampa can move the chains on the backs of RBs Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell, I expect for veteran signal caller Baker Mayfield to take some shots downfield this week. If he can connect, Tampa’s offense has a chance to keep this one close and even secure the upset. If not, Chi-town will enter the BYE week with an elite 7-2 record. What about you? Which players will you be focused on when Tampa visits Soldier Field?!

title: Chicago Bears Week 9 Flashbacks: A Pair of Wins Against Rivals and a Defensive Masterclass
summary: Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 9 performances from Chicago Bears history! 1.) 1990, Bears @ Buccaneers: Testaverde throws it to everybody November 4, 1990 | Bears win 26-6 The Bears entered Week 9 of the 1990 season at 7-1 and firmly in control of the NFC Central. Tampa […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WI - NOVEMBER 04: Josh McCown #12 of the Chicago Bears looks for a receiver against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on November 4, 2013 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. The Bears defeated the Packers 27-20. (Photo by Jonathan Daniel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Climb aboard the Gridiron Time Machine as we revisit three memorable Week 9 performances from Chicago Bears history! 1.) 1990, Bears @ Buccaneers: Testaverde throws it to everybody November 4, 1990 | Bears win 26-6 The Bears entered Week 9 of the 1990 season at 7-1 and firmly in control of the NFC Central. Tampa Bay quarterback Vinny Testaverde probably wishes this particular Sunday had gone a little differently. After a scoreless opening quarter, Chicago finally broke through with a 12-yard touchdown run from Brad Muster. Neal Anderson added another score later in the quarter, while Kevin Butler’s 30-yard field goal sent the Bears into halftime with a 17-0 advantage. The offense did its part, but the defense completely took over the afternoon. Testaverde completed just 10-of-24 passes for 149 yards while throwing five interceptions and losing a fumble. Rookie safety Mark Carrier grabbed two of those interceptions within a two-minute span late in the second quarter, helping set up 10 Chicago points. Richard Dent, Shaun Gayle and Ron Rivera each added interceptions of their own. Jim Harbaugh quietly put together a solid afternoon on the other side, completing 14-of-23 passes for 213 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions. His 19-yard scoring strike to Dennis Gentry helped extend the lead to 23-0 in the third quarter. Chicago piled up 378 yards of offense, including 187 on the ground, while controlling the football for more than 38 minutes. Tampa Bay did not finally reach the end zone until the fourth quarter, long after the game had been decided. The Bears walked out of Tampa with a 26-6 victory and an 8-1 record. Five interceptions, six total takeaways and another dominant performance from a defense loaded with familiar names. That sounds like a pretty good Sunday against Tampa Bay. 2.) 2013, Bears @ Packers: McCown gets it done at Lambeau November 4, 2013 | Bears win 27-20 Walking into Lambeau Field without your starting quarterback is generally not an ideal recipe for success. The Bears found a way anyway. With Jay Cutler sidelined, veteran backup Josh McCown made his first start since the end of the 2011 season against a Packers team sitting atop the NFC North. The complexion of the game changed almost immediately when Shea McClellin sacked Aaron Rodgers on Green Bay’s opening possession. Rodgers suffered a fractured left collarbone on the play and did not return, leaving Seneca Wallace to finish the game. That turned Monday Night Football into a battle of backup quarterbacks, and McCown was more than ready for it. He completed 22-of-41 passes for 272 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. Brandon Marshall caught seven passes for 107 yards and a score, while Matt Forte rushed for 125 yards and another touchdown. Green Bay managed to turn a 17-10 halftime deficit into a 20-17 lead in the third quarter without Chicago’s offense touching the football, scoring a touchdown before recovering a surprise onside kick. McCown answered. He found Alshon Jeffery for a six-yard touchdown late in the third quarter to put Chicago back in front 24-20. From there, the Bears put together a clock-killing fourth-quarter drive that eventually ended with a Robbie Gould field goal and a 27-20 victory. McClellin finished with three sacks, matching his career total entering the night, while Chicago’s defensive ends combined for five sacks overall. The win snapped Green Bay’s six-game winning streak against the Bears and created a three-way tie atop the NFC North at 5-3. A backup quarterback, Lambeau Field and Monday Night Football. Not a bad time for one of the best performances of McCown’s Bears career. 3.) 2018, Bears @ Bills: The defense does the scoring November 4, 2018 | Bears win 41-9 The 2018 Bears were beginning to figure out just how dangerous their defense could be when they traveled to Buffalo in Week 9. The Bills got the full experience. Chicago’s offense managed just 190 total yards, Mitchell Trubisky threw for only 135 yards, and the Bears possessed the football for less than 26 minutes. Naturally, they scored 41 points. After a scoreless first quarter, Jordan Howard punched in a one-yard touchdown to give Chicago the lead. Then the defense decided to handle the scoring itself. Eddie Jackson stripped tight end Jason Croom, recovered the football and raced 65 yards for a touchdown. On Buffalo’s next possession, Kyle Fuller broke up a pass that Adrian Amos intercepted. Watch the full game below: One possession later, Fuller did it again. This time the deflection landed in the hands of Leonard Floyd, who returned the interception 19 yards for another touchdown. Chicago had forced turnovers on three straight Buffalo possessions, scored twice on defense and suddenly held a 21-0 lead. Howard added another touchdown before halftime to make it 28-0. The Bears defense finished with four takeaways, three interceptions and four sacks. Jackson and Floyd accounted for 14 points by themselves, while the Bills offense scored just nine. Chicago cruised to a 41-9 victory, improving to 5-3 and maintaining its lead in the NFC North. There may not be a stat that sums up the 2018 Bears better than this one: 41 points. Just 190 yards of offense. Sometimes the easiest way to fix an offense is to let the defense score instead. Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs .

full_text: Aug 4, 2026; Nashville, TN, USA; Tennessee Titans defensive lineman Jordan Elliott (95) goes through drills during training camp at Vanderbilt Health Football Center. Mandatory Credit: Steve Roberts-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect According to NFL insider Jordan Schultz , the Chicago Bears intend to work out former Tennessee Titans defensive tackle Jordan Elliott next week. The soon-to-be 29-year-old is a 6’5″, 325-pounder with 65 starts and 102 games played in his career, who was released by the Titans on October 20. On Thursday, October 15, Elliott had an altercation at practice with his teammate, offensive lineman JC Latham, and he was told to leave the field. He left the facility, went to his car in the players’ parking lot, and grabbed a gun. Another teammate, defensive lineman John Franklin-Myers, de-escalated the moment without further incident. Aaron Wilson of Houston’s KPRC 2 and Sports Talk 790 reported on the situation a couple of weeks ago. “This was so crazy,” an NFL source said. “Jordan has been having a lot of problems away from the building and obviously he brought it to work with him. There was no reason for him to go off like that. Everyone thought that was wild. To overreact like that is absolutely crazy. We’re just glad that no one got hurt and it’s over.” Elliott has been dealing with personal family issues and sources said he brought that frustration and anger with him to the workplace, Titans coach Robert Saleh previously said that Elliott has been dealing with “personal stuff.” It’s against NFL rules to bring a gun onto team property, and the League is investigating the situation. His former head coach, Robert Saleh, discussed the incident at length after they released him. #Titans HC Robert Saleh says Jordan Elliott having a gun was, in a way, a “small sign of a cry for help,” considering he had no prior issues and is a father and a hard worker. Saleh referenced two suicides in the NFL over the past year and expressed concern about players… https://t.co/q9lj5zEzdC pic.twitter.com/DlhVRnOsI0 — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 21, 2026 “These kids go through a lot. I will stand on the table for Jordan’s character. My message to 31 other teams: If you need a hell of a run-stopping DT that can help for a playoff run, give me a call. I’ll tell you everything you need to know about him. He’s a good man. Had a terrible lapse in judgment.” The Bears will have a walk-through at Halas Hall on Saturday and host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football. Elliott would likely work out next week at Halas Hall, as the Bears will be on their bye following the Bucs game.

title: Bucs at Bears Q&A: Bears look to continue their dominance
summary: The Chicago Bears haven’t trailed in a game since October 11th. They haven’t trailed with Caleb Williams since September 20th. They look to continue their domination against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football. The Bucs have won 3 of their last 4 and look to continue their winning ways against the Bears. To […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers warms up prior to the game against the Atlanta Falcons at Raymond James Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears haven’t trailed in a game since October 11th. They haven’t trailed with Caleb Williams since September 20th. They look to continue their domination against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers on Sunday Night Football. The Bucs have won 3 of their last 4 and look to continue their winning ways against the Bears. To get you set for this game, we chatted with Ira Kaufman, a long-time Bucs reporter (and Hall of Fame voter), currently with JoeBucsFan, for insight on the Bears. Here’s that Q&A. 1. Do the Tampa fans have any confidence in Todd Bowles? I know the Bucs are just a half game out of first, but this is a team that is 5-12 over their last 17 games. Todd Bowles remains an unpopular figure for much of Buc Nation. Fans aren’t happy with his clock management or his placid demeanor on the sidelines, suggesting he is being out-coached on a regular basis. A recent poll on the joebucsfan.com website revealed that more than 70 percent of voters have little or no confidence in Bowles, who is 38-38 since replacing Bruce Arians in 2022. 2. I feel like if Tampa is going to be competitive this week, Baker Mayfield is going to have to be effective in the passing game. Is he at a point where he can do that with the injured thumb? He’s only thrown 14 passes the last two weeks. Mayfield said this week that his injured right thumb has progressed to the point he no longer needs to wear a glove for support. Since he returned, Mayfield has thrown sparingly as Tampa Bay relied on a powerful ground game to defeat Carolina and Atlanta, climbing back into the race for the NFC South title. 3. The Bucs have certainly been powered by their running game, and the Bears have been susceptible to giving up some yards on the ground this season. Enter Jeffery Simmons. How do you think the Bucs can run the football against the Bears’ new front with Big Jeff? We just saw Simmons make an immediate impact as the Bears shut down Seattle on the road Monday night. However, the Seahawks don’t have an elite running back like Bucky Irving, who is averaging 5.0 yards per carry. Add in Kenneth Gainwell and a physical offensive line, and it’s fair to say Chicago’s rush defense faces a major challenge. It’s the best way for the Bucs to keep Caleb Williams and company watching from the sidelines. 4. Who is a lesser-known player on the Bucs offense and one on the Bucs defense that you think could have an impact in this game that fans may not know a lot about? The Bucs are looking for a No. 1 target to emerge in the wake of Mike Evans’ departure to the 49ers. Rookie Ted Hurst has shown flashes as a big-bodied WR who can get downfield. He earned Mayfield’s trust during an impressive training camp, and he could be a factor Sunday night. On defense, second-year pro David Walker is developing into a dynamic pass rusher who could pressure Williams into mistakes. 5. The Bucs defense has been playing excellent football. What is the key to this unit that sets them apart? Bowles overhauled his defense in the offseason, adding veterans like Al-Quadin Muhammad, A’Shawn Robinson, Alex Anzalone, and rookie Josiah Trotter. It took a few weeks, but this revamped unit has grown comfortable with the aggressive, blitzing schemes Bowles is known for. Cornerbacks Jacob Parrish (league-leading 13 pass breakups) and Zyon McCollum have been exceptional.

title: Chicago Bears vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers: Keys for a Chicago victory
summary: Get ready for an old-school NFC Central showdown. Not many of us are old enough to remember when the Chicago Bears and Tampa Bay Buccaneers were division rivals. And I don’t really think this game is going to be like those old battles. In those days, the Bucs were usually not very good. And in […]
full_text: TAMPA, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Calijah Kancey #94 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers makes a tackle against Kyle Pitts Sr. #8 of the Atlanta Falcons during the first half of the game at Raymond James Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Tampa, Florida. (Photo by Mike Carlson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Get ready for an old-school NFC Central showdown. Not many of us are old enough to remember when the Chicago Bears and Tampa Bay Buccaneers were division rivals. And I don’t really think this game is going to be like those old battles. In those days, the Bucs were usually not very good. And in the years where they were good, by the late ‘90s, the Bears were lousy. The matchup this Sunday should be a good game. The Bucs’ defense is very good by DVOA and several other metrics. The Bears’ offense has been playing great, putting up points on everyone. So what’s it going to take for Chicago to go into their bye week on a four-game winning streak? We asked our team. Sam: The Bucs have a top-5 defense. They’ve also played some weird games that can be criticized, not unlike some of Chicago’s early-season results. They played in an absolute monsoon and didn’t need to complete a pass. The week prior, they took advantage of the Panthers’ run defense and could again give Baker a week off. If the Bears play their game — sustain drives, score early and often — the Bucs will have a hard time playing from behind. If the Bucs can shut down the Bears’ average-looking run game and Mayfield can actually complete passes, then it will be a close one. Jeff Berckes: Ben Johnson and Dennis Allen have done a great job overall this season creating game plans that put the Bears in a great position to succeed. The Bucs are a team the Bears should beat as long as they don’t experience a letdown after the big road win in Seattle and peeking ahead to the bye. This is a straightforward “keep building” game for Caleb and the offense by grinding the Bucs defense to a fine dust with long drives until the explosives break the game open. On defense, I expect Dennis Allen to continue his weaponization of his early Christmas present, Jeffery Simmons, and playing off the havoc he creates. This is a “don’t get cute, keep the foot on the gas” game for me. Josh: The Bucs crushed the Falcons on the ground, which should serve as a warning sign for the Bears, who lack PFF all-pro Gervon Dexter. More seriously, the Bears are still struggling against the run, and their corners are suspect, so they need to focus on play disruption on defense. Dennis Allen needs to keep mixing it up to unsettle Baker Mayfield. On offense, Caleb just needs to Caleb it and Ben just needs to stay aggressive. ECD: Offense: Repeat the same game plan as the one executed against the Seahawks and let Caleb Williams cook. The Bucs’ EPA numbers are very impressive, but I’m not terrified of this defense. Especially since their best player in YaYa Diaby will be out due to his MCL sprain. Defense: A much easier assignment as the Bucs rank in the bottom third of the league in most statistical categories. Let the front four led by Jeffery Simmons and a recharged Montez Sweat destroy their game plan before it even has a chance to get going. Special Teams: Don’t take any unnecessary risks. The Bucs’ special teams unit might be the best in the league, particularly in kick coverage. What do you think are the keys to the game? Are you worried about the Bucs’ defense?

title: 2027 Bears mock draft: Post-Jeffery Simmons trade picks
summary: If you’ve been a Bears fan for long enough, you know the drill by now. The 2027 NFL Draft figures to be another year where they don’t have a first-round pick, having traded their first-rounder this year and in 2028 to the Titans for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. I say this not to disagree […]
full_text: KNOXVILLE, TN - OCTOBER 17: Alabama Crimson Tide defensive back Zabien Brown (2) tracks the play during the college football game between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Alabama Crimson Tide on October 17, 2026, at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, TN. (Photo by Bryan Lynn/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you’ve been a Bears fan for long enough, you know the drill by now. The 2027 NFL Draft figures to be another year where they don’t have a first-round pick, having traded their first-rounder this year and in 2028 to the Titans for All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons. I say this not to disagree with the trade; I’m highly in favor of it, and Simmons was absolutely dominant in his debut when the Bears beat the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks on Monday. But in years past, Chicago has entered drafts without first-round picks multiple times, thanks in part to trades the team has made for players like Jay Cutler, Khalil Mack, and Justin Fields. Barring an unforeseen trade for a first-round pick, the Bears won’t make their first pick in 2027 until Day 2, where they currently sit near the bottom of the second round for their first selection of that weekend. That makes projecting prospects to Chicago in mock drafts a little more difficult, as it requires a deeper level of research than the surface level of having to know which top-ten prospect might end up on the team. Luckily for you guys, I have you covered. Here is my first Bears mock draft after the Jeffery Simmons trade, for which I used the PFN mock draft simulator to generate the picks for the other 31 NFL teams. Round 2: Zabien Brown, CB, Alabama Now that the Bears have a superstar at defensive tackle, their biggest need on the roster is arguably at cornerback. It’s likely they see a different group at the position in 2027, too; Jaylon Johnson could be released to free up significant cap space, and Tyrique Stevenson arguably hasn’t shown enough consistency to earn a long-term extension as he approaches impending free agency next offseason. To pair up with Kyler Gordon and Malik Muhammad, Chicago will need to bring in a new cornerback. An intelligent and scrappy cornerback, Zabien Brown is a quick processor who acts upon his diagnoses in coverage with impressive urgency and ideal physicality at the catch point. He’s a willing and capable tackler who’s sticky in man coverage and understands his assignments well in zone coverage. He doesn’t stand out as elite in an aspect of his game, which drops him to Day 2 for me, but he’s a well-rounded cornerback with a strong game who could be a good starting cornerback for years to come. Round 3: Mateen Ibirogba, DT, Texas Tech After trading for Simmons, the Bears definitely have a stronger defensive tackle room than they did going into the regular season. However, Grady Jarrett stands out as a potential cap casualty this coming offseason, and they don’t have a true standout alongside Simmons on the roster currently. It wouldn’t be surprising at all if they use another early-round draft pick on an interior defender. Mateen Ibirogba was originally an edge rusher at Georgetown who eventually bulked up to play defensive tackle, excelled and transferred to Wake Forest, where he would continue to excel before earning a presumably hefty NIL sum to go to Texas Tech. His previous EDGE experience shows in his pass-rushing chops, as he’s an explosive interior defender with impressive get-off speed and a deep arsenal of push-pulls, cross-chops, and club-swims needed to shed blocks. Though his anchor against the run is average, he has legitimate upside as an interior rusher on passing downs. Round 5 (via Falcons): Antwan Raymond, RB, Rutgers As good as the Bears’ offense currently is, I don’t think I could imagine Ben Johnson going one whole draft without securing another skill position player. Roschon Johnson is currently in the last year of his rookie contract, and in the carries we’ve seen him have over the last few weeks with Kyle Monangai injured, he doesn’t seem to have the decisiveness in between the tackles or the explosiveness to warrant another contract. This could make Chicago look for a new third-string running back in 2027. I see Antwan Raymond developing into a high-end backup or a decent spot starter at running back, which is good value in Round 5. He has a low center of gravity and makes precise movements in the open field, taking sharp angles to open running lanes and making smart cuts to evade defenders. He plays with ideal patience and tempo variance out of the backfield, and he’s also a willing and physical pass protector. Though his breakaway speed isn’t elite and could limit his big-play potential, he has enough short-area quickness and agility to make up for it. Round 6: Tobi Osunsanmi, EDGE, Indiana How the Bears approach the defensive end position and what archetype of player they look for could depend on how they address this offseason. Dayo Odeyingbo and Montez Sweat are two potential cap casualties who would free up a ton of cap space, but Odeyingbo looked good before getting hurt, and Sweat is coming off of his best performance of the year in Week 8. If they keep both, they could look to throw a speed rusher into the mix as depth. As of this writing, Tobi Osunsanmi leads the Big Ten with 10.0 sacks and 15.0 tackles for loss through his first nine games with Indiana. He’s a little smaller than the typical Dennis Allen edge rusher at 6’2” and 250 pounds, and he had a season-ending injury to close out 2025 at Kansas State. But he’s a twitchy edge rusher with good bend at the top of his arc, a high motor in pursuit, and proper hand activity needed to stack and shed blocks at the point of attack. Round 7: Aidan Banfield, OG, North Carolina With a seventh-round pick, you’re really only looking for depth options. If you can get a good long-term backup out of this pick, it would be tremendous value. The Bears have drafted at least one offensive lineman every single year that Ryan Poles has been their general manager, and I don’t see that trend stopping in 2027. Aidan Banfield is only a junior, so there’s no guarantee he declares for this year’s draft. However, the three-sport high school athlete is explosive coming off the line of scrimmage and demonstrates good mobility changing direction against stunts and inside speed rushes along the interior. He demonstrates ideal spatial awareness in pass protection and can execute double-team and chip block assignments well, too. Once he gets to the NFL, he’ll need to get stronger and work on his pad level, but there’s potential for him to be a very good backup in the pros.
