title: Broncos vs. Panthers: 3 Players to Watch
summary: The Denver Broncos take on the Carolina Panthers on Sunday for their Week 9 matchup. If they can achieve a victory, they will be 7-2 before their bye week. In order to win and keep their spot atop the AFC West, the Broncos need these three players to play at a high level. Nik Bonitto […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - OCTOBER 15: Linebacker Nik Bonitto (15) and defensive end Zach Allen (99) of the Denver Broncos celebrate a shared sack of quarterback Sam Darnold (14) of the Seattle Seahawks during second half of a 17-14 overtime Broncos win on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026, at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo. (Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Denver Broncos take on the Carolina Panthers on Sunday for their Week 9 matchup. If they can achieve a victory, they will be 7-2 before their bye week. In order to win and keep their spot atop the AFC West, the Broncos need these three players to play at a high level. Nik Bonitto — Edge Rusher Finding a way to rattle Bryce Young is one of my big keys to the game. So far this season, the Panthers’ offensive line has struggled to protect him. He has already been sacked 23 times—almost as many as last season—and he is getting pressured on over 40-percent of his drop backs. Edge rusher Nik Bonitto is one of the players who needs to show up big on Sunday. After posting back-to-back seasons with double-digit sacks, the fifth-year pro is having a slower start to the 2026 season. Compared to 2025, Bonitto is experiencing a dropoff across the board relative to sacks, hurries, quarterback hits, and pressures. Left tackle Rasheed Walker has been a liability for Carolina thus far. More often than not, Bonitto will be tasked with going up against him on Sunday. If he can have a big day and win his one-on-one opportunities versus Walker, that should definitely help slow down the Panthers’ offense which ranks Top 10 in many respects. Malcolm Roach — Defensive Lineman The Broncos boast a deep rotation along their defensive line. That has kept their line fresh and taken a big burden off of All-Pro Zach Allen’s shoulders. However, their depth will be tested on Sunday with Eyioma Uwazurike being ruled out. That means someone else is going to have to step up and be a dominant force in the trenches. I’ve got a feeling Malcolm Roach will be that player. In eight games , the seventh-year pro has 24 tackles, 3.5 sacks, 5 tackles for loss, and 12 quarterback hits. Roach has always been a quality run defender, but his ascent as a pass rusher has been a great development for the team. Being able to put pressure on Young (as mentioned above) will be critical. Though limiting running back Chuba Hubbard’s impact will be important too. Hubbard is on pace for a career season. He sports a great 4.6 yard per carry average and has 540 rushing yards with 5 rushing touchdowns on the season. Denver will need Roach to be quick off the snap and make some plays in Carolina’s backfield to slow him down. J.K. Dobbins — Running Back In a few articles this week, I’ve advocated for rookie running back Jonah Coleman to be the focal point of the Broncos’ rushing attack against the Panthers. Carolina’s defense has been awful stopping opposing rushing attacks in the first half of the season. That’s why it makes sense to pound the rock on the road. Even if I’m bullish on Coleman deserving a majority of the reps, that doesn’t negate this being a big game for Dobbins. It absolutely is. He has struggled this season and is sporting a career low 3.3 yard per carry average. If he can’t find a way to improve going up against one of the NFL’s worst run defenses, when can we reasonably assume he will get on track? Denver needs a strong running game to be legitimate Super Bowl contenders. Earlier in the week, Head Coach Sean Payton mentioned he was pleased with what he had seen from Dobbins thus far. However, rumors have swirled for weeks that the Broncos may be in the market to add to their stable of backs prior to the November 10th. How Denver’s run game looks, in particular Dobbins, against the Panthers might have an impact on whether or not they are buyers at the position before the deadline.

title: Future Broncos: 3 Prospects to Watch in Week 10 of NCAA Football Season
summary: Week 10 of the NCAA Football season is upon us. After a multi-week hiatus from talking prospects to give my thoughts on the NFL trade deadline and last week’s mock draft—it’s back to the grind to highlight some options for the Denver Broncos in the 2027 NFL Draft. For this installment, I decided to make […]
full_text: MADISON, WI - NOVEMBER 08: Wisconsin Badgers linebacker Sebastian Cheeks (15) celebrates a turnover during a college football game between the Washington Huskies and the Wisconsin Badgers on November 8, 2025 at Camp Randall Stadium in Madison, WI. (Photo by Dan Sanger/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Week 10 of the NCAA Football season is upon us. After a multi-week hiatus from talking prospects to give my thoughts on the NFL trade deadline and last week’s mock draft—it’s back to the grind to highlight some options for the Denver Broncos in the 2027 NFL Draft. For this installment, I decided to make it focused on defense. Jaylen McClain — Safety — Ohio State The Broncos have gone through a lot of injuries in their secondary this season. Multiple starters at cornerback and safety have missed a few games. They’ve had to really embrace the next man up mentality in their defensive backfield. Even so, they have performed well as a unit. However, the future of the group is uncertain with a handful of players scheduled to be free agents at the end of the season. We all know General Manager George Paton loves drafting defensive backs. With nine picks in this year’s draft, I have no doubt at least one of them will go to the backend of the Broncos’ defense. Just to be clear, I’m not advocating for drafting a safety with a premium selection. However, Future Broncos serves as an exercise to highlight good prospects that fit the team at any position of need. One player that is flying up draft boards is Ohio State safety Jaylen McClain. As a freshman, McClain (6’0”, 203 pounds) appeared in fifteen games for the National Champion Buckeyes and posted 15 tackles. Last season as a sophomore, he earned a starting role in their secondary. He didn’t disappoint and notched 53 tackles and allowed just a 67-percent passer rating when targeted. This season, he has improved even more. Through eight games, the junior safety has posted 37 tackles, 1 sack, two interceptions, and a forced fumble. The big play aspect of the game [forcing turnovers] that was missing earlier in his career finally has started to show out. Ohio State Defensive Coordinator Matt Patricia deploys McClain in a variety of fashions. He has the athleticism and talent to be a true centerfield type safety in the NFL. He doesn’t just excel in coverage; McClain is aggressive against the run and has been disruptive when used on blitzes. Does that sound like a player that would fit Denver’s’ defense? Absolutely. Though I question whether or not Denver would make the premium investment it would take to select him if he declares. He seems like a sure-fire Top 50 pick. You can catch McClain in action when the #11 ranked Buckeyes host Oregon this afternoon. Sebastian Cheeks — Edge Rusher — Wisconsin Prospect development certainly isn’t linear. Sometimes it takes a few seasons for players to hit their stride to showcase their potential to play at the next level. Wisconsin fifth-year senior edge rusher Sebastian Cheeks is one of those players. Cheeks (6’3”, 243 pounds) spent his first two years at North Carolina where his impact was limited to just 11 games due to a shoulder injury. In 2024, he transferred to the Badgers in order to get more playing time and try to revitalize his collegiate career. He played in 23 games in his first two seasons with Wisconsin but was still mostly a backup. This season, Cheeks has been dominant after earning a starting role. In fact, he is looking like one of the best pass rushers in the entire nation. In eight games , Cheeks has notched 31 tackles, 8 tackles for loss, 6 sacks, and two forced fumbles. He is currently posting an impressive 23.9% pressure rate—the best of any draft eligible defender in this class. My biggest question mark with him is how well he set the edge as a run defender in the pros at his size. It’s not necessarily a liability now, but it may be going up against NFL talent every Sunday. While I do think the Broncos have much larger and immediate needs than edge rusher, but you can never have enough pass rushers. If Cheeks keeps dominating, he will easily be a Day 2 pick half a year down the road. You can catch Cheeks in action this afternoon when the Badgers host Rutgers. A.J. Holmes Jr. — Defensive Lineman — Texas Tech The Broncos certainly have one of the deepest defensive lines in the National Football League. Whether or not Denver opts to invest significant draft capital next Spring remains to be seen. They have utilized third-round picks the past two drafts to bolster the unit’s long-term potential. However, Eyioma Uwazurike is a free agent and D.J. Jones carries a hefty cap hit for a player that sees only 40-percent of the defensive snaps. Winning in the trenches is a formula for success. I’m a strong advocate of always adding firepower to the offensive and defensive lines. A prospect that has made a monumental impact this collegie season is Texas Tech defensive lineman A.J. Holmes Jr. Holmes Jr. (6’3”, 300 pounds) spent his first three seasons at Houston. A reserve and depth player for his first two years, he was 12-game starter for them in 2024 and posted 40 tackles, 8.5 tackles for loss, and 2 sacks. In 2025, he transferred to Texas Tech for more exposure and to get on the radar of NFL scouts and general managers. He started the season as a backup for Joey McGuire’s squad but finished out the last eight games of the year as a starter in the Red Raiders’ defense. He had a quality season and posted 38 tackles, 9 tackles for loss, 4.5 sacks, with 2 fumble recoveries, and 1 forced fumble. This season, Holmes is playing the best ball of his life with the Red Raiders. At the midway point of the season, he already has 25 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, and 7.5 sacks and 1 forced fumble. He leads all interior defensive lineman in the nation with a whopping 33 quarterback pressures. His physical traits may not be elite. Though he makes up for them with an incredible motor, feisty demeanor on the field, and having a wide variety of pass rushing moves. He lines up all over their defensive front and is just as disruptive going up against tackles as he is interior offensive linemen. If Holmes Jr. continues to play this great, he will certainly be an All-American and a good bet to be selected in the Top 50 picks in the 2027 NFL Draft. You can catch Holmes in action tonight when the 13th ranked Red Raiders host West Virginia.

title: Detroit Lions vs. Miami Dolphins preview: 3 key stats
summary: As the Detroit Lions approach the midway point of their season, it’s been a weird and challenging week to care as deeply about football or celebrate the Vikings win. Most Lions fans, media members, and those within the franchise have been clinging to the progress reports and updates on team captain Jack Campbell, who remains […]
full_text: Oct 30, 2022; Detroit, Michigan, USA; Detroit Lions linebacker Malcolm Rodriguez (44) sacks Miami Dolphins quarterback Tua Tagovailoa (1) during the first quarter at Ford Field. Mandatory Credit: David Reginek-USA TODAY Sports As the Detroit Lions approach the midway point of their season, it’s been a weird and challenging week to care as deeply about football or celebrate the Vikings win. Most Lions fans, media members, and those within the franchise have been clinging to the progress reports and updates on team captain Jack Campbell, who remains hospitalized with a neck injury suffered in Week 8. The player who was awarded last season’s media Good Guy of the Year award had just welcomed his first child with his wife, Megan, a son named Cooper, in July. And here was the new dad laid up in a hospital bed, still without full movement of his upper body. It was tough to harness that same giddy, football-frenzied feeling for the upcoming game until fans were reminded why this is such a likable team, as Campbell, the player who perfectly embodies this city and this franchise, remained at the forefront of players’ and coaches’ minds throughout the week. They spoke about how they’re playing for 46. Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard said, “Let’s play and prepare like 46. The way you honor him is to wipe those tears from your eyes and make sure you prepare and play like him.” That’ll get you on board to root for the boys quickly. And suddenly, just like the countless games down the stretch in 2024 that were continually billed as “trap games,” you feel reassured that the Lions won’t let the 1-6 Miami Dolphins sneak up on them. They’ll be looking to fight and take care of business against the team that once called Dan Campbell its head coach and had Sheppard as one of its defensive anchors. The Dolphins are going through a rebuilding period, but head coach Jeff Hafley and general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan both come from Green Bay and are all too familiar with the Lions. They have their talent-deficient unit losing but competing, with a number of young players who could become foundational pieces, much like the early Dan Campbell Lions. This week’s preview will examine three key stats and matchups Detroit needs to control to keep its three-game winning streak alive, avoid giving the Dolphins life, and make 46 proud. Note: Unless otherwise indicated, all statistics are sourced from NFL Pro, FTN Fantasy, Pro Football Reference, SumerSports, or Pro Football Focus. Good Golly, Miss Ollie This week’s preview will focus entirely on how the Lions’ defense will coalesce to cover for the absence of Jack Campbell, and how the Dolphins’ offense will understandably try to attack a defense without its green dot. Linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske are expected to handle the primary linebacker snaps, all with expanded roles and added responsibilities. That becomes particularly important given Miami’s recent success pounding the rock with Ollie Gordon since the De’Von Achane injury. The Dolphins comparisons to the early Dan Campbell-era Lions have been prevalent this week, and one reason for that is Miami’s reliable and developing offensive line. From left to right, Patrick Paul, Kadyn Proctor, Aaron Brewer, Jonah Savaiinaea, and Austin Jackson form an above-average unit with a good mix of proven, reliable veterans and young, ascending players. They’ve started to give the Dolphins a fighting chance by being imposing and winning at the line of scrimmage. Since Week 4, the Dolphins have shifted their rushing approach, leaning into their offensive line and Gordon’s preferred running schemes by utilizing power concepts on 13.8% of runs (5th) and man/duo concepts on 20.7% of rushing attempts (15th), with considerable success. With power, which features a backside pulling guard attacking the frontside like a runaway freight train, Miami has averaged 5.7 yards per carry (7th), +0.219 EPA/rush (6th), a 56.3% rushing success rate (5th), and a 25.0% explosive run rate (4th) since Week 4. Power runs will require Detroit’s linebackers to not only process and flow quickly, but also meet the pulling guard in the hole without giving up ground and scrape from the backside. The linebackers need to be firing on all cylinders to match Miami’s physical, downhill approach. The same goes for defending man/duo concepts, where the Dolphins’ offense has churned out 5.1 yards per carry (5th), +0.122 EPA/rush (5th), a 50.0% rushing success rate (5th), and an 8.3% explosive run rate (15th) since Week 4. Interestingly, teams haven’t really tested the Lions’ defense with power runs this season, with only 3.1% of rushing attempts (31st) coming on power concepts. Detroit has faced just one such rush since Week 4, which went for minus-4 yards. The Lions have fared well in the small sample size, allowing only 3.4 yards per carry (t-11th) and no explosive plays on their limited snaps defending power. Teams have, however, tested the Lions’ defense up the gut with man/duo concepts, running them on 31.3% of rushing attempts (5th). Detroit has countered that volume by cleaning up those physical runs, allowing just a 33.3% rushing success rate (4th) and 0.6 yards after contact per rush (2nd). An underrated key to preventing the Dolphins from outmuscling Detroit up the middle with power and man/duo concepts will be whether Tyleik Williams can play with his hair on fire against All-Pro center Aaron Brewer. Brewer understands leverage and angles better than most centers in the league, but he’s also a pivot player who stands just 6-foot-1 and 290 pounds. If the 6-foot-3 Williams, who notably lost a ton of weight this spring to get down to just 325 pounds, can win at the point of attack, overpower Brewer into the backfield, disrupt rushing lanes and timing, and congest the flow of the run play, it’ll go a long way toward making the linebackers’ jobs much easier. God Forbid a Willis Gets a Little Motion While the Dolphins’ offense under second-year holdover offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik, formerly of the Houston Texans, doesn’t do much well outside of some aspects of its run designs, it does one thing often enough that it might challenge the Detroit Lions’ defense. The Dolphins’ offense uses pre-snap motion on 74.1% of its snaps, the second-highest rate of any team in the NFL. The league average is only 59.2%, while the Lions’ offense, for comparison’s sake, sits at just 54.5% (24th). What’s interesting is that the Dolphins aren’t particularly better at rushing or passing the football with or without pre-snap motion, remaining bottom 10 in most metrics. The prevalence of the pre-snap motion itself is what’s important here. The Lions’ defense hasn’t been tested as frequently against pre-snap motion this season, and when it has, there have been some struggles. Detroit has faced pre-snap motion on only 52.1% of its defensive snaps, the second-lowest rate in the NFL. The Lions have actually excelled at defending the run against pre-snap motion, restricting opponents to -0.16 EPA/rush (4th) and just a 36.7% rushing success rate (4th). Detroit has managed to shut down offenses trying to gain an advantage in the numbers game, manipulate gap assignments, or use motion to stretch the defense geometrically, get defenders out of position, and create rushing lanes. However, issues arise in pass defense against pre-snap motion. Even if the Dolphins haven’t been particularly successful using it, there are still some concerns for Detroit. Opponents have passed on 63.6% of plays featuring pre-snap motion against the Lions’ defense, the highest pass-to-run ratio in the NFL on such plays. Against pre-snap motion, Detroit’s pass defense has allowed +0.22 EPA/dropback (29th), a 54.1% passing success rate (26th), and an 11.6% explosive pass rate (27th). The Lions’ coverage unit will need to communicate effectively and trust one another, particularly with a new green dot in either Derrick Barnes or…

title: Lions, Dolphins Week 9 injury designations: Lions rule out 5 starters
summary: The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) have declared their Week 9 injury designations, and the Lions will be missing multiple starters, including one on offense, three on defense, and one not yet cleared from his injury list—all of which we knew ahead of time, based on coach Dan Campbell’s comments throughout the week. […]
full_text: Detroit Lions center Cade Mays (64) warms up ahead of the game between Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions (5-2) and Miami Dolphins (1-6) have declared their Week 9 injury designations, and the Lions will be missing multiple starters, including one on offense, three on defense, and one not yet cleared from his injury list—all of which we knew ahead of time, based on coach Dan Campbell’s comments throughout the week. Let’s look at Friday’s practice report and get you up to date on what we know. Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded . Ruled OUT C Cade Mays (ankle) — Preparing for Juice Scruggs to start EDGE DJ Wonnum (concussion) LB Jack Campbell (neck) CB D.J. Reed (hip) S Kerby Joseph (knee, PUP) — Days remaining in injury evaluation clock: 11 Mays is dealing with a low ankle sprain, which typically keeps players out at least a week, and potentially as long as a month, so him being ruled out of this game was expected. How quickly he recovers is still to be determined, but the Lions have been highly fortunate to have Juice Scruggs stepping into the starting center role, and they’ve been planning on him starting since the beginning of this week. Wonnum is still working through the NFL’s concussion protocols and won’t be able to return in time for this game. With head injury recovery times varying by individual, it’s unclear how long he will need before he is cleared. Second-round rookie Derrick Moore is expected to increase his role in Wonnum’s absence, and Campbell is seeing improvement: “It was unfortunate we lost Wonnum, but yet, now (Moore) gets more reps. And the reps that he got are valuable, man. There’s no way to duplicate real in time game reps against good opponents and you see growth, you see growth. I saw growth in practice yesterday. So, the more he plays, the better he’s going to get. And we love where he’s going right now.” Jack Campbell continues to improve, per Dan Campbell, but he should be considered out indefinitely until otherwise clarified. “Jack continues to improve, which is all great news,” Dan Campbell said on Friday. Reed said he felt good in the locker room following the game, but he was not cleared to practice this week and will miss this game. Campbell noted that he’s very confident with the team’s depth: “(Ennis) Rakestraw is getting better. Rock (Ya-Sin) looks healthy and is playing good football. (Roger) McCreary, too. So, I just feel like these guys are starting to play pretty good football for us. And (Khalil) Dorsey, man, Dorsey’s contributing in a big way. So, I like where we’re at and it’s really a pretty depthwise, it’s a pretty strong room. So yeah, I don’t like the though of not having Reed, but at the same time, I’m encouraged. I’m encouraged. I think we’ll be OK here.” Joseph is looking “better than anticipated,” according to safeties coach Jim O’Neil, but Campbell made it clear earlier in the week that the plan was to keep him out for another game, then continue to ramp up his participation levels next week, as he nears a return. “It’s been great. Two weeks ago, it was classroom work, where we were really locked in. Then it was walkthrough and individual. Yesterday was his first team practice and he looked a lot better than what I anticipated him looking (like). So it was very encouraging. So now he’s gotta stack multiple days. He’s got to stack them, so today will be a big day for him, but he looked awesome yesterday at practice,” O’Neill said on Friday. Questionable RB Sione Vaki (ankle) — added to the injury report on Friday RB Jacob Saylors (neck) WR Amon-Ra St. Brown (rib) Vaki was unexpectedly absent from Friday’s practice and has been given a questionable designation heading into this weekend’s game. Beyond that, the extent of his injury is unknown, and we may have to wait until Saturday—to see if he travels with the team—or even game time on Sunday, to find out his availability. Saylors has dealt with a neck injury for two weeks and couldn’t finish Week 7’s game against the Vikings because of it. Look for the Lions to be cautious in his return, but with Vaki also questionable, the Lions could end up with a depth issue at running back. St. Brown was injured in Week 7 but told the media on Thursday that, “I’m a little banged up, but I’ll be alright,” and is anticipating playing against the Dolphins. Not listed with an injury designation LB Amen Ogbongbemiga (toe) CB Rock Ya-Sin (cramps) S Brian Branch (concussion) Ogbongbemiga was estimated to have been a limited participant on Wednesday and a full participant after that, and with him not carrying an injury designation, he should be good to go, giving the Lions special teams work and linebacker depth. Ya-Sin dealt with cramps earlier in the week but still practiced in full each day. He’s potentially in line to challenge for a starting role this week with Reed sidelined. Branch is nearing the end of the NFL’s concussion protocol, and Campbell said he expects him to be cleared and ready to play on Sunday. “I think (Brian Branch) BB’s going to be good here. We’ll get through today, and I think we’ll be OK.” Dolphin s’ injury designations Coming soon.

title: Lions safety Kerby Joseph looking ‘better than anticipated’
summary: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won’t play this week, as he continues to ramp up from a knee injury that cost him over a year of football activities. But as he continues to get more work in and get close to his return to the field, Joseph is starting to turn heads. Last week, the […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MI - AUGUST 08: Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph (31) participates in pass coverage drills during the Detroit Lions Training Camp afternoon practice session on August 8, 2022 at the the Detroit Lions Training Facility in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Detroit Lions safety Kerby Joseph won’t play this week, as he continues to ramp up from a knee injury that cost him over a year of football activities. But as he continues to get more work in and get close to his return to the field, Joseph is starting to turn heads. Last week, the Lions started his 21-day evaluation clock, getting him worked into walkthrough practices while getting additional reps with teammates after practice. This week, he got his first taste of team action, and he was already doing things Lions safeties coach Jim O’Neill wasn’t expecting. “It’s been great. Two weeks ago, it was classroom work, where we were really locked in. Then it was walkthrough and individual. Yesterday was his first team practice, and he looked a lot better than what I anticipated him looking (like),” O’Neil said. “So it was very encouraging. So now he’s gotta stack multiple days. He’s got to stack them, so today will be a big day for him, but he looked awesome yesterday at practice.” O’Neil credited a lot of people in Joseph’s recovery. There’s the medical staff that has outlined and executed a recovery plan for the safety. There are players like Dominic Lovett and Jackson Meeks, who have stayed after practice to help get Joseph caught up on the reps he’s missed in practice during his ramp-up. But more than anyone, O’Neil credits Joseph’s perseverance through the difficult last couple of years. “He’s worked his ass off. He has. He’s gone through a mental battle, he’s gone through a physical battle, and he’s in a great place right now,” O’Neil said. “And I’m excited for him, and I know how hard he’s working. I know how hard it must be to be at the top of your game and then have it taken away from you. He’s grinded to get back to the level that he’s used to playing at and at his standard.” The next step for Joseph is simple: stack days. It’s not just about how his knee responds to a heavier load, but how Joseph himself can continue to play and grow. As O’Neil is quick to point out, Joseph hasn’t really played at a Pro Bowl level in nearly two years, as he was battling through this knee injury even when he was playing in 2025. But if the Lions can get the 2024 Kerby Joseph back—along with Brian Branch’s continued progress now that he’s back from his 2025 Achilles injury—then Detroit’s back-end could look a lot different and better soon. “As we get guys back, guys like with Kerby’s skillset or (Thomas) Harper’s skillset, that just opens up the door to do more stuff with Branch,” O’Neil said. “He can go down, he can do dime roles, he can play nickel roles. You can use him more of a chess piece as we get some guys back in the defense and in that secondary.”

title: Has the Detroit Lions defense turned a corner?
summary: What a difference a month can make. After a historically bad start to the season, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has helped the defense find their sea legs over the course of the last four weeks. With that said, there is still plenty to improve upon for a unit that has even more to […]
full_text: What a difference a month can make. After a historically bad start to the season, Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard has helped the defense find their sea legs over the course of the last four weeks. With that said, there is still plenty to improve upon for a unit that has even more to play for with the loss of All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell during their Week 8 win over the Minnesota Vikings. There were some around the fan base and media who were ready to move on from Sheppard if things didn’t improve—especially after the loss to the Carolina Panthers where they appeared to be out-schemed from the jump. After some tough conversations as well as some schematic and personnel tweaks, the Lions’ defense is beginning to settle in dating back to their Week 5 whooping of the Arizona Cardinals. That brings us to today’s Question of the Day: Do you believe the Lions’ defense has turned a corner? My answer: Despite a three-game sample size not being the largest to go off of, I do belive this unit has begun to figure things out. It still isn’t perfect, and there are still too many missed assignments for my liking, but you can do a lot with the way the Lions’ front is playing. Their star players up front, like defensive end Aidan Hutchinson and defensive tackle Alim McNeill, are making their presence felt nearly every time the ball is snapped. Beyond those two, other members of the defensive line like rookie Skyler Gill-Howard and second year defensive tackle Tyleik Williams are playing some really good football. And while there are still things to clean up in the secondary, cornerback D.J. Reed’s play has really leveled out, star defensive back Brian Branch is back in the mix, and the team opened up All-Pro safety Kerby Joseph’s 21-day window last week. If they can continue to defend the run well and cut down on the blown coverage moments that have plagued them through seven games, I think that will be enough to make them a contender down the stretch. Continue to improve so that you are playing your best, and most sound football in December and into January. When you have an offense like Detroit does, that’s all you really need. What about you? Do you think the Lions’ defense has turned a corner? Let us know in the comments below. Join the conversation! title: Detroit Lions offer firm defense of Brian Branch’s play despite fines
summary: In his first game back, Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch received a fine for improper use of his helmet on this play against Packers tight end Tucker Kraft. The following week, Branch had another helmet-to-helmet collision, this time with teammate DJ Wonnum. The collision knocked both Wonnum and Branch out of the game with a […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - NOVEMBER 01: Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch (32) takes the field prior to the Detroit Lions versus Minnesota Vikings game on Sunday November 1, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In his first game back, Detroit Lions safety Brian Branch received a fine for improper use of his helmet on this play against Packers tight end Tucker Kraft. Hey @nfl can y'all do something about this??? pic.twitter.com/2CKGCkTsbS — Easton Butler (@Easton__Butler) October 25, 2026 The following week, Branch had another helmet-to-helmet collision, this time with teammate DJ Wonnum. The collision knocked both Wonnum and Branch out of the game with a concussion. #BrianBranch #DJWonnum Both @Lions players to locker room One carted, one on own power 2 head injury checks from friendly fire pic.twitter.com/yCsiIoB20r — David J. Chao – ProFootballDoc (@ProFootballDoc) November 1, 2026 Violent collisions with his helmet are nothing new with Branch. He’s been fined six times for impermissible use of his helmet, twice for hit on a defenseless receiver, and he was ejected from a game after a particularly violent head-to-head collision vs. the Packers in 2024. Despite the two notable collisions through two games, Lions safeties coach Jim O’Neil offered an impassioned defense of Branch’s play. “We coach eyes-up tackle, but we also coach—we’re going to play the game violently,” O’Neil said. “That’s the way the game was meant to play. That’s one of the reasons BB is who he is. I mean, he’s got an old-school mentality. He’s explosive. He’s going to play the game violently. We talk about defending every blade of grass, whether it’s on the sideline—you’re not going to tiptoe the sideline on us. If a running back’s on his way down, we’re going to beat him to the ground and hit him. “I thought BB did a great job on that play. He lowered his target. Obviously, when the receiver drops, as well, sometimes it’s head-to-head. We’ll continue to coach eyes-up tackle, but I love the way Brian Branch plays, and we’re not going to do anything to change that. We’re going to continue to try to help him with his technique, but we’re not going to change his mentality at all.” Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell made a similar argument about Branch. “Once he’s going, he’s going for his target and then that target drops. And so, that ends up where it goes,” Campbell said. “You can certainly say go lower, but now you have got to be careful. You start going real low, then you start taking out knees and stuff, and you don’t want any of that. So, just keep your eyes up, see what you hit, try to drop it just a little bit.” Branch is progressing through concussion protocol, and barring any setback, the Lions expect him to play this week vs. the Miami Dolphins. That’s good news for Detroit, because O’Neil compared Branch’s versatility to having three extra players on defense. “I think as we get into the third, fourth, fifth game here, he’s going to catch his groove,” O’Neil said. “He’s such a unique piece, because he can play like a linebacker, he can play like a corner, he can play like a safety. It’s like having three extra guys up on game day, because of what he can do for the defense.”

title: Lions vs. Dolphins: 3 key matchups
summary: The Detroit Lions (5-2) take their talents to South Beach to take on the Miami Dolphins (1-6). Fresh off a three-game win streak, including two in a row against the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, the Lions have reestablished themselves as true NFC North contenders. Despite the back-to-back-to-back victories, the Lions still find themselves […]
full_text: The Detroit Lions (5-2) take their talents to South Beach to take on the Miami Dolphins (1-6). Fresh off a three-game win streak, including two in a row against the Green Bay Packers and Minnesota Vikings, the Lions have reestablished themselves as true NFC North contenders . Despite the back-to-back-to-back victories, the Lions still find themselves currently in third place in the division. This week, the Chicago Bears take on the rising Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and the Minnesota Vikings host Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills on “Monday Night Football.” If the Lions take care of their business, there is a realistic opportunity that Dan Campbell’s team will sit alone at the top of the standings. From just about every performance and talent metric, the Lions should have the edge in this matchup. But digging deeper, the Dolphins are rebuilding in a way that should remind Lions fans of the Dan Campbell led 2021 team. In what could typically be labeled a “trap game,” often the NFL rears its powerful element of parity into the equation. To avoid that, the key matchups will come down to not necessarily the talent on the field, the grit of the players to determine the ultimate outcome. Let’s dive in to the three key matchups centered on the intangible traits that will make or break Sunday’s matchup in south Florida. Gritty rookies in key roles Breaking the normal structure of the article here as this first key matchup really is not a direct positional or players matchup, but the comparative play of the key rookies on each team. While many readers here at Pride of Detroit are familiar the Grit Index, for newer readers, it is the NFL Draft metric that Erik Schlitt and I have created to grade prospects on their intangible qualities. In the 2026 NFL Draft, seven teams drafted players in the elite tier of the Grit Index with a score of 9+. The Detroit Lions and Miami Dolphins were two of those teams. There were 30 players with a 9+ score on this year’s GRIT Index (top ~7.5%) Only 2 teams drafted 3 or more players within this Elite tier: — Chicago (4 – Thieneman, Roush, Jones, Elliott) — Detroit (3 – Miller, Abney, Gill-Howard) (2 – BAL, IND, LV, MIA, PIT) — Between The Numbers – Anthony (@BtwnTheNumbers) April 26, 2026 For the Lions, it was Blake Miller, Keith Abney, and Skyler Gill-Howard. For the Dolphins, it was Jacob Rodriguez and Michael Taaffe. You could call it coincidence, but I am not surprised that each of these five rookies have become key contributors for their respective teams. In fact, Rodriguez and Taaffe are first and second, respectively, in snaps played on the entire Dolphins roster. Similarly, Miller, Abney, and Gill-Howard lead the Lions 2026 rookie draft class in snap counts on the season. They key here with all five of these players is which one will either rise to the occasion, or which one will be a potential liability? Rookies go through growing pains and not all progress is linear. Will Taaffe rise to the occasion against the Lions elite offensive weapons? Will Rodriguez command and communicate the defense to his teammates as the green dot linebacker against the creatively-detailed Lions offense run by offensive coordinator Drew Petzing and Jared Goff? Will the Lions rookies take their strong starts to the next level, or will it be a game filled with growing pains coming off a three-game win streak? The play of these rookies will go a long way in determining the outcome of the game. The Lions’ linebacker room This is a big week. At this point, we’re all aware of and have been in the emotional waiting room following the updates and progression after Jack Campbell’s traumatic neck injury against the Vikings. The impact, though, is most significantly felt by those players closest to him. The key matchup is not how fellow linebackers Derrick Barnes, Malcolm Rodriguez, and Trevor Nowaske fill in Jack Campbell’s shoes, no player will be able to do that for this team. And I don’t suspect they are trying to. The key is how Barnes, Rodriguez, and Nowaske can play as the best version of themselves and as a unit while battling this adversity on and off the field. Derrick Barnes wept in the locker room. Malcolm Rodriguez spent the first night "hugging my family." Even Alex Anzalone was hurting in Tampa Bay. But the season continues, and "he doesn’t want us to feel sorry for him." "Prepare and play like 46." https://t.co/Fv9KTOtsMo — Will Burchfield (@burchie_kid) November 5, 2026 In my view, having Kelvin Sheppard as defensive coordinator, former linebacker coach, and former linebacker himself, he is in a unique position to lead these players through this storm. Sheppard has expressed nothing but confidence in the group. “I raised these other guys that are about to play. Malcolm Rodriguez and Derrick Barnes, those are my little brothers and they know the standard. They both have worn the green dot before. So, this isn’t like a first-time ordeal for either one of them, because that load might get shared. We’re still working through that, but I’m confident in either one of them.” I don’t expect this group to be perfect as each player adapts to their adjusted roles. But I do expect each to play with passion and grit. I expect them to prepare and play like 46. Zach Sieler vs. Lions interior offensive line Lastly, turning to the leader of the Dolphins, captain Zach Sieler is not only the fins most disruptive player on defense, he is the heart and soul of the team. 🎥 Jeff Hafley on Zach Sieler's leadership: "It's valuable to me, it's valuable to the young players… he's one of the best people ever. There's not a much better person out there than Zach Sieler. He does everything the right way." ( @MiamiDolphins ) #PhinsUp pic.twitter.com/gal8hkUSCF — FinsXtra (@FinsXtra) October 5, 2026 Dan Campbell has emphasized Sieler’s impact. “Defensively, Sieler’s really the anchor in there. You know, he’s played good football for a really long time, man. Smart, crafty, powerful, can get an edge in the pass game.” Relentless in both the run and pass game, Sieler will present a challenge to the youth of the Lions interior offensive line. With starting center Cade Mays not practicing and a wave of injuries on defense , the Lions can control the game if Christian Mahogany, Juice Scruggs, and Tate Ratledge can continue to win the line of scrimmage along the interior. In a game where, On Paper, the Lions have a distinct advantage, players like Sieler can lead the charge in a spoiler’s effort. Three key matchups. Three opportunities for grit to win the day.

title: Lions vs. Dolphins 5 Qs preview: Is Miami mirroring Detroit’s 2021 culture rebuild?
summary: The Detroit Lions head to South Beach for a Week 9 interconference matchup against a young, rebuilding Miami Dolphins team. We had the pleasure of connecting with Kevin Nogle, the Managing Editor of Phinsider to give us some insight into this Miami team ahead of Sunday’s kickoff. We learned about the local sentiment surrounding head […]
full_text: Dan Campbell guides the Lions through workouts during a spring minicamp. 2022-06-10 Dan Campbell | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Detroit Lions head to South Beach for a Week 9 interconference matchup against a young, rebuilding Miami Dolphins team. We had the pleasure of connecting with Kevin Nogle, the Managing Editor of Phinsider to give us some insight into this Miami team ahead of Sunday’s kickoff. We learned about the local sentiment surrounding head coach Jeff Hafley’s foundational reset, how offensive coordinator Bobby Slowik is tailoring the offense to quarterback Malik Willis, and how Ollie Gordon is handling the backfield workload in De’Von Achane’s absence—plus what Miami needs to do to keep pace with Detroit’s offense. 1. Miami arguably made more changes to their organization than any other team in the NFL this offseason. New head coach, new quarterback, the changing out of long-tenured skill position players—it was a massive overhaul in South Beach. Although the Dolphins are off to a 1-6 start, how much of that was expected from a team that underwent so many changes this offseason? It’s early, but do you get the sense that new head coach Jeff Hafley is the right guy for this rebuild? This year is about setting up the franchise for the future, and while losses are never fun, the struggles were expected. This is the league’s youngest team, and they are facing a steep learning curve. Miami has 14 rookies on the roster, plus another seven first-year players. This is clearly a reset of the team’s foundation, and there will be growing pains. The Dolphins’ schedule has also been brutal this year. They started the year against the Las Vegas Raiders, San Francisco 49ers, Kansas City Chiefs, and Minnesota Vikings, not facing a team that had a loss until Week 5 against the Cincinnati Bengals, who were 2-2 coming into that game. Through Week 8, Miami has faced the league’s toughest schedule, with a combined opponent winning percentage of .589. The schedule is not an excuse, but with such a young team, it is another variable to consider. Obviously, things can change, but Hafley has instilled confidence in the fanbase so far. The Mike McDaniel era had some fun moments, but it quickly fell apart and the team never adjusted (and McDaniel still does not seem to have made adjustments as the Los Angeles Chargers struggle this year). I think Hafley’s focus on making the Dolphins physical, allowing the younger players to gain experience, and the team’s ability to make adjustments, learn from mistakes, and continue to fight even in losing situations indicate he is the right guy for this role. Lions fans saw Dan Campbell build a culture out of tough losses back in 2021; that is exactly the phase Hafley and the Dolphins are in right now. 2. From the outside looking in, Malik Willis was dropped into a tough situation given the pieces around him in the offense—and it looks like, predictably, the passing game has struggled so far. The Dolphins rank 26th in passing DVOA and EPA/pass. How has Bobby Slowik tried to tailor this offense to Willis’ strengths? What’s working, what’s not working, and how much of that is related to a new quarterback in a new system versus the lack of talent personnel-wise? I think we are starting to see Willis find some comfort in the offensive system, and he is starting to play better. Despite being a third-round pick in 2022, Willis has played in only 29 career games, starting just 13. He is a league veteran but really has the starting experience of a rookie. At times, he still seems bothered by the speed of the game, but the experience he is getting this year is already making a difference in his play. I think one of the biggest issues we have seen from Willis is a desire to be a pocket passer. He stays in the pocket longer than he should, trying to find the perfect pass rather than taking something shorter or throwing the ball away to avoid a sack. The offensive line is not doing him any favors, but he has taken multiple sacks by running out of bounds instead of throwing the ball away. He seemed to want to avoid using his legs, but has opened up that part of his game in the last couple of weeks. Slowik, like McDaniel before him, has an offensive system built on quarterback accuracy and timing. He uses bootlegs, run-pass options, and play-action passes to get Willis out of the pocket and seeing open receivers. They also seem to be using some half-field concepts, keeping Willis looking in one area and working from deep to shallow rather than having him search the entire field for receivers. The youth on the roster – especially with wide receivers Caleb Douglas, Chris Bell, and Kevin Coleman Jr. – do not always create separation, and drops have also been an issue. When the primary target is not open on time, a young quarterback hesitates, and behind an evolving offensive line, hesitation leads to sacks. That all relates back to the discussion of Miami’s reset this year. The potential for talent is on Miami’s roster, but they still need to grow individually and together. The coaching staff is clearly working on the balance between youth and system – relying on a more basic system as the players learn. 3. Losing De’Von Achane in the first month of the season felt especially cruel for this offense that was already so limited on difference makers. The Dolphins rank 9th in EPA/rush (-0.03) but rank near the bottom of the league in rush success rate (26th) and rush DVOA (26th), suggesting that their run game is a boom-or-bust attack. Is that a fair assessment of Ollie Gordon’s performance this year? The Dolphins also rank 26th in stuffed rate (22.8%) which is the percentage of runs that earn zero or negative yards. Are those stuffed runs more of an indictment of the offensive line or the coaching/play calling? That seems like a fair assessment. Gordon has been a lot of fun to watch as he breaks out this year, but he is a power-back who works extremely well as a change-of-pace option behind Achane. When he finds space, he is able to break it for a big gain, but it really is boom or bust on each run. Part of that is Gordon and his abilities. Part of that is the offensive line finding space to get him free. And part of that is opposing defenses planning to stop the run. Miami has had success this year, averaging 131 rushing yards per game, and they have topped 100 yards in five of seven games, including one game over 150 yards and another over 200 yards. They also have two games with 74 yards rushing each. Boom or bust. The offensive line—especially last week with Kadyn Proctor out with a concussion—still has work to do to come together as a unit. I think play calling is part of it, but not necessarily because the plays are wrong, but rather because the player is wrong. The rushing attack was built for Achane’s skill set, complemented by Gordon. Now, it is a Gordon-led unit and some of the designs are clearly meant for Achane’s speed over Gordon’s power. We have seen that evolve as Slowik has adjusted to Gordon, but there is an obvious difference between the two players and there will likely be a boom or bust aspect to the Dolphins’ ground game all season. The outside zone, stretch concepts were designed for Achane’s elite sideline-to-sideline track speed. Gordon is a one-cut, downhill runner. The Dolphins have pivoted to more gap and inside-zone looks to match Gordon’s style, but until defenses are forced to back out of the box, stops will linger. 4. Hafley brings his decades of experience coaching defense to Miami, and the numbers related to personnel deployment and coverage usage are pretty interesting through eight weeks. Miami lines up in base personnel 51.7% of snaps, second-most in the NFL, and they’re utilizing zone coverage 78.8% of the time (10th in the NFL). How much of these numbers overlap with the talent available on the current roster? In other words, does it feel like Hafley’s trying to put his players in the best spots…

full_text: (Photo by Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Green Bay Packers have announced their initial game statuses for Sunday’s action against the New England Patriots, following a week of practice. Five players have already been ruled out: tight end Josh Whyle (concussion), offensive lineman Travis Glover (knee), offensive lineman Sean Rhyan (ankle), linebacker Zaire Franklin (shin), and edge defender Micah Parsons (knee). Parsons remains on the physically unable to perform list, while the other four players are on the 53-man active roster. With four scratches already, the Packers are down to 49 options for their 48 players on game-day already, and that’s if their questionable players suit up: running back MarShawn Lloyd (knee) and cornerback Keisean Nixon (groin). Running back Chris Brooks, who is on the injured reserve at the moment but has his practice window open, is also listed as questionable. Green Bay is not likely to carry more than three running backs or eight offensive linemen on the 48-man game-day roster, so I bet there’s at least one call-up from the practice squad this week, most likely to help on special teams while Isaiah McDuffie and Ty’Ron Hopper are full-time starting linebackers. This has been what the team’s plan has been in recent weeks. On the Patriots’ end of the injury report, receiver A.J. Brown (ankle/knee) and running back TreVeyon Henderson (illness) have been ruled out for Week 9. Players listed as questionable by New England are safety Kevin Byard III (chest), cornerback Carlton Davis III (neck), tight end Hunter Henry (foot), receiver Mack Hollins (calf), tackle Morgan Moses (foot), safety Brenden Schooler (hamstring) and offensive lineman Greg Van Roten (hamstring). title: NFL Draft: Many 4th-year seniors are expected to return to college
summary: The Athletic’s Dane Brugler has reported that NFL scouts “are preparing” for a high number of fourth-year seniors to return to college football in 2027, which will impact the 2027 NFL Draft. This is part of the inevitable evolution of the college landscape, as the NCAA decided to allow for “five-for-five” this past offseason. Five-for-five […]
full_text: (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) The Athletic’s Dane Brugler has reported that NFL scouts “ are preparing ” for a high number of fourth-year seniors to return to college football in 2027, which will impact the 2027 NFL Draft. This is part of the inevitable evolution of the college landscape, as the NCAA decided to allow for “five-for-five” this past offseason. Five-for-five plays out exactly how you think. College players have five years of service available to them before they’ve exhausted their NCAA eligibility, no matter whether they took a redshirt year or not. What this means is that true seniors, players who got on the field for four years without burning a redshirt, are no longer getting pushed out of the NCAA, but actually have another year of eligibility. I first got wind of this upcoming trend in October, so I decided to look at the upcoming class and how it would impact it. My finding: It could impact it a lot. Out of the top 40 prospects on the consensus board (checked on October 12th, when I last dug into the data), only one player (Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss) was a fifth-year player. In essence, every non-Chambliss in that portion of the draft will be treated like an underclassman in previous classes and would have to declare for the draft, passing up available college eligibility, to be entered in 2027. Some notable players who are considered to be “seniors,” but still have eligibility in college next season, if they want it, are: Minnesota iOL Greg Johnson Oregon iDL A’Mauri Washington Clemson ED Will Heldt Missouri OL Cayden Green Oregon ED Matayo Uiagalelei Kentucky OL Lance Heard Missouri ED Damon Wilson Jr. Arkansas ED Quincy Rhodes Jr. LSU ED Pincewill Umanmielen LSU S Ty Benefield Oregon OL Iapani Laloulu Florida State WR Duce Robinson Miami RB Mark Fletcher Alabama S Bray Hubbard BYU RB LJ Martin Oregon ED Teitum Tuioti LSU LB Whit Weeks South Carolina WR Nyck Harbor Indiana CB A.J. Harris Out of the top-100 prospects in this class (again, going off the 10/12 consensus board), only 17 are fifth-year seniors. These are the top three-round players who are for sure going to be in the 2027 class: #9: Trinidad Chambliss, QB, Mississippi #41: Carter Smith, OL, Indiana #44: Ahmad Moten Sr., iDL, Miami #47: Kenyatta Jackson, ED, Ohio State #51: Devan Thompkins, iDL, Alabama #54: Jayden Maiava, QB, USC #60: Omarion Miller, WR, Arizona State #67: Clev Lubin, ED, Louisville #74: Bear Alexander, iDL, Oregon #76: DJ McKinney, CB, Notre Dame #78: Jacarrius Peak, OL, South Carolina #80: Emmanuel Oyebadejo, iDL, Florida #85: Zereoue Williams, OL, Utah #88: A.J. Holmes Jr., iDL, Texas Tech #94: PJ Williams, OL, SMU #98: Ben Roberts, LB, Texas Tech #100: Jamari Sharpe, CB, Indiana That’s it. The other 83 prospects in the top-100 are either fourth-year seniors (now eligible to return to the NCAA for another year under five-for-five) or underclassmen (who have always had extra eligibility). Keep an eye on declarations this year, because they will decide the strength of the upcoming class. If a lot of players go back, as expected, the 2028 class will be much stronger than 2027, due to the talent bottleneck. The 2028 class might be the strongest class since 2011, when the NFL instituted a rookie salary scale — which disincentivized players returning to school. With $40 million college rosters, the prospect of declaring for the NFL draft, when the top third-round pick (Carson Beck) made $2.7 million this year, is a lot less urgent.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Packers still plagued by missed opportunities
summary: The Green Bay Packers don’t appear to have a problem finding open receivers. Receivers catching the ball, however, is unfortunately a problem.  We’ve seen the stat six hundred times already, but here it is once more for posterity: Through eight games, Green Bay has recorded 23 dropped passes, eight more than any other NFL team. […]
full_text: (Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers don’t appear to have a problem finding open receivers. Receivers catching the ball, however, is unfortunately a problem. We’ve seen the stat six hundred times already, but here it is once more for posterity: Through eight games, Green Bay has recorded 23 dropped passes, eight more than any other NFL team. And don’t look now, but that’s already more than the Packers had all of last season. As Jordan Love continues to put together an outstanding year, drops are becoming impossible to ignore. The biggest surprise in all of this is Matthew Golden, who was drafted in part specifically because he is incredibly sure-handed. In his first training camp, months removed from a season where Packers receivers again struggled to make tough catches, Golden reportedly caught everything. In 2026, he has nine drops. But this isn’t exclusively a Golden problem. The issue has spread throughout a receiving group that has otherwise demonstrated plenty of big-play potential. Ok, let’s stop piling on. There’s reason for optimism. Christian Watson and Golden have shown the ability to make tough catches generate explosive plays. Tucker Kraft has, too — and I’d expect him to start accumulating impressive plays as he continues to regain confidence following a return from a knee injury. The talent is there, we’ve seen the proof before, and Love clearly has confidence in his receivers. That’s what makes the problem so frustrating. Green Bay doesn’t necessarily need to find another receiver before the November 10 trade deadline. It needs the very talented receivers already on the roster to catch the dang ball. Until then, they’ll continue to be a streaky offense with a quarterback leading the league in passing yards. If the pass catchers can turn it around, though, the passing attack could graduate to the “most dangerous in the league” conversation. That’ll also be necessary for this team to survive the NFC North and do damage in the playoffs. I dunno, can we go back to making them catch bricks or something? Packers lead NFL in drops by a huge margin The Green Bay Packers currently hold a wide and possibly insurmountable lead for dropped passes as the midway point of the 2026 season approaches. Packers must be buyers at trade deadline The NFL trade deadline is Tuesday. The Packers haven’t been buyers in a long time but there is a green-and-golden opportunity to make a move in the wide-open NFC. ICYMI: Packers-Patriots preview Justis Mosqueda dives deep to help get you ready for Packers at Patriots. Packers give Micah Parsons boost in return from ACL injury The defense just needed to hold the line until Parsons could return from injury, but what they’ve accomplished is far more impressive. Packers discussion in the Feed Parsons is set to return, and the team has needs elsewhere. As the trade deadline approaches, should the Packers consider trading an edge rusher? title: Desmond Howard, Reggie White and more highlight Packers’ best moments against Patriots
summary: The New England Patriots are the epitome of what good ol’ Mike McCarthy would have called an “uncommon opponent.” They’ve been around for more than 50 years, but the Packers have only encountered them 13 times, and that counts their matchup in Super Bowl XXXI. But there’s still no shortage of big statistical performances on […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - JANUARY 26: Desmond Howard #81 of the Green Bay Packers returns a kickoff while pursued by Mike Bartrum #86 of the New England Patriots during Super Bowl XXXI January 26, 1997 at the Louisiana Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana . The Packers won the game 35-21. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots are the epitome of what good ol’ Mike McCarthy would have called an “uncommon opponent.” They’ve been around for more than 50 years, but the Packers have only encountered them 13 times, and that counts their matchup in Super Bowl XXXI. But there’s still no shortage of big statistical performances on the Packers’ side of these matchups, and, as always, looking back gives us a great chance to Remember Some Guys. And that remembering takes us all the way from the unremarkable days of the late 1980s to the Super Bowl and beyond. Most passing yards – 368 ( Aaron Rodgers, 2014 ) Aaron Rodgers and Tom Brady squared off exactly once when both teams were at anything resembling full strength, and it was a game for the ages. Aaron Rodgers barbecued the Patriots’ secondary to the tune of 368 yards and two touchdowns, including a magnificent 45-yard catch and run by Jordy Nelson just before halftime . Most rushing yards – 136 ( Ahman Green, 2002 ) The Packers traveled to New England on a rainy October day in 2002 to face off against the defending Super Bowl champs and came away with a convincing 28-10 win . Ahman Green fueled most of the offensive effort, carrying 31 times for 136 yards, scoring a touchdown as well. He also added 21 more yards and a touchdown on three catches. 136 yards wouldn’t even be Green’s best day of the 2002 season. By the time he ran over the Patriots, he’d already put up a 155-yard day against the Atlanta Falcons in the season opener. Most receiving yards – 132 ( Sterling Sharpe, 1994 ) You could always count on Sterling Sharpe to do great things, even in a losing effort. In 1994, the Packers came up short against the Patriots, allowing a game-winning drive and a go-ahead field goal with just seconds remaining . But Sharpe held up his end of the bargain, recording 132 yards and a touchdown on nine catches. Whatever happened down the stretch, he wasn’t to blame! Most points scored – 18 ( Brent Fullwood, 1988 ) One of the most obscure names on our list today, Fullwood scored three touchdowns in a 1988 beatdown of the Patriots . The final score was 45-3, but amusingly, Fullwood didn’t get in on the action until the Packers were already up 17-3. But a 33-yard run midway through the third quarter started the deluge, and he added touchdown runs of seven and 31 yards in the fourth quarter to get the blowout really rolling. He finished with a spectacularly efficient 118 yards and three touchdowns on 14 carries. Sacks – 3 ( Reggie White, 1996 ) The Minister of Defense had famously never won a championship at any level when he joined the Green Bay Packers, but he more than did his part in Super Bowl XXXI. He took down Drew Bledsoe three times to put the game away late , including two on back to back plays to close out the third quarter. But fans of a certain age will remember that White’s performance, great as it was, was hardly the only standout play that day. More on that in a second. Solo tackles – 11 ( Marques Anderson, 2002 ) In the same game where Ahman Green ran wild in New England, Marques Anderson did plenty of work on defense. The rookie safety racked up 11 solo tackles (and an interception) to fuel a defensive effort that suffocated Tom Brady and the Patriots. Interceptions – 2 ( Ron Pitts, 1988 ) Brent Fullwood did the bulk of the damage on offense in the Packers’ 1988 beatdown of the Patriots, but Ron Pitts set the table on defense. He ended two Patriots’ drives with interceptions, but he had company. The Packers intercepted Patriots quarterbacks Doug Flutie and Steve Grogan five times that day to cement the all-around blowout. Return yards – 244 ( Desmond Howard, 1996 ) We couldn’t not mention this one. Reggie White was great in Super Bowl XXXI, but Desmond Howard was transcendent. He piled up 244 total yards on kickoff and punt returns, including a 99-yard touchdown that’s etched into Packers’ lore , and was named Super Bowl MVP for his efforts.
author: Jon Meerdink

title: There is a lot for the Colts to consider as they move forward this season.
summary: I have to admit that I have started and stopped writing this two or three times. I don’t think that I have anything new to add in this stomach churning segment of the season. Much has been discussed about our desire to see both the offensive and defensive leaders of the team relieved of their […]
full_text: I have to admit that I have started and stopped writing this two or three times. I don’t think that I have anything new to add in this stomach churning segment of the season. Much has been discussed about our desire to see both the offensive and defensive leaders of the team relieved of their duties. Not for the purpose of seeing a drastic improvement and unlikely playoff run, but simply a “We have seen enough” feeling. We’ve ran the cycle of every player that we’d like to trade or keep, and how much we’d expect to get in return. I’d throw my hat in the ring, but the honest truth is that it would be a guess. I really struggle understanding firing CB, then putting Dodds in charge of the who stays and who goes decisions. Maybe CB refused to make decisions for the next regime and that was his last act. I know that someone has to do it and maybe Carlie is keeping plausible deniability, by allowing the current admin to make these calls. I will say that I would bench Jones, but intend to keep him next year. He can’t do what he needs to do with his physical limitations. He will be past those limitations by the start of next season. A new GM could find Jones a better option than others who might be available and not as expensive as many suggest. At minimum, that GM gets a year to form his own opinion. If a rookie is brought in, I can’t see it being one that you are ready to throw to the wolves immediately, especially with the AR wounds still pretty fresh. As far as team building, I do not know who has Carlie’s ear right now? She has a very important decision regarding who is tasked with getting the Colts off the mat and back in the fight. She has had to have made some contacts with a person or persons that she feels that she can trust, but I do not know who that might be? I also do not quite understand her desire to continue to be on the sidelines and tuned in. What can she pick up by listening to Shane and Lou? If she did decide to meddle, she could get away with it pretty easily this season. I don’t think her presence is necessarily inspiring the players to give their best effort. The information that she needs to be gathering right now, is who will be the next eyes, ears, and voice of the franchise. I think she has picked up enough to have her expectations as to what she wants to hear from a GM, during the interview process. I think a view from the suite, might give her a different perspective. She can listen if she wants, it is her business to run. This is the time of the season when the “lay down” banter begins. I’ve never been a proponent and even less this year, when it doesn’t affect the first round pick. It appears that Shane and Lou will be allowed to keep doing things that don’t work, so the best you can do is protect players from getting hurt during a season that essentially means nothing. There are lots of lame ducks that are not going to get off of the ground. Honestly, I do not think we need to avoid winning, as it is going to occur naturally. It is time to see who has some pride in their craft. Do not reward lack of effort with playing time. You can live with some mistakes, if they are mistakes of aggression and excitement. I’m not proposing cutting players, but there are lots of incentives that players can’t reach, if they are not on the field. Maybe someone on the bench, or a practice squader emerges as a player? It is hard for bench players to show anything after camp is over. The NFL barely lets you have contact in practice, so how can you show what you have learned in the film room? Give them their shot. So, while we are not considering what has to be done to make the playoffs, there are still many considerations, far more than I have mentioned, which will shape the path forward. I’m normally not one to punt, but if you realize that punting can be a strategic play, maybe it is more palatable this season. We as fans might be a little more patient during this time. Many recently blasted the organization for the return they got for Q. As we find out that he had an injury, prior to the trade, maybe we should consider that we don’t know the whole story on nearly anything.

title: Former Colts All-Pro OG Quenton Nelson to undergo cleanup surgery and will miss at least a few weeks
summary: Former Indianapolis Colts All-Pro offensive guard Quenton Nelson, who was traded last week to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 3rd round pick and 2028 fifth round pick, will undergo minor cleanup cartilage surgery on his balky knee and miss at least a few weeks—although he’ll not be placed on injured reserve at this time: […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 02: Quenton Nelson #53 of the Seattle Seahawks in action against the Chicago Bears at Lumen Field on November 02, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Former Indianapolis Colts All-Pro offensive guard Quenton Nelson, who was traded last week to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 3rd round pick and 2028 fifth round pick, will undergo minor cleanup cartilage surgery on his balky knee and miss at least a few weeks—although he’ll not be placed on injured reserve at this time: #Seahawks G Quenton Nelson will have surgery to clean out some cartilage in his knee, sources say, as fragments had been causing an issue recently. The plan is for Nelson to avoid Injured Reserve, and his timeline is a few weeks. Seattle has two games, then a Week 11 bye. pic.twitter.com/AZyUFzg7Kj — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 6, 2026 The Seahawks have two games and then their BYE week, so the hopeful expectation for Seattle must be that Nelson could be ready in 3 weeks’ time as opposed to the minimum 4-game period of inactivity that any stint on injured reserve requires before any ensuing activation. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald indicated that Nelson had the knee condition prior to arriving in Seattle via trade, having suffered it in on the road in Week 7 against the Minnesota Vikings while still formerly a member of the Colts. However, he aggravated the knee injury further, during the Seahawks’ 34-17 Monday Night home loss against the Chicago Bears. It’s unfortunate timing for the playoff hopeful Seahawks and Nelson, who was rather unsurprisingly very impressive during his Seahawks debut on primetime . The future Hall-of-Famer figured to be a ‘plug-and-play’ elite left guard for Seattle in no time and didn’t skip a beat during his Pacific Northwest debut. What is interesting is that it seems as though both the Colts and the Seahawks knew of Nelson’s initial knee condition, which likely came up in his physical. Although to be fair, it worsened this past Monday Night. Perhaps that may have been some of interim GM Ed Dodds’ eagerness and motivation in moving Nelson well before the trade deadline, knowing that his knee condition could eventually lead to the perennial All-Pro and pending NFL free agent missing games down the road in 2026. It’s hard to say for sure at this time. Nelson has been incredibly durable in his Canton-bound NFL career to-date, having only missed 4 starts—all of which occurred during the 2021 campaign with the Colts. We wish Big Q a speedy recovery the rest of the way.

title: Colts rookie LB CJ Allen will be handling important defensive duty on Sunday for first time
summary: Indianapolis Colts rookie starting linebacker CJ Allen, who was originally a top candidate to don the infamous green dot during training camp, will assume such duties for the first time in his NFL career on Sunday at home against the Dallas Cowboys. As starting veteran linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) was already ruled out, the green […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 01: CJ Allen #53 of the Indianapolis Colts reacts after a play during the game between the Jacksonville Jaguars and the Indianapolis Colts on November 1, 2026 at EverBank Stadium in Jacksonville, Fl. (Photo by David Rosenblum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Indianapolis Colts rookie starting linebacker CJ Allen, who was originally a top candidate to don the infamous green dot during training camp, will assume such duties for the first time in his NFL career on Sunday at home against the Dallas Cowboys. As starting veteran linebacker Akeem Davis-Gaither (knee) was already ruled out, the green dot duties at the 2nd level of the Indy defense will now transition to Allen, who at MIKE, will be making his 2nd career NFL start. With Davis-Gaither unlikely to be re-signed as a veteran free agent at year-end, it’s quite possible that the Colts will let Allen don the defense’s lone built-in radio speaker and handle communicating the defensive play-calling to his on-the-field Indianapolis teammates the rest of the way. There’d be no real reason not to, unless it goes poorly. Allen was one of the few silver linings during last Sunday’s blowout road loss the Jacksonville Jaguars, recording a team-high 10 tackles to go along with a sack. He projects to be a potential key piece to the Colts defensive core if he can continue to improve and develop after such an encouraging debut start last weekend. That being said, he’ll be handling an important job duty, and one that was already the center of an unnecessarily self-inflicted controversy to start the Colts’ disappointing 2026 season—as veteran safety Cam Bynum initially handled green dot duties in the Colts Week 1 loss to the Baltimore Ravens. There was a number of breakdowns and Colts defensive players being out of position, as Bynum was forced to run from down the field and the backend of the Indy secondary to relay the defensive play-calling to his teammates, which didn’t provide them as much opportunity to communicate and get set pre-snap. At that time, the Colts were the only team not to use a linebacker for handling green dot duties, and it cost them in Week 1. Here’s hoping Allen’s green dot debut goes a lot smoother!

title: Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 9): Colts confidence falls to 19%, fans favor Taylor trade
summary: The latest SB Nation Reacts survey paints an increasingly bleak picture of fan sentiment surrounding the Indianapolis Colts, with just 19 percent of fans expressing confidence that the franchise is headed in the right direction. That’s another significant decline from last week’s 31 percent and a staggering 28-percentage-point drop from the 47 percent recorded just […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 1: Running back Jonathan Taylor #28 of the Indianapolis Colts runs for a first down in the second quarter against the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Jacksonville, Florida. (Photo by Parker S. Freedman/Getty Images) | Getty Images The latest SB Nation Reacts survey paints an increasingly bleak picture of fan sentiment surrounding the Indianapolis Colts, with just 19 percent of fans expressing confidence that the franchise is headed in the right direction . That’s another significant decline from last week’s 31 percent and a staggering 28-percentage-point drop from the 47 percent recorded just two weeks ago, shortly after the firing of general manager Chris Ballard. Whatever optimism emerged following Ballard’s dismissal appears to have disappeared almost as quickly as it arrived. The Colts have lost four consecutive games, falling to 2-6 following Sunday’s humiliating 42-7 defeat against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Indianapolis was thoroughly outplayed in virtually every aspect of the game, trailing 28-0 at halftime before suffering its most lopsided loss of the season. With the offense continuing to struggle under Daniel Jones and the defense showing little consistency, there has been very little on the field to suggest that a turnaround is approaching. The organization’s recent roster overhaul has only added to the uncertainty. Indianapolis traded Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner last week, parting ways with two of its most accomplished veterans in exchange for future draft capital. While those decisions may ultimately benefit the franchise in the long run, they also signal that the Colts are increasingly focused on rebuilding rather than competing this season. With no first-round selection in the 2027 NFL Draft and several important roster questions still unanswered, fans understandably have concerns about how quickly the organization can return to contention. The decline in confidence does not necessarily mean fans oppose the direction ownership has chosen, particularly given the frustration surrounding the previous regime. However, the results suggest that meaningful organizational changes alone have not been enough to restore faith in the franchise. Indianapolis still needs to demonstrate that it has a realistic plan for building a competitive roster, and the decisions made over the next several months could go a long way toward determining whether that confidence eventually returns. Elsewhere in this week’s survey, fans were asked whether the Colts should trade star running back Jonathan Taylor ahead of the November 10 deadline, and the results were surprisingly decisive. An overwhelming 73 percent of respondents supported moving Taylor , despite the 27-year-old remaining one of the NFL’s premier running backs and arguably the most important player on Indianapolis’ offense. The results reflect just how much the conversation surrounding the Colts has changed over the past several weeks. Taylor remains an elite offensive weapon and is under contract through 2028, but with Indianapolis potentially several years away from seriously competing again, there is a legitimate question about whether his remaining prime seasons align with the organization’s rebuilding timeline. Multiple contenders have reportedly expressed interest, and with the Colts believed to be seeking a first-round selection or a comparable package, moving Taylor could provide valuable draft capital for whoever takes over as general manager. There is still a strong argument for keeping him, particularly with the Colts already lacking established offensive weapons and potentially facing another quarterback change in the coming years. Taylor has also maintained that he wants to win in Indianapolis and has not requested a trade, making his situation different from some of the other players reportedly seeking opportunities elsewhere. Nevertheless, the survey results suggest that a substantial majority of participating Colts fans would support another major trade if it helps accelerate the franchise’s rebuilding process. Whether Indianapolis ultimately receives an offer compelling enough to move Taylor remains to be seen, but with the deadline rapidly approaching, the organization faces another decision that could significantly shape its future.
