full_text: As the once perceived 17-0 Los Angeles Rams sit at 4-4, someone needs to be blamed, and according to fans surveyed, Sean McVay deserves more than his fair share. Over 67% the fans polled blame McVay as being a “part of the problem” for the team’s struggles, as opposed to around 32% expressing that McVay is “not a problem” . To go so far as to say the Rams could do better at head coach than McVay may be foolhardy, but to say that McVay could be doing a better job as his team sits 4-4? That seems fair. McVay would likely agree, he could be doing a better job. If you doubt McVay in Week 9 against his former Washington Commanders, then you should make a bet on FanDuel . Bet responsibly. Of course, coaching only gets you so far, yet, in the NFL coaching may be more important than any other sport. McVay is one of the best NFL coaches we’ve seen. Even if he never wins another game, what he’s done since entering the league in 2017 has changed the NFL. Despite the historical relevance McVay has at the NFL level, football is a “What have you done for me lately business?” Lately, McVay has helped guide his team from 2-4 to 4-4. If he keeps winning, if the Rams keeps winning, the fans will believe, and McVay will be seen as a solution, not a problem. Do you believe this team is headed in the right direction? Speaking of belief in the Rams, how confident are you that this team is headed in the right direction? According to fans surveyed, their confidence in this team is a coin flip with 51% of fans saying this team is headed the right way, while 49% are not so positive. Coaching aside, the Rams on paper, despite with the loss of Jaylen Watson , have a stronger roster than the Commanders. The Rams should win even if McVay doesn’t bring his A-game on Sunday. Though, games aren’t played on paper, otherwise the Rams would be 17-0 instead of 4-4. Jayden Daniels in terms of talent, has it. He can give the Rams fits if they don’t contain him. But for the second time this year, Myles Garrett should be suiting up for the Rams , and perhaps he’ll have a better showing than Week 1 and actually earn a sack, or a tackle, or anything. Garrett doesn’t have any real stats for L.A. after his lone game against the San Francisco 49ers, which didn’t go well for the entire team. Maybe Week 9 is L.A. rookie CJ Daniels’ chance to breakout , maybe Kyren Williams and Blake Corum each score, or maybe Washington’s own rookie Sonny Styles puts down a sack or two. If you want to bet on it, FanDuel should have you covered. McVay and the Rams can change the tone of their season with a win on Sunday to get to 5-4. A loss, and L.A.’s season may officially be spiraling. If you feel any type of way about the Rams or another team, check out FanDuel .

title: Puka Nacua is shouldering an immense load for the Rams offense
summary: Los Angeles Rams’ star Puka Nacua is one of the best in the business and, in recent years, has been featured as much as nearly any receiver in the NFL. This season, though, his usage has surpassed even his previous lofty production. The fourth-year pro is currently just seventh in the NFL in total targets […]
full_text: (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images Los Angeles Rams’ star Puka Nacua is one of the best in the business and, in recent years, has been featured as much as nearly any receiver in the NFL. This season, though, his usage has surpassed even his previous lofty production. The fourth-year pro is currently just seventh in the NFL in total targets with 74 of them, but that’s through just six games played. He’s first by a sizable margin in targets per game, with quarterback Matthew Stafford throwing at his All-Pro receiver 12.3 times per game. On a per-game basis, no one is being thrown at more often than Nacua. Is that sustainable? For comparison’s sake, Dallas Cowboys wide receiver CeeDee Lamb leads the league in total targets with 92, but is averaging just 11.5 per game. Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who at times has been the only functional piece of the Seattle Seahawks offense this season, is averaging 11.1 targets per game. Puka keeps climbing. 📈 With 4,756 receiving yards through his first 50 career games, Puka Nacua now ranks second all-time at that mark, surpassing Hall of Famer Lance Alworth and trailing only Justin Jefferson. https://t.co/c863uCkvK1 @RamsNFL @AsapPuka @BYUfootball pic.twitter.com/sa71gULtQY — Pro Football Hall of Fame (@ProFootballHOF) November 3, 2026 Nacua’s rate isn’t just a league-best this year, it’s in historic territory in terms of target share. According to Next Gen Stats, only three players since the turn of the century have averaged more targets per game than Nacua. That includes Julio Jones at 12.7 with the 2015 Atlanta Falcons, Marvin Harrison at 12.8 with the 2002 Indianapolis Colts and Terrell Owens at a staggering 13.1 targets per game for the 2005 Philadelphia Eagles. That’s two Hall of Famers and another who’s a shoo-in, by the way. Idk if it's the calf or the play calling, but absolutely nothing downfield for Puka Nacua the last two weeks. pic.twitter.com/zT9qW0DmoU — Cameron DaSilva (@camdasilva) November 2, 2026 It’s not necessarily a negative to have your passing game run through one player at a stark rate. And it’s not as if Nacua is the only worthwhile part of the offense, either, considering L.A.’s ground game has been excellent again this season, once again placing in the top 10 in the NFL in EPA/rush and the top five in success rate. Part of the reason for the higher-than-usual target share for Nacua is his quarterback. Stafford isn’t pushing the ball down the field nearly as often as he’s done over the course of his career. Nacua is a big-play threat, of course, but he’s not a burner, and he’s dangerous on the routes and concepts Stafford has been more comfortable with in 2026. Some questions and answers with Rams OC Nathan Scheelhaase on the state of L.A.'s WR room around Puka Nacua right now. (Worth noting: The trade deadline is 5 days away.) pic.twitter.com/iWXsN89ARl — Nate Atkins (@NateAtkins_) November 5, 2026 All of this is a bit of a high-wire act for Los Angeles. Nacua is a dazzling player, but on the off chance an opposing defense finds a way to limit him, what’s the changeup in the passing game? Right now, the Ram receiving the second most targets this season is Kyren Williams, a running back. Third? Davante Adams, who’s on injured reserve . Tight end Tyler Higbee slots in fourth with just 27 targets so far this season. This is emphasizing two things: Nacua is phenomenal, and the Rams really do need more help at wide receiver. A superstar acquisition is an exciting proposition , but even a decent starter would do the trick at this point. Puka Nacua has proven he can carry nearly the Rams’ entire passing game on his own. That probably won’t change without a drastic shakeup to the roster.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: Myles Garrett expected to play in Week 9
summary: The Los Angeles Rams will activate pass rusher Myles Garrett in time to return this Sunday against the Washington Commanders, according to multiple reports on Friday. The veteran defensive end has missed all but one game this season with a knee injury, an ailment that caused him to miss most of training camp and seven […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams will activate pass rusher Myles Garrett in time to return this Sunday against the Washington Commanders, according to multiple reports on Friday. The veteran defensive end has missed all but one game this season with a knee injury, an ailment that caused him to miss most of training camp and seven games this year. However, L.A.’s long awaited return for the player who they invested so much into over the offseason appears to be two days away. The Rams desperately needed good injury news this week and Garrett’s expected return against the Commanders is just what the doctor ordered. #Rams star Myles Garrett, working his way back from knee surgery that landed him on Injured Reserve, is on track to be activated ahead of Sunday’s game at the #Commanders , per me and @MikeGarafolo . Garrett has practiced all week and all indications point towards him playing. A… pic.twitter.com/hoOhpOJL4y — Ian Rapoport (@RapSheet) November 6, 2026 What can be said about Myles Garrett that hasn’t been said 100 times this year already? He is the reigning Defensive Player of the Year after recording a historic 23 sacks last season. The Rams just put Jaylen Watson on season-ending IR but they hope to have both Garrett and Trent McDuffie on the field on Sunday, a pairing we’ve only seen once this year. That was a 27-7 loss to the 49ers in Week 1, but L.A. had to travel across the world for that game. McDuffie has been one of the top-five cover corners in the NFL this season and Garrett is no doubt one of the top-five edge rushers. The Rams’ defense has been good enough, but many expected it to be the best in the league after trading two first-round picks, Jared Verse, and more to acquire these two players. The defense now gets a chance to show what they’ve really become this year.

But with the Rams missing Davante Adams, they have desperately needed production on the perimeter. CJ Daniels number is likely to be called with Konata Mumpfield and Jordan Whittington producing next to nothing in the passing game. title: CJ Daniels can help wake up a drowsy Rams passing game
summary: At first glance, the Los Angeles Rams passing offense seems healthy and productive. They currently sit third in the NFL in passing yards and attempts, while standing second in completions. The numbers say one thing, but clearly, over the last two games, quarterback Matthew Stafford hasn’t looked comfortable targeting wide outs not named Puka Nacua. […]
full_text: At first glance, the Los Angeles Rams passing offense seems healthy and productive. They currently sit third in the NFL in passing yards and attempts, while standing second in completions. The numbers say one thing, but clearly, over the last two games, quarterback Matthew Stafford hasn’t looked comfortable targeting wide outs not named Puka Nacua. Actually, the passing offense (under 200 yards) has been uninspiring against three consecutive lower-tier teams It is time rookie CJ Daniels gets his chance in the Rams offense . Even with the heavy dose of multiple tight end formations, a 45% rate, the need for more production out of L.A.’s secondary wide receivers is glaring. Stafford’s fluster has been particularly noticeable in the past two games since Davante Adams went to the Injured Reserve List. In theory, Daniels place on the active roster in the past two games is in response to Adams’ absence, but he’s only received five offensive snaps, all in mop-up situations with the Rams running out the clock. Opposite Nacua, the L.A. offense has instead made do with holdovers Tutu Atwell, Konata Mumpfield, and Jordan Whittington to the tune of three catches on nine targets for 65 yards. Even with a heavy dose of multiple tight end formations, a 45% rate, the need for more production out of L.A.’s secondary wide receivers is glaring. I wish they let CJ Daniels get some play time.. https://t.co/Gf95Mg9TdG pic.twitter.com/1toiolQwNF — Rams Tapes 🇵🇷 (@RamsTapes) October 2, 2026 What CJ Daniels brings to the table The L.A. scouting department loves players who can step up from lower competition schools and be successful with bigger programs. Daniels played at Liberty, a Conference USA program, for four seasons (one redshirt), improving his production numbers every year. He jumped through the 2024 portal to LSU and proffered a solid SEC season that was cut short by injury after nine games. Granted a sixth year of eligibility for 2025, he moved to the ACC Miami Hurricanes for a final season that ended in the College Football Playoff National Championship Game. After a trade that moved the Rams up 10 draft positions, Daniels was taken at #197 of Round 6 in the 2026 Draft. Daniels checks off a lot of boxes that make up what the Rams look for in a wide receiver, the intangibles as well as physical makeup. His character is toughness, football IQ, and reliability. At 6’ 2” 202 lb. with almost 32” arms, Daniels has stellar hands (zero drops in his senior year at Miami) and outstanding body control led him to convert contested catches at a 75.6 percent percent clip over his last three college seasons. Not particularly fast or bursty, 4.58 forty and 1.61 10 yard split, his change of direction/ short area agility (7.03 3cone) are average, as is his flexibility/ balance (4.27 shuttle). Daniels creates separation with feints/fakes, change of speed, and sharp cuts out of breaks. He tracks balls well, and sports solid hand/eye coordination. He can really extend to get after the ball, but needs to be consistent as a pro, NFL cornerbacks will swipe the ball from body catchers and hesitant reach. He was considered a willing and successful run blocker. CJ Daniels motions in and blocks..gets nose in there, a mess with others,but maybe getting to speed in blocking? pic.twitter.com/XtI8yfggCF — Jim Youngblood 53 (@53_jim70721) November 3, 2026 Daniels pro film is from preseason games and it coincides quite well with his college profile. He projects as a reliable, competitive support piece, not a star playmaker. He has formational versatility, can find soft areas of zones, and his cuts at speed will help him against man coverage, but early in his career he may struggle if he can’t release off the line of scrimmage clean. Not a lot of giddy-up with the ball in his hands, but his aggressive play style could help him break sloppy tackles. Are fans the only ones considering a WR change? Excepting those periods where the offense has been in hurry up mode. It has been clunky for portions of every game without regard to competition, Adams injury has only exacerbated the situation. The Rams need at wide receiver has fueled pundits to weigh in on rumors about the addition of big names, Josh Downs, Brian Thomas, Jr. and Jajuan Jennings amongst others. But there’s a huge hurdle to overcome. Without re-working established contracts, L.A. simply doesn’t have the cap space, which according to overthecap.com stands at a paltry $8k, to bring in a veteran or promising youngster. The L.A. braintrust does not appear particularly interested bringing in receiver help from another team. Sean McVay weighed in on the the contributions of the receiver unit over the past two games and whether, or not he was actively looking for an WR upgrade from other teams with Nate Atkins of The Athletic. “All I care about is winning,” McVay said. “We’re 2-0 in those games,… I think there are a lot of ways that you can impact the game, not exclusive to just catching the football…The first five drives (Sunday vs the Chargers) were not good at all, but there were a lot of reasons for that. None of them that I thought had to do with the other receivers.” “I would never rule out opportunities to get better, but at what opportunity cost?” McVay said. “…What are the resources that you would be willing to give up when you’re looking at it as a whole? I understand the question, I just don’t know that there’s enough information or people that are out there that are available that would accommodate …” Sub-par production out of the current Rams receivers not named Puka Nacua or not, all the signs clearly point to the Rams plowing forward with in-house wide receivers. Just as clearly, it is time for CJ Daniels to get his shot at re-invigorating the Rams secondary targets.

title: The Rams officially going with two kickers, sign Joshua Karty
summary: The Los Angeles Rams rolled with two kickers in Week 8, and they are doing it again as they made it official before Week 9 by signing Joshua Karty and Brandon McManus to their roster. Karty is expected to handle kickoffs, while McManus will handle field goals. Karty botched two kickoffs last week by not […]
full_text: The Los Angeles Rams rolled with two kickers in Week 8 , and they are doing it again as they made it official before Week 9 by signing Joshua Karty and Brandon McManus to their roster. Karty is expected to handle kickoffs, while McManus will handle field goals. Karty botched two kickoffs last week by not hitting them into the landing zone, setting up the opponent at the 40-yard line due to penalty. McManus has been flawless on his attempts since joining the Rams. He’s been fine, but the team hasn’t seen if McManus can handle a high-pressure kick such as a game winning one. All things come in time, the Rams will find out if McManus can handle it or not, they’ll also see if Karty can improve, but their kicking position is still a question mark despite all their changes. It’s clear that as the Rams continue to make changes, they don’t exactly know what they are doing. But they are trying. Points for trying. Then again, points for trying, doesn’t always lead to points on the field. Rams sign Joshua Karty to active roster and bring back former 3rd-round CB (ramswire) “The kicking carousel continues to spin for the Los Angeles Rams . On Thursday, the Rams announced they have signed Joshua Karty from the practice squad to the 53-man roster, giving them two kickers on the active roster; Brandon McManus is the other. Additionally, the team reunited with cornerback David Long Jr., who Los Angeles drafted in the third round back in 2019. Long has been signed to the practice squad, taking the spot vacated by Karty’s promotion. It’s surprising that the Rams signed Karty to the 53-man roster after elevating him for the first time last week. They could have used a temporary elevation on him twice more, but perhaps they want to reserve their practice squad promotions for players at another position.“ Rams Midweek Report: A Concerning Trend on Offense, Matthew Stafford’s Elbow, and Trade Buzz (si.com) “There is certainly some context to that as Davante Adams and Puka Nacua have each missed games. Terrance Ferguson has also been out since Week 3. At the same time, the Rams haven’t pushed the ball down the field very often. Through eight weeks this season, the Rams’ passing game has an explosive play rate of just 4.1 percent. At this point last year, the passing game had an explosive play rate of 17.5 percent and it was 18.2 percent for the season. The passing game is less than one-fourth as explosive as it was last year. That lack of explosiveness certainly helps explain some of the Rams’ troubles scoring consistently. Picking up yards hasn’t been an issue. The Rams also rank sixth in touchdown rate once they get into the red zone.“ Commanders Daily: The Rams Have More Than Film on Jayden Daniels (si.com) “When asked if Kingsbury and Johnson could share their knowledge of Washington’s personnel with the Rams’ defense, Blough’s response was direct: “I think so. I think everybody in every role shares information. And yeah, they certainly know our guys. We know what they know about our guys, and we kind of go from there.” There’s no getting around the fact that the Rams will come equipped with information on Washington’s strengths and tendencies from a year ago. Kingsbury and Johnson helped prepare Daniels each week, which gave them a chance to see what he handled well and what needed more work. That experience can help the Rams make sense of what they’re seeing from him in Blough’s offense now. They will certainly know the assistant that Blough was; hell, they’ll know Dan Quinn even better. That’s the type of familiarity Washington’s staff will need to account for.“ Rams can’t waste any more time achieving a sustainable offense (ramblinfan) “Complicating the matter is the fact that injuries are depleting the team. The Rams have played most of the season without up-and-coming tight end Terrance Ferguson. Now Davante Adams is on injured reserve. And much to fans’ horror, even durable Matthew Stafford is suffering from arm soreness . LA is facing a midseason crisis. Yes, the offense can gain yards and remains one of the NFL’s best. But it lags at 10th place in scoring. The Rams haven’t converted moving the football into points on the scoreboard. The strategy that has carried the offense to Week 9 won’t work going forward. The strain on the few entrusted playmakers is taking its toll.“ Commanders defense faces major challenge in Rams WR Puka Nacua (sports.yahoo) “Not only is Nacua very talented, but Rams head coach Sean McVay really moves Nacua around. “Oh, they do a great job the way they move him; the way they utilize him,” Jones said. “He’s in the run game, because he is physical,” Jones said. The Rams run the ball well, and the second-level blocking of Nacua has certainly helped Rams ball carriers. In addition, the Rams occasionally will hand off the ball to Nacua. In 2025, he ran ten times for 105 yards and five rushing first downs. But make no mistake, Nacua is still one of the real workhorses in the NFL. He hurts opposing defenses with his ability to go into the middle, catch short passes and sometimes get beat up, and sometimes break free for larger yardage. Though Nacua was injured in the opener and missed the next two games, he has still collected 56 receptions, 26 receiving first downs and three touchdowns.“ Washington Commanders vs. Los Angeles Rams: 3 reasons for optimism (sports.yahoo) “A steady ground game could create more manageable third downs and make play-action more effective. It would also give Washington a way to extend possessions and limit opportunities for Matthew Stafford and the Rams’ offense. Washington’s defense is showing it can produce game-changing plays The Commanders’ defense delivered a performance against Philadelphia that offers encouragement heading into a tougher assignment. They recorded five sacks, including one that produced a fumble recovery deep in Eagles territory. Rasul Douglas also intercepted a fourth-down pass, helping the Commanders finish a game in which they scored 27 unanswered points.“ LA Rams vs Washington Commanders: Three Matchups to Watch (sports.yahoo) “Jayden Daniels is playing really well over the last two weeks, ranking top ten in multiple categories and leading the league with zero turnovers. Through five games, he has thrown for 976 yards, six touchdowns, and zero interceptions on a 62.8% completion rate — and he has added 236 rushing yards and two scores on the ground. Daniels was 16-of-29 for 217 yards in the Sunday night win over Philadelphia, and he followed a 199 passing yard, 103 rushing yard, two score performance from week five with that gritty showing. Now he faces a Los Angeles Rams defense that will test whether the momentum is real. The Rams have shown they can pressure the quarterback and take away one side of the field, so Daniels’ ability to extend plays, work through progressions, and hit the deep ball will all be on display.“ Commanders vs Rams predictions, picks, odds for NFL Week 9 game Sunday (azcentral) “Which team has the best chance to win the game according to NFL Week 9 win probabilities ? Check out The Arizona Republic’s score projection for the Sunday football game, as well as Rams vs. Commanders picks , odds and win chances for the NFL Week 9 game , which can be seen at 11 a.m. MST on FOX ( stream with FUBO ).“ Rams pass rush poses major test for Commanders (cbssports) “Even absent Garrett, with Donald drawing attention in the middle, Young has been able to flourish. He’s got 4 1/2 sacks this season. “When you allocate resources to one elite premium player, he’s gonna get a one-on-one matchup,” Blough said. “We gotta be able to win on the perimeter. And he’s elite pass rusher, really good bull rush in this league and we gotta be ready for him.” While Young provides a challenge on the edge, Donald, who doesn’t have a sack this season, still can have a massive impact on how an opposing offense operates with an interior rush.“ Comment of the day: Feed post of the day:

title: Las Vegas Raiders-San Francisco 49ers FEED Topic: Who gets more touches between Mike Washington Jr., Ashton Jeanty?
summary: Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak made headlines during last week’s game against the New York Jets. Not for himself, but a decision he made with Las Vegas’ backfield. Kubiak didn’t just switch the Raiders’ lead running back between rookie Mike Washington Jr. and second-year pro Ashton Jeanty; he turned Washington into the feature […]
full_text: (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak made headlines during last week’s game against the New York Jets. Not for himself, but a decision he made with Las Vegas’ backfield. Kubiak didn’t just switch the Raiders’ lead running back between rookie Mike Washington Jr. and second-year pro Ashton Jeanty; he turned Washington into the feature back with 25 carries and made Jeanty the third-down option with just two carries and three catches. Now, heading into the Week 9 matchup against the San Francisco 49ers, the question arises of whether the workload split between Washington and Jeanty will continue . Some have speculated that Kubiak’s decision was punitive-based. Ahead of last week’s game, Jeanty gave the Jets ‘bulletin board material’ by saying that a few players on New York’s defense “don’t really want to tackle”. While the first-time head coach is still establishing his identity, he’s made it clear that he takes a ‘no-nonsense’ type of approach and doesn’t divulge much to the media to avoid situations like this. So, there’s reason to believe that the running back’s comments irked Kubiak and played a role in the former’s workload last Sunday. However, this Sunday will give us a better answer to see if the 25-to-2 (or 12.5-to-1) ratio of carries, or a similar type of split, continues. On Monday, the head coach indicated that the workload between the two backs could vary game to game. “I think it’s always a moving target,” he replied when asked if the Raiders will have a shared backfield moving forward. “See where your team’s at, and who’s playing the best ball at the time. And it’s a 17-game regular season where things change every week. And they’ve been changing at guard…That’s the NFL. “We have a young roster, and we’re going to give guys opportunities and see what fits us best. But your 11, whether you’re playing really well or not playing well at all, it’s always going to change a little bit.” Despite those comments, it’s hard to deny that the Raiders’ rushing attack did a better job of staying on schedule last week. Washington had 83 yards on his 25 carries, which comes out to 3.3 ypc. That’s pretty comparable to Jeanty’s 3.1 ypc for the season. But the rookie’s average was brought down by a handful of stuffed runs near the goal line. Also, Vegas’ EPA per rush was 0.11 points better last week than the team’s season average, and its success rate on the ground was 7.2% higher, per Sumer Sports . That being said, Washington’s lack of success in the red zone can’t be ignored. He’s averaging 1.2 ypc (17 attempts for 21 yards) inside the 20-yard line, per Sumer , and is viewed as more of a home-run hitter out of the backfield. Granted, Jeanty isn’t much better in the scoring area — 1.6 ypc (22 attempts for 36 yards) — but it is an improvement on a slightly bigger sample size. Also, he’s arguably the better option at getting the tough yards of the two backs. So, maybe Klint Kubiak’s formula moving forward is to have the rookie help get the offense into the red zone and then have the second-year pro take over with fresh legs. Of course, we won’t know the answer until Sunday’s game, which is why the topic is this week’s game day FEED discussion. Meanwhile, the 49ers have a very good defense that is great at stopping the run. San Francisco ranks fifth in the NFL with 89.0 rushing yards allowed per game and is second in EPA per rush allowed at negative 0.17 . Especially since the Jets were missing their best run defender last week, defensive tackle T’Vondre Sweat, this weekend will be a true test to see if the Raiders’ rushing attack improves with Washington as the lead back. So, for this week’s game day discussion on The FEED , we’ll be keeping tabs on how the carries are divided up in Las Vegas’ backfield. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on FOX (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

title: Raiders Week 9: 49ers explosive offense, stingy defense are imposing
summary: At 6-1 overall, it’s no surprise the San Francisco 49ers boast a Top 10 offense and defense at this particular juncture of the 2026 season. The Niners have the fourth-best scoring offense of the 32 NFL teams at 197 points per game and accumulated the sixth-highest total yards at 2,600. In addition, the team’s defense […]
full_text: (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images At 6-1 overall, it’s no surprise the San Francisco 49ers boast a Top 10 offense and defense at this particular juncture of the 2026 season. The Niners have the fourth-best scoring offense of the 32 NFL teams at 197 points per game and accumulated the sixth-highest total yards at 2,600. In addition, the team’s defense allows the sixth-least amount of points at 139 and the fourth-least amount of yards at 2,095. The Las Vegas Raiders’ Klint Kubiak and Rob Leonard will certainly have their hands full when the Silver & Black head to Santa Clara for a Week 9 matchup with the 49ers. The head coach and defensive coordinator, respectively, are the play callers for offense and defense and have the headset and play sheet to combat their counterparts in San Francisco head coach Kyle Shanahan and defensive coordinator Raheem Morris. Of the Raiders combo, Leonard has the tougher challenge trying to stymie Shanahan’s explosive offense that hasn’t skipped a beat even though injuries change the lineup. “Yeah, they do. They’re fundamentally sound, man,” Leonard said of the 49ers offense. “They’re a clean operation, and they got some good players. Quarterback’s playing at a high level, good tight end, running backs, and the offensive line is really good. So, that’s what jumps out to me, how fundamentally sound they are, and they’re able to put a lot of pressure on you.” With an accurate and collected quarterback in Brock Purdy, Shanahan funnels the offense through his signal caller and it’s one that attacks every level of the opposing defense. Very physical in the trenches, the offensive line buys Purdy the time to go through his progressions and get the ball to a target like tight end George Kittle. The 33-year-old veteran leads the team with 34 catches for 425 yards and five touchdowns and shows no signs of slowing down — as evidence by his 56-yard catch-and-run below: GEORGE. KITTLE. DENvsSF on CBS/Paramount+ Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/fynYAzwRMn — NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026 Shanahan’s ground game is domineering ranking eighth-best in yards (892) and third in rushing touchdowns (10) and bolsters his ability to open the full play book to deploy on the opponent. Christian McCaffrey paces the run game with 84 carries for 389 yards and eight touchdowns. Spell back Kaelon Black has 57 totes for 233 yards and a score while Purdy has scrambled for 161 yards and a touchdown on 32 attempts. As fundamentally sound Leonard says the 49ers are on offense, his Raiders defense must be equally as coherent — something Las Vegas has tumbled down the rankings as it lost four-straight games before a Week 8 win against the New York Jets to get to 4-4 overall. The Silver & Black are giving up the second-most points (230) and third-most yards (3,055). Leonard’s unit is ranked 25th against the pass with 1,884 yards allowed and 31st against the run with 1,171 yards yielded. The defensive play caller knows his crew has a lot to work on and can’t afford a lapse against a quality team like the Niners. Especially with San Francisco’s penchant to run outside zone runs and a multitude of pre-snap motions to create chaos. To combat this, Leonard is likely to use more single-high safety alignments for run fits and creatively blitz to ground the 49ers. Then — now don’t gasp if this brings past pain with the Raiders — maintain eye discipline is vital. The motions Shanahan habitually uses is intended to break coverages that end up explosive plays. Las Vegas can ill-afford to get “caught looking” against San Francisco, a team that’s deployed 21 personnel (two running backs and one tight end) to perfection at times this season. How Leonard counters with personnel is going to be intriguing. Perhaps going into sub packages built on speed and athleticism that brings slot corner Taron Johnson in the lineup is the route to go. Safeties Treydan Stukes and Jeremy Chinn have shown the ability to stop the run while Johnson is both a steady cover man and tackler over the middle. “Stack plays,” Leonard said when asked what was stressed during practice this week. “Really focusing on us, our alignment, our assignment, key technique, fundamentals, and it’s especially that time of the year where it’s hard to really out-scheme people. Everybody knows who they are, so you have to go out and execute.” DeForest Buckner vs Nick Bosa on the sled for the first time since the 2019 season! Both return to 49ers practice on the same day. A massive shot in the arm for this SF team pic.twitter.com/OZekoK5gNn — David Lombardi (@LombardiHimself) November 4, 2026 The chess game between the Raiders offense and 49ers defense is the marquee matchup for the Silver & Black. Unlike the defense, Kubiak concocted the sixth-best scoring offense in the league (221 points) that’s generated the 12th most yards (2,739). The aerial attack is third-best in the NFL with 2,121 yards and 19 touchdowns. Morris, meanwhile, is the architect of Niners’ sixth-ranked defense in points allowed (139) and fourth-ranked in yards allowed (2,095). Under Morris’ command, San Francisco has the fifth-best run defense allowing 623 yards and the second-least rushing touchdowns (three). With Las Vegas unable to get a consistent ground game going (31st in yards at 618), expect Kubiak to dial up creative passing concepts to get tight end (in-name-only) Brock Bowers loose against a 49ers defense that’s 11th-best in yards allowed (1,472) and 17th most touchdowns given up (10). “It’s a talented bunch. Been together for a long time. Experienced bunch,” Raiders offensive coordinator Andrew Janocko said of the 49ers defense. “It’s a team that have a lot of familiarity with playing against them last year. They’re well coached, well prepared. They attack the football. They’re very opportunistic. So, it’ll be a heck of a challenge for us against one of the best teams in the league.” With how disciplined 49ers defenders play, Las Vegas must win their blocking assignments to keep veteran quarterback Kirk Cousins upright to throw. And to ensure a more productive run game by establishing its own outside zone runs, the offensive line must anchor and push forward and not get stonewalled or driven backwards. A ground game that gains positive yards consistently allows play action to be truly effective — which is a staple of Kubiak’s offense. Head-to-Head Sunday’s clash marks the 16th time the Raiders and 49ers have met. The Niners lead the all-times series 8-7 (all regular season games) and the Las Vegas variant of the Silver & Black have played the Red & Gold only once: Back on New Year’s Day in 2023 which the 49ers won 37-34. San Francisco is riding a two-game win streak with the 2023 meeting the latest one and a 34-3 victory over the then-Oakland Raiders in 2018 being the other. The Raiders last win over the Niners arrived in 2014 — a 24-13 win in Oakland. Quote of Note “Another top five defense in the league. Feels like I’m saying that every week the last several weeks. I don’t know who the bottom five defenses are, but we’re not playing them. So, maybe someday. But what a challenge.” —Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Kirk Cousins on the Week 9 matchup

title: Battle of the Bay: Raider Nation versus Niner Gang
summary: The San Francisco 49ers host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday at Levi’s Stadium. The focus on this used to be bragging rights for Raider Nation vs. Niner Gang as both teams were Bay Area rivals until the Raiders moved to Las Vegas.  In the grand scheme of things, it’s just another game on the […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers host the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday at Levi’s Stadium. The focus on this used to be bragging rights for Raider Nation vs. Niner Gang as both teams were Bay Area rivals until the Raiders moved to Las Vegas. In the grand scheme of things, it’s just another game on the schedule for both teams. However, it’s a bigger game for the Raiders than the 49ers, as the Raiders need a statement win against a top team. Bringing a (4-4) record back to the Bay is cool and all, but for a fringe team on the outside looking in, it’s a measuring stick. Head coach Klint Kubiak is no stranger to playing and defeating the 49ers, but he is also a member of the Kyle Shanahan coaching tree. Black O vs Red D The strength of the Raiders is in their offense, specifically their passing game. However, since making the switch to Mike Washington Jr. as running back 1, with former first-round pick Ashton Jeanty as a complementary back, the rushing attack has picked up steam and a season-high 38 points were scored. Against the 49ers, the Raiders face one of the toughest defenses they have seen all season. As if that weren’t enough, it’s a defense starting to get its fangs back. While the 49ers defense may not be as great as it once was, it’s still plenty good enough to bully the Raiders offense. Fred Warner is still amongst the top dogs at linebacker, Dre Greenlaw is hitting anything not in the same colored jersey before and after the whistle. Nick Bosa is finally feeling healthy and the reacquisition of DeForest Buckner is ready to challenge the Raiders’ pass protection and newfound success on the ground. Where the game will be won Shanahan has turned the 49ers into perennial playoff contenders behind both an ever-evolving offense and a ferocious defense. Just when teams think they have the offense pegged, they find a different way to exploit the matchups and personnel and break them down. Kubiak was Shanahan’s former passing game coordinator. Now, his little brother, Klay Kubiak, is the offensive coordinator for the 49ers. Klay benefits from experimenting against a Top-5 NFL defense in practice every day. Sunday, he will be calling plays against one of the most underperforming defenses in the league. Furthermore, the 49ers offense relies on scheming players open, utilizing rhythm, timing and deception. All things that Rob Leonard and the Raiders’ defense have struggled with over the last five weeks. Leonard’s seat has to be getting hotter and hotter each week another team drops 30+ on his defense. Yes, this was the murderers’ row stretch of opponents. There are no excuses for losing; you are what your record says you are, and the Raiders are a .500 team because the offense is good and the defense isn’t. Sure, Leonard has the unenviable task of trying to corral a supremely efficient offensive machine. But they don’t call it “The Battle of the Bay” for no reason. Raider Nation v. Bang Bang Let’s be honest, life has been hard for Raider Nation. All the losing and watching members of the Nation convert to the Bang Bang Niner Gang. Why? Because the 49ers have had their stuff together and just kept winning. Growing up in the Bay Area, this rivalry means a little something extra. It is a little bit more personal than a divisional matchup because most Bay Area families and friends are split down the middle. Knocking those smug looks off the faces of the Niners Faithful just really warms the hearts of members of Raider Nation. The bragging rights silence endless ridicule and incessant reckless rambling, but not only that; it allows the Nation to hold their heads high no matter how the season ends, provided the 49ers don’t win it all.

title: Raiders wide receiver Week 8 snap and production review
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ won 38-33 at the New York Jets on Sunday. Let’s review how their wide receivers fared: Tre Tucker Tucker played a team high 54 percent of the snaps, a team high. Still, it was a season low for him. He had no receptions on one target. This came after a two-game […]
full_text: (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ won 38-33 at the New York Jets on Sunday . Let’s review how their wide receivers fared: Tre Tucker Tucker played a team high 54 percent of the snaps, a team high. Still, it was a season low for him. He had no receptions on one target. This came after a two-game stretch in which he had 10 catches for 200 yards and three scores. Jalen Nailor: The starter played 46 percent of the snaps, a week after he played 75 percent of the snaps. He did, however, have his best game as he caught four passes on four targets for 38 yards and a score. Maybe less is more for Nailor, who had eight catches for 75 yards on 20 targets going into Sunday’s game. Jack Bech: The 2025 second-round draft pick returned from a four-game stint on the injured reserve. He played 40 percent of the snaps. Yet, he wasn’t targeted. Dareke Young: He played five offensive snap. He didn’t have any targets. Cody White: White played two snaps with no targets. He was released Wednesday and tight end Carter Runyon was activated. Then, Thursday, White was re-signed and Runyon was released. Conclusion: Nailor was the only Las Vegas wide receiver with a reception and they were targeted just five times. However, tight end Brock Bowers had six catches for 87 yards while lined up as a receiver, according to Next Gen Stats, the most for an NFL tight end in 10 seasons. We will see if that trend continues. But the Raiders need to get the ball to Tucker and Bech needs to show he deserves to be on the field. With White gone, maybe Dont’e Thornton or Malik Benson will be active Sunday.

title: Brock Bowers’ numbers will just keep going up
summary: The working relationship between new Las Vegas Raiders’ head coach and offensive playcaller Klint Kubiak and star tight end Brock Bowers is already working brilliantly and it will likely only get better. This offseason, an impressed Kubiak famously called his new toy a football robot from heaven. So far, their results together have been pretty […]
full_text: (Photo by Al Bello/Getty Images) | Getty Images The working relationship between new Las Vegas Raiders’ head coach and offensive playcaller Klint Kubiak and star tight end Brock Bowers is already working brilliantly and it will likely only get better. This offseason, an impressed Kubiak famously called his new toy a football robot from heaven . So far, their results together have been pretty unworldly. Bowers already has 41 catches for 547 yards. He missed the first two games of the seoans with a knee injury and the 2024 No. 13 overall pick is still second in the NFL in receptions among tight ends. His 13.3 per catch average is leading the NFL among tight ends. Bowers is on pace to have 102 catches for 1,366 yards and 12 touchdowns in 15 games. When he broke every rookie tight end record, Bowers had 112 catches for 1,194 yards and 5 touchdowns in 17 games. Kubiak is using Bowers as a wide receiver often and they are exploiting defenses. The working relationship is only going to get better and expect Bowers’ eye-popping numbers to only get more gaudy.

summary: The 4-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Kickoff is set at 1:25 p.m. PT. full_text: (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 4-4 Las Vegas Raiders play at the 6-1 San Francisco 49ers on Sunday. Kickoff is set at 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to an upset victory: Stop McCaffrey: The Raiders have been getting gashed weekly on the ground. Christian McCaffrey awaits. This can get ugly. Get turnovers: This is how Las Vegas can pull off an upset. They need to get back to their early-seaosn ways of creating multiple turnovers. Red-zone offense: The Raiders are likely going to have to score a lot of points in this game. So, they can’t settle for field goals. They were four-for-four in the red zone in a win at the Jets last wee after being a combined three-for-10 in the previous two games, which were both defeats. They need to cash in when they can. Better cornerback play: The Jets and Geno Smith picked on the Raiders’ cornerbacks last week. Brock Purdy can be a surgeon. We need to see a bounce-back game from this group. Beat a good team: We know the story of the Raiders so far this season. They can’t beat good teams but they take care of business against lousy teams. At some point, they must beat a quality opponent. This is as good as any week to start.

After a disappointing 9-8 record in 2025 leading to a fourth-place finish in the NFC North, Detroit is looking to return to the form that brought them back-to-back division titles in 2023 and 2024. The NFC North is a tough division, however, with all four teams above the .500 mark and having won at least five times already this season. How will Sunday’s game play out? This week, I am not as bullish on the Dolphins’ chances. The Lions are the better team in this matchup, and I think they’ll cover the 6.5-point spread, even with the injuries they are facing. Miami will play the Lions tough, and they might keep it close for much of the game, but in the end, I think the Lions pull away. Prop Bets Any time touchdown scorer: Ollie Gordon II Yes: +100 The Dolphins running game ran into a speedbump against the Patriots. It will not be easy, Detroit has the ninth-ranked rush defense in the league, allowing just 96.6 yards per game. The Dolphins will have to be deliberate in getting the ball to Gordon, continue to feed him even if they are getting stuffed early, and make this a physical game. In the end, I think Gordon will be able to find the endzone at least once in this game and this prop hits. Sam LaPorta receiving yards: 48.5 Over : -114 Under: -114 Miami has struggled covering tight ends this season, and they face another who could cause problems in LaPorta. They have allowed four tight ends to surpass the 48.5 yards mark (T.J. Hockenson, 119 yards; George Kittle, 80 yards; Mason Taylor, 62 yards; Travis Kelce, 59 yards) and would have had five on that list if Hunter Henry had not been injured in the second quarter Patriots game (3 receptions, 30 yards when he departed). Unless Miami comes with a different scheme to handle tight ends, LaPorta reaching 49 yards receiving seems likely. title: Miami Dolphins vs. Detroit Lions: Three Reasons Why
summary: The Miami Dolphins will be back in Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium to face the Detroit Lions this Sunday.  The good news? For the first time all season, the Dolphins will not have to go back out onto the road after a home game.  The bad news?  They face a hot Detroit Lions team.  Do […]
full_text: The Miami Dolphins will be back in Joe Robbie Hard Rock Stadium to face the Detroit Lions this Sunday. The good news? For the first time all season, the Dolphins will not have to go back out onto the road after a home game. The bad news? They face a hot Detroit Lions team. Do they have a chance? Mebbe . 3 REASONS FOR HOPE MALIK WILLIS IS IMPROVING Locked On Dolphins covered an aspect of this much more deeply than I can in an article, so I’ll let you watch for yourself . Willis was nothing short of atrocious the 1st 5 games. He had moments but was overall bad. But in the past 2 games, we have seen Willis take a step forward. I’ve listed my preferred stats in previous posts so let’s compare Willis’ 1st 5 games to the last 2 games in those stats. In the 1st five games, Willis had a completion percentage of 56.2% – completing 73 of his 130 attempts. In the last 2 games, Willis has a completion percentage of 66% – completing 35 of 53 pass attempts. In the 1st five games, Willis had a YPA of 6.53. In the last 2 games, he has a YPA of 7.91. He threw 2 TDs on 130 attempts for a TD% of 1.5%. In the last 2 games, he has 4 TDs on 53 attempts, for a TD% of 7.5%. Weeks 1-5, he had 4 INTs in 130 attempts for an INT% of 3.1%. The last 2 weeks, he has 1 INT in 53 attempts, which is an INT% of 1.9%. This is drastic improvement across the board. Two games don’t erase the previous five and I’m not saying he has suddenly gone from Joe Dirt to Joe Montana. But I said in the offseason he should be considered an “experienced rookie”. And like most rookies, there has been bumps in the road but also some growth. The next step is to maintain that growth and sustain these increased averages. But not only is there statistical improvement, he has become a vocal leader. Willis is a reserved man and doesn’t have a fiery disposition. But his interaction with Ollie Gordon II on the sideline after Gordon’s penalty and what was said after that shows a level of leadership I haven’t seen from a Dolphins’ quarterback in YEARS. It’s an impressive display for a young QB trying to find his footing and become a great player and a franchise QB. They don’t HAVE to listen to him, but that interaction shows that they do. THE REST OF THE OFFENSE IS GETTING BETTER The Dolphins started the season very rough on the offensive side of the ball. The were averaging 11.5 PPG the 1st 4 weeks of the season. In the last 3 games, they average 23.7 PPG. That would be 12th best if that were the season. In the 1st 4 games, they average 267.5 yards per game. In the last 3 games, they averaged 320 yards per game. Getting Caleb Douglas back helped, but we’ve also seen development and improvement from other WRs like Malik Washington – who is creating more separation than I would have expected – and Kevin Coleman Jr., who roasted a Pats DB for his 2nd TD of the season. Greg Dulcich is getting more involved. Gordon had a rougher day at the office against a stout NE run defense, but he is still on pace for a 1000-yard season and maybe he gets double digit TDs. It’s a young and growing offense that will have its fair share of issues, like we saw in the 3rd quarter last week. But they are getting better and now face… THE LIONS DEFENSE IS STRUGGLING So far this season, the Dolphins have faced 4 of the top 10 scoring defenses. They have faced 4 of the top 10 passing defenses in passing yards allowed. They have faced 3 of the top 10 rushing defenses in yards per attempt allowed. The Lions will not be any of those. The Lions have the 31st ranked pass defense in yards allowed, with 1936, and 32nd in passing yards per game allowed at 276.6. They are 26th in passer rating allowed at 101.0, 22nd in completion percentage allowed at 65.9, and 19th in YPA allowed at 7.3. They are tied for last with 18 passing TDs allowed. They have the 2nd highest ADOT for defender at 9.5, meaning teams are passing deeper on them. They are solid tacklers, with the fewest missed tackles at 15 and are 5th in YAC allowed, but the Dolphins should have some success in the air against the Lions. On the ground, the Lions are 6th in rushing yards allowed at 676 but also have the 3rd fewest attempts against them at 163. They allow 96.6 rushing yards per game and allowed 4.1 YPC. As a scoring defense, the Lions rank just ahead of Miami (25.9 PPG), allowing 25.7 PPG. Miami’s offense will have opportunities to move the ball and score. 3 REASONS FOR CONCERN THE LIONS’ PASS RUSH IS STILL STRONG Overall, the Lions’ defense looks like a weakness Miami could exploit. But the Lions can get after the QB very well. The Lions have 3 players with 4 or more sacks, led by standout edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson. One of those players is IDL Alim McNeill and strong interior pass rushers have given Miami issues. McNeill is ESPN’s top IDL pass rusher, with a win rate of 27%. As a team, the Lions rank 3rd in PRWR at 59%. Perhaps Kadyn Proctor’s return can mitigate that problem, but after last week, I’m skeptical. The Lions as a team are third in sacks with 24 and tied for 10th in pressure percentage at 24.8%. The Lions don’t blitz at a high rate, ranking 17th at 25.7%, so most of those pressures are generated with a 4-man rush. Miami’s OL will need to play much better than last week if they want to capitalize on the weaknesses of the Lions defense. MIAMI’S PASS RUSH FACES A TOUGH TEST The Dolphins’ defense has slowly started to move up the rankings of pressure percentage, currently 22nd at 21.1%. They are still on the bottom of the barrel in terms of sacks, tied with KC and NYG with 9. However, they have had at least 2 sacks in 3 of the past 4 games. Chop Robinson has come on with 4 sacks and leads the league in pressure percentage individually and has the best pass rush win rate . Unfortunately, the Lions have one of the best OLs in the league at stopping pressure. They rank 7th as a team in PBWR at 54% (see the previous link). PFF ranks them 1st and highlighted that the Lions’ OL only allowed 4 pressures last week to the league leading Vikings, who get a pressure 35% of the time. Both of Detroit’s OTs are top 20 in PBWR (Paul has dropped out of the top 20). The Dolphins and Jeff Hafley may need to get creative with pressure packages and blitz plans in order to get to Jared Goff. THE LIONS ARE A VERY DANGEROUS OFFENSE The Dolphins have faced some scary offenses this season, but none present the total package that Detroit presents. The Chiefs have Mahomes and Walker, but don’t have elite receivers. Cincy has Burrow and elite WRs, but their run game isn’t special. The Lions have all of it. They’re 4th in the league in total yards at 2768, but the 3 teams ahead of them have played an additional game. They average 395.4 yards per game and 5.9 yards per play, tied for 5th. They are 4th in passing yards per game at 264.0 and 7th in rushing yards per game at 131.4. Goff is completing 67.7% of his passes, 5th best. He’s thrown 15 TDs and only 1 INT. Jahmyr Gibbs is 2nd in the league in attempts with 157, and 2nd in rushing yards with 773. He has 8 rushing TDs, tied with several for 3rd, and leads the league in both yards per game at 110.4 and attempts per game at 22.4. Gibbs also has 2 receiving TDs. Amon-Ra St. Brown is 5th in the league in receptions with 53, 10th in yards with 571, and tied for 6th in TDs with 5. One of those he is tied with is his teammate Jameson Williams. Williams doesn’t have the volume, with only 27 catches, but has 437 yards, meaning a 16.2 YPC average. Of WRs with more than 20 catches, only Tee Higgins, Christian Watson, Rome Odunze, and Tre Tucker have a higher YPC average. TE Sam LaPorta is tied with Williams and Gibbs in targets with 44 and has added 31 catches, 367 yards, and 3 TDs. Those 4 players are Detroit’s primary weapons. Only one other RB on the team – Sione Vaki – has any rushing attempts and all other pass catchers have 36 combined targets. The Lions know who they are, what they have, and they lean heavily on it. They are successful with it.…

title: 5 Things I Think I Think About the Miami Dolphins After Week 8
summary: Let’s start with the bad news. The Miami Dolphins are 1-6, having scored the second-fewest points in the entire league. (Who’s scored the fewest? Thank you for asking. It’s the winless Los Angeles Chargers, whose offense is led by our old friend, Mike McDaniel. There’s a lesson in there somewhere.) Young, developing teams can be […]
full_text: Let’s start with the bad news. The Miami Dolphins are 1-6, having scored the second-fewest points in the entire league. (Who’s scored the fewest? Thank you for asking. It’s the winless Los Angeles Chargers, whose offense is led by our old friend, Mike McDaniel. There’s a lesson in there somewhere.) Young, developing teams can be hard to watch sometimes, but they can also be rewarding if you know what to look for. So with that in mind, here are five things I think I think after Week 8. There’s a Good Team in There Somewhere For one glorious half, the Dolphins looked like a quality, well-coached football team. Their defense forced a fumble deep in Patriots territory. After trading field goals through most of the first half, they drove 70 yards for a touchdown, spreading the ball around to Greg Dulcich, Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman before connecting with Malik Washington for a short touchdown just before the break. Perhaps unsurprisingly, things unraveled in the second half. The Patriots made adjustments the Dolphins couldn’t counter, and (as we’ll discuss shortly) Miami made so many self-inflicted mistakes that it couldn’t overcome them. But it’s hard not to wonder: If the Dolphins can build a double-digit lead over a playoff contender like the Patriots while making so many unforced errors, what happens when they stop making them? That Said, the Dolphins Are Still Making Rookie Mistakes Playing against a Mike Vrabel-led team isn’t going to be easy. Any lapses in communication on either side of the ball are going to be exploited, and the Dolphins weren’t exactly on their A game. On one of Malik Willis’ five (!) sacks, Douglas and Bell ended up running to … the same area of the field. After stopping the Patriots’ offense to open the second half, the Dolphins had a chance to extend their lead. Instead, on third-and-9, Willis’ pass at the sticks doinked off Dulcich’s helmet. And at the end of the third quarter, two defenders covered the option on Drake Maye’s goal-line read-option, leaving Maye free to waltz untouched into the end zone. It didn’t cost them much, I suppose, but a wide-open Jaylen Wright also dropped an easy pass. (And no, I’m not emotionally ready to talk about Ollie Gordon’s unsportsmanlike penalty.) These are fixable mistakes, but they cost the Dolphins a winnable game against a division opponent. Malik Willis Is Becoming Part of the Solution OK, so 19 points doesn’t seem like much of an answer to the torches-and-pitchforks crowd around these parts three weeks ago. And even after two games of noticeable improvement, I don’t think we’re anywhere near being able to say, “Hey, let’s not spend an early-round 2027 pick on a quarterback.” That said, 21-of-32 for 211 yards, two touchdowns and a deflected interception? That’s “pass”able (ha ha) for a quarterback playing with little help from the running game and under pressure for much of the afternoon. More to the point, Willis is starting to do what professional quarterbacks do: throw the ball away, take the easy yards when they’re there and avoid putting the ball in harm’s way. (Though I see we’re still sliding behind the line of scrimmage for a sack instead of throwing the ball away, so there’s still some growth that needs to happen.) It’s a small thing, but a necessary one if you want to see continued development. I’m eager to see how he performs against the Lions this week. Kadyn Proctor’s Importance Is No Longer Theoretical In my Tracking the Guards series, I’ve talked a lot about how people who understand offensive line play have been impressed with Proctor’s development this year, even if his PFF grades don’t always reflect it. But if you really want to judge how well a player is performing, look at how the team does when he’s not in the lineup. Proctor missed the Patriots game while in concussion protocol. His replacement, Jarrett Kingston, played fine, but Proctor’s absence was noticeable. Without him, the Dolphins’ running game lacked its power. There were far fewer instances of linebackers getting neutralized, and the Patriots’ safeties and second-level defenders had a much easier time disrupting the offense. Proctor is expected back in the lineup against the Lions, and it’s clear the team needs him. It’s Not Always Pretty, but the Rebuild Seems To Be Working Just look at all the players 25 or younger who are either starting or playing meaningful snaps: Patrick Paul. Caleb Douglas. Malik Washington. Kevin Coleman. Chris Bell. Kadyn Proctor. Jacob Rodriguez. Michael Taaffe. Chris Johnson. Chop Robinson. Jordan Phillips. Jonah Savaiinaea. You could probably throw in Kenny Grant, Dante Trader, Jason Marshall and Zeek Biggers, too. That’s an incredible amount of development time, and it’s time that isn’t being spent (or wasted) on players like Jonnu Smith or Jalen Ramsey. And, with a few notable exceptions, they’ve largely stayed healthy, too. They’re getting the reps they need to grow into the players we want them to be. Those reps are also producing penalties and blown assignments, but that’s part of the growth process, too. So, yeah, 1-6 isn’t much fun, and it’s definitely not fun listening to pundits talk about how the Dolphins’ future opponents are going to have a field day playing them. But the growth and talent development are exciting to watch, and to me, much more rewarding than what we’ve seen in recent years: older players underperforming and getting hurt. I like this version better.

According to Miami’s head coach, Jeff Hafley, Proctor will return to the team’s starting lineup this Sunday […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NV - SEPTEMBER 13: Miami Dolphins offensive tackle Kadyn Proctor (74) walks off of the field after a NFL regular season game between the Las Vegas Raiders and Miami Dolphins at Allegiant Stadium, Sunday September 13, 2026 in Las Vegas, NV. (Photo by Jordon Kelly/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Miami Dolphins’ starting left guard, rookie Kadyn Proctor, missed the team’s week 8 contest against the New England Patriots due to a concussion the young player suffered the previous week in a win over the New York Jets. According to Miami’s head coach, Jeff Hafley, Proctor will return to the team’s starting lineup this Sunday when Miami hosts the Detroit Lions. Speaking with the South Florida media on Friday, Hafley said, “ Proctor is clear, ” when asked about the rookie’s availability for Sunday’s game. In his absence, Miami’s offensive line struggled against a stout Patriots front — allowing 5 sacks and managing just 74 yards rushing on 20 attempts (just 3.7 yards per carry). Proctor’s return against the Lions provides a bit of intrigue — as Detroit was heavily rumored to be big fans of the Alabama product coming out of college. Numerous mock drafts had the Lions taking him with the 17th pick in the 1st round of the 2026 NFL Draft — before Dolphins’ general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan pounced and took Proctor with the 12th pick. The Lions settled for right tackle Blake Miller out of Clemson. We will continue to keep you updated on all things Miami Dolphins as the team looks to secure their second victory on the season when they host Jared Goff, Jahmyr Gibbs, Amon-Ra St. Brown and the rest of the Detroit Lions on Sunday.

title: Week 9 Preview: From Wentz We Were
summary: The Minnesota Vikings return home to U.S. Bank Stadium to face the Buffalo Bills in a rematch of the most memorable regular-season game in years: a thrilling 33-30 overtime road win in 2022. Will the Vikings repeat their magic on Monday Night? Hey, can you believe it’s already November? Time sure does fly, doesn’t it? […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 13: Justin Jefferson #18 of the Minnesota Vikings catches a pass in front of Cam Lewis #39 of the Buffalo Bills during the fourth quarter at Highmark Stadium on November 13, 2022 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Timothy T Ludwig/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings return home to U.S. Bank Stadium to face the Buffalo Bills in a rematch of the most memorable regular-season game in years: a thrilling 33-30 overtime road win in 2022. Will the Vikings repeat their magic on Monday Night? Hey, can you believe it’s already November? Time sure does fly, doesn’t it? VIKINGS ON OFFENSE There’s not much more to say that I didn’t cover a few days ago. To be honest, I’m exhausted by it all. Sitting here in Week 9, still sorting this mess out, is really an indictment of Kevin O’Connell and the entire offensive staff. Things need to be fixed, and fast. The Kurt Warner film breakdown video below has been circulating here at the DN and across social media over the past few days. To recap, Kyler Murray has made some nice plays, but he’s missing far too many opportunities. It simply hasn’t been good enough, especially given the weak defenses he’s been facing. Per ESPN’s Bill Barnwell, Murray’s 44.9 QBR through Week 8 ranks just 26th when adjusted for the cupcake units he’s faced. In true Vikings fashion, the schedule was set up beautifully for the offense to find its rhythm before things got tougher, and we flushed the opportunity down the toilet. The last time we faced anything that resembled a “good” defense was the Tampa Bay Buccaneers five weeks ago. As I’m writing this, it’s official: Kevin O’Connell announced that Carson Wentz will start Monday night in place of the injured Murray. Max Brosmer will be the backup. Hmmm. Oh, I’ll just say it: If Wentz plays well, barring an injury or trade, he’ll remain the starter. I believe KOC may have said otherwise, but may I present, as Exhibit 1A, past statements about young quarterbacks and a fella named J.J. McCarthy. Wentz should be an upgrade over his season in the system, given his proven ability to move the ball efficiently. He passed for over 300 yards twice in four starts last year before KOC famously threw him out there against the Chargers in Week 8, while uttering the famous words of Ivan Drago: “If he dies, he dies.” He also, of course, played essentially two games for us this year, going 23-for-39 (59%) for 276 yards (7.08 avg), 3 TDs, and 0 INTs (though a couple of possible ones were dropped). That’s good for a 106.4 QB rating. That’s…okay, but he’ll need to do more if he’s indeed the guy from here on out. Unlike Murray, he does have a proven track record of getting the ball to Justin Jefferson, at least. So that’s something. No doubt Jefferson smiled when he heard the news. Enter the Buffalo Bills, and, will you look at this, another weak defense for us to possibly step on a rake against. Yippee. They rank 23rd in EPA/play, 24th in points allowed (25.9), 24th in total yards allowed (352.1), and 30th in passing yards allowed (254.7). They’re better against the run (10th), but that may be more about how easily teams have been able to pass against them. Wentz should have opportunities against a porous Bills pass defense, so for goodness’ sake, let’s hope we can finally see some life. The fans need it, and, most of all, an overstressed defense needs it. The pressure to hold teams under 20 to have any shot at winning games, given an offense channeling leather-helmet-era output, has to take its toll. VIKINGS ON DEFENSE Brian Flores and company face what may be their toughest challenge to date in containing Josh Allen and the Bills offense. The Lions are great, but Allen’s mobility and ability to extend plays add an enormous challenge. While he may not be Jahmyr Gibbs, James Cook III is no slouch, averaging 5.1 yards per carry and 101 yards per game. Their receiving corps is solid, if unspectacular. Khalil Shakir, Keon Coleman, and old Viking nemesis D.J. Moore lead the wideouts, while tight end Dalton Kincaid leads the Bills in receiving yards per game (57.3) and can be a real red-zone menace. But let’s be real: the Bills offense is Josh Allen. For my money, he’s the league’s best quarterback, and he’s playing like it. He’s leading an attack that’s 1st in EPA/play, 2nd in total yards, 2nd in yards per play, 3rd in rushing yards, and 10th in passing yards. They’re also near the top of the league in red zone and 3rd-down percentages, respectively. This is a true strength-vs.-strength battle against the Vikings’ defense. They remain 1st in EPA/play, points per game, success rate allowed, Pass EPA/play, and passing yards allowed. They’re only 2nd in yards allowed per game. What gives, Flores!? Of course, we’ve been vulnerable to the run in a couple of games this year, and the unit’s rankings took a hit after giving up a whopping 230 yards to the Lions last week. We’re now 17th in rushing yards allowed per game and are giving up 4.5 yards per carry. If my concern level for the offense is a 10, I’d put this at a solid 2 right now. They’ll get this straightened out soon enough, but, as noted, this week will bring another challenge. Indeed, you’d think the two priorities for this week would be, first, to keep Cook contained on early downs, which would repeatedly force Allen and the Bills’ offense into the pressure cooker of 3rd-and-long against the blitz and our elite coverage unit. Second, to (as much as possible) keep Allen contained in the pocket in those likely passing situations. If he buys himself time outside the pocket, more often than not you’re toast. Conversely, I’d be shocked if the Bills don’t test our shaky run defense early and often in this one to avoid those very scenarios. In addition, what makes the Bills’ offense so dangerous is their ability to convert 4th-and-short situations with Allen, who, at over 6’ 5” and nearly 240 pounds, is nearly impossible to stuff at the line of scrimmage. This can not only extend drives but also frustrate and demoralize a defense. If we’re to win this one, I can’t see us doing it without creating a turnover or two. The good news is that Allen does suffer from a bit of Stafforditis – i.e., elite QBs who are prone to throwing some head-scratching INTs. Hopefully, the pressure Flores will bring will help. James Cook has also had problems holding onto the ball this year, with four fumbles already, so there’s that, too. PREDICTION Wentz starting gives me a bit more confidence we can pull off the upset, but I can’t, in good conscience, pick the Vikings to win this game until I see something – anything – that resembles consistency from the offense. Scoring 24 points consistently shouldn’t be this difficult with our skill players. Wentz did make the most of the short fields the Packers gave us in Week 1, getting us to 39 points. Sure, there were TD drives of 1 play for 1 yard, 3 plays for 14 yards, and 6 plays for 28 yards. But we also had a 9-play, 83-yard scoring drive! It’s like the ‘98 Vikings and ‘99 Rams rolled into one! Holding Allen and the Bills offense under 20 in this game may require Flores to paint another masterpiece like the Week 17 game against the Lions last year at U.S. Bank Stadium. Can it happen? Absolutely. Will it happen? Ehhh, you can’t count on it. Regardless, it’d be nice not to have to rely on that every week, wouldn’t it? My guess: Wentz injects some much-needed life into the offense, but we come up short. Reverse psychology initiated. Buffalo Bills: 26 Minnesota Vikings: 24

Note: only starters on IR are listed. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. title: O’Connell Must Adapt or the Offense Stays Stuck
summary: The Minnesota Vikings face a quarterback crisis: Carson Wentz starts Monday with Kyler Murray injured. Kevin O’Connell made it official — Wentz will start against the Buffalo Bills while Murray recovers from hamstring tightness suffered against the Detroit Lions. But is this a one-week stopgap or a soft benching? On this episode of The Real […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - OCTOBER 25: Head coach Kevin O'Connell of the Minnesota Vikings looks on prior to the start of the game against the Indianapolis Colts at U.S. Bank Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by David Berding/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Minnesota Vikings face a quarterback crisis: Carson Wentz starts Monday with Kyler Murray injured. Kevin O’Connell made it official — Wentz will start against the Buffalo Bills while Murray recovers from hamstring tightness suffered against the Detroit Lions. But is this a one-week stopgap or a soft benching? On this episode of The Real Forno Show , Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano break down what the Wentz start means, the mounting frustration with O’Connell’s offensive scheme, the looming trade deadline, and the J.J. McCarthy situation that won’t go away. This is for any Vikings fan searching for answers during a season that started 6-0 and now feels like it’s slipping through their fingers. Tyler Forness doesn’t mince words about the state of the offense. After Wes Phillips publicly blamed player execution for the offensive struggles, Tyler pushed back hard: “At a certain point, the execution isn’t on the players, it’s on the coaches.” He compared O’Connell to a brilliant physics teacher who couldn’t connect with his students: “Who cares if you’re smart? The ones who design systems and call plays that get first downs, field goals, touchdowns — that’s who the smartest guys in the room are. It’s time to put the ego away, Kevin.” The core issue is that O’Connell’s system demands anticipatory throws over the middle of the field — throws that Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold made routinely but Murray consistently turns down. As Tyler put it: “The problem isn’t that he can’t see. The problem is that he can see and isn’t throwing it.” Meanwhile, Justin Jefferson is averaging fewer than seven targets per game, a number Tyler finds unacceptable given that Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba are seeing 12 targets a game elsewhere. On Wentz, Tyler is measured: “He’s good enough to keep you stable for a game or two. He’s one of the top five backup guys I would want.” But he’s clear-eyed about the ceiling: “Carson Wentz is what he is, and he’s been that way for years now.” Key Points from the Episode: Carson Wentz will start Monday vs. Buffalo Bills; Max Brosmer backs up. Kyler Murray’s hamstring injury is not considered long-term. Tyler does not believe this is a soft benching — O’Connell explicitly committed to Murray as the starter when asked by Dan Mizutani. Wes Phillips’ comments blaming players for poor execution drew sharp criticism from Tyler, who argued the coaching staff needs to look inward. O’Connell showed he could adapt to Murray’s skill set before the bye week, then reverted to his preferred system afterward — what Tyler called the “arrogant part of this whole conversation.” The Vikings lack the cap space to make splash trades at the deadline. Nolan Teasley has four paths: stand pat, add a small piece, make a blockbuster, or sprinkle in minor upgrades. Tyler’s dream trade target: Jalen Carter. A realistic target: a blocking tight end or nose tackle like Grover Stewart via a late-round pick swap. J.J. McCarthy is done in Minnesota. Tyler revealed: “They were done with J.J. McCarthy. They were done the second they named him the third-string quarterback.” The decision stemmed from off-field processing concerns, not talent — Tyler described the relationship with O’Connell as “oil and water.” The 2024 Vikings parallel the 2017 season’s quarterback uncertainty with Teddy Bridgewater, Case Keenum, and Sam Bradford — different details, same anxiety. Listen: View Link Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: If you’re a Vikings fan trying to make sense of a season that started with Super Bowl aspirations and now has you questioning everything, this episode of The Real Forno Show is essential listening. Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano deliver the unfiltered film analysis, cap-space breakdowns, and trade-deadline speculation you won’t find anywhere else in the Vikings media landscape. Subscribe on YouTube, join the Discord, and become a paid subscriber for behind-the-scenes trade-deadline intel Tyler shares only with members. Fan with Us!!! Tyler Forness @TheRealForno of Vikings 1st & SKOL @Vikings1stSKOL and A to Z Sports @AtoZSportsNFL , with Dave Stefano @Luft_Krigare producing this Vikings 1st & SKOL production, the @RealFornoShow found at the @BleavNetwork . So here’s the question, Vikings fans: Do you trust Kevin O’Connell to fix this offense, or is it time to admit the system is the problem?
