title: 3-Point Stance: Patriots’ trade deadline isn’t time for a youth movement
summary: Are the New England Patriots sellers at the NFL trade deadline? Last week, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer highlighted defensive tackle Christian Barmore and cornerback Carlton Davis as potential Patriots trade candidates ahead of the deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10. According to Breer, if a deal is struck, New England’s motivation would be centered around adding […]
full_text: Are the New England Patriots sellers at the NFL trade deadline? Last week, Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer highlighted defensive tackle Christian Barmore and cornerback Carlton Davis as potential Patriots trade candidates ahead of the deadline on Tuesday, Nov. 10. According to Breer, if a deal is struck, New England’s motivation would be centered around adding draft capital and transitioning into a younger roster. Though based on his response when speaking with the media on Wednesday, head coach Mike Vrabel appears to disagree with that approach. “I think sometimes national reports have the tendency to do that. I have not shared that information with anybody,” Vrabel said. “This time of year, I think that all these things kind of get drummed up. So, we’re focused on trying to prepare for [the Green Bay Packers on Sunday] and make the corrections from [last week]. “This is business as normal here, so I don’t know where a lot of these things come from. Certainly not from any conversations with me.” Regardless of whether or not the Patriots strike a deal involving either player, trading almost any impact contributor on the roster while sitting at a 5-3 record at the regular season’s midway point is certainly questionable. At the least, a deal of that stature calls for a corresponding “buying” move. Sure, New England’s depth in multiple areas will be a largely discussed topic throughout the offseason regarding the team’s roster-building process. And rightfully so. Vrabel said it himself after a preseason victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, stating at the time that he doesn’t think his team is “very deep.” But sending away either Barmore or Davis simply doesn’t make sense at this time. Especially for a franchise still in contention for the AFC East title. Trading Barmore creates another need In 2023, Barmore posted his best season as a pro, recording 8.5 sacks, 16 quarterback hits and pressuring those passers 49 times. He also consistently disrupted opposing run offenses, forcing 13 tackles for a loss and totaling 64 combined takedowns. That season-long performance earned the Patriots’ 2021 second-round draft selection a four-year, $84 million contract extension the following offseason. Currently in year two of that new deal, Barmore’s production hasn’t entirely matched the monetary value of his contract, especially in run defense. From just last season, the 27-year-old has seen his involvement in that facet of the defense drop from 62.8% to just 36%. Still, New England evidently continues to view Barmore as a producer when rushing the quarterback, heavily using the defensive tackle during pass-rush downs and critical third-down plays. Barmore’s overall reduced role also doesn’t mean he’s expendable. Trading him shuffles the defensive line, forcing Cory Durden into a new, pass-rush-heavy role and 34-year-old DaQuan Jones, who has contributed as a relief piece for the primary starters, into a heavier workload. Davis’ departure would leave a hole in the secondary As for Davis, the cornerback hasn’t shown signs of regression. But the soon-to-be 30-year-old, entering the final year of his contract with a mighty injury history and owed $22 million in 2027, plays directly into the youth-movement argument. Nonetheless, shipping him off to another franchise creates a glaring hole in the cornerback room. That decision then forces Vrabel and the defensive coaching staff to decide between starting substitute Charles Woods opposite Christian Gonzalez or pulling Marcus Jones away from his natural nickel-cornerback position. With several offenses in the Patriots’ remaining schedule currently ranking top 10 in passing yards per game, that potential decision seems counterproductive. Davis, who recently returned to the starting lineup last week after missing four games, played a significant role in New England’s divisional round victory against the Houston Texans in the playoffs last season, intercepting C.J. Stroud twice. The offseason offers a better time to make a move It’s true that the Patriots’ defense has struggled to deliver on the expectations surrounding their offseason additions of Dre’Mont Jones, All-Pro safety Kevin Byard and second-round pick Gabe Jacas. But much like the rest of the roster, that group has dealt with injuries. Last week’s matchup against the Miami Dolphins marked the first game the starting cornerback trio of Gonzalez, Davis and Jones all played together since Week Three. While the healthy defense didn’t put together a flawless performance, the unit signaled improvement, sacking Malik Willis on five occasions, logging an interception and forcing the Miami offense into four three-and-out possessions. Teams can afford slow starts, and while there’s no guarantee New England will find its stride later in the season, the ability to play its best football down the stretch is what ultimately matters the most. In Barmore’s case, as the Boston Herald’s Andrew Callahan put it , the Patriots seemingly want “out of the Barmore business.” An offseason deal, rather than a midseason trade, allows New England greater flexibility to reallocate resources and explore replacements to replicate or improve upon Barmore’s production while spending less. Even though eventually moving Barmore or another established contributor makes sense for the team’s long-term roster construction, the Patriots’ timing of a potential trade should account for the franchise’s current position in the AFC playoff picture.

summary: New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson revealed Friday that he has been dealing with a neurological medical condition that resulted in hospitalization. Henderson was first listed on the injury report with an illness last Thursday, Oct. 29, and has been away from the team since. Head coach Mike Vrabel said the team has not […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - DECEMBER 01: Head coach Mike Vrabel of the New England Patriots speaks with TreVeyon Henderson #32 prior to the game against the New York Giants at Gillette Stadium on December 01, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Maddie Meyer/Getty Images) | Getty Images New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson revealed Friday that he has been dealing with a neurological medical condition that resulted in hospitalization. Henderson was first listed on the injury report with an illness last Thursday, Oct. 29, and has been away from the team since. Head coach Mike Vrabel said the team has not yet decided whether Henderson will be placed on a reserve list. For now, the focus remains on supporting the 24-year old through his recovery. “I know that he is well loved and respected on our football team,” Vrabel said. “I’m just trying to make sure that TreVeyon, he’s cared for and that the recovery plan is intact and he’s comfortable with it and that his wife Kenzie is cared for and understand what was going on through the process. “Support him the best way that I know how is just to care for him, listen to him and do whatever we can to get healthy and get back and help this football team and do what he loves.” Henderson was ruled out for Sunday’s game against the Green Bay Packers, marking the second consecutive game he will miss due to illness. With Henderson sidelined, the Patriots signed Lan Larison from the practice squad last week to join Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner on the active roster. Kiner has since assumed Henderson’s No. 2 role behind Stevenson. “Corey’s worked really hard, and I think that his spark and energy going back to the Jets game has been noticeable,” Vrabel said. “Being able to run, kick off returns, provide impact there. He’s a great teammate. He’s got great energy. I love seeing him in the building each and every day. So, hopefully his role can continue to grow and be able to help us out there.”

title: Patriots RB TreVeyon Henderson provides medical update, reveals recent hospitalization
summary: New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson, who had been out since last Thursday due to an illness, took to social media on Friday to provide an update on his medical situation. “Recently, I experienced an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days,” Henderson […]
full_text: New England Patriots running back TreVeyon Henderson, who had been out since last Thursday due to an illness, took to social media on Friday to provide an update on his medical situation. “Recently, I experienced an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms that required hospitalization for several days,” Henderson wrote in the statement. “During that time, I underwent extensive medical testing and evaluation. While the results of my comprehensive medical testing have comeback positive and reassuring, the cause o f this remains unknown and unexplainable.” “I will continue working closely with specialists and physical therapists to focus on my recovery, as these symptoms have affected my strength, coordination, and some of my physical functions. I am committed to doing everything necessary to return to full health. My health and long-term well-being remain my foremost priority.” 🙏🏽 pic.twitter.com/l52XuixPOc — TreVeyon Henderson (@TreVeyonH4) November 6, 2026 Henderson, 24, joined the Patriots as a second-round selection in the 2025 NFL Draft and burst onto the scene as a big-play threat. Serving in tandem with veteran running back Rhamondre Stevenson, he finished his rookie campaign with 1,132 scrimmage yards and 10 touchdowns. His second NFL campaign, however, has been a challenge. Henderson suffered an ankle injury in late August that forced him out multiple weeks into the regular season. He returned in Week 2 against the Steelers — a game that saw him score a 39-yard touchdown reminiscent of his 2025 form — but has touched the ball only 57 total times for 248 scrimmage yards and that one score since then. Along the way, he also suffered a high ankle sprain and has missed time due to his current illness. That illness first came up last week leading up to New England’s game in Miami. Henderson was a full participant in practice on Wednesday before being absent the following two days and into the game. He was also a non-participant in practice so far this week. The Patriots will host the Green Bay Packers at Gillette Stadium on Sunday. In light of his statement,Henderson’s participation appears to be in doubt.

title: Patriots will have their hands full against Packers’ explosive passing game
summary: The Green Bay Packers offense has had its ups and downs this season, as evidenced by the fact it is ranked 20th in points (21.4) and 18th in yards per game (331.6) as well as 17th in expected points added per play (0.010). One area that has consistently yielded positive results so far, however, has […]
full_text: The Green Bay Packers offense has had its ups and downs this season, as evidenced by the fact it is ranked 20th in points (21.4) and 18th in yards per game (331.6) as well as 17th in expected points added per play (0.010). One area that has consistently yielded positive results so far, however, has been its deep game. No team in the NFL has had more explosive plays in the passing game than the Packers, who have had 33 plays of 20-plus yards so far this season. Quarterback Jordan Love, meanwhile, is tied for the league lead with 17 completions of 20-plus air yards, and tied for third in average depth of target (9.8). The New England Patriots therefore know what’s in store this Sunday. “This team lives off of taking shots,” said safety Kevin Byard. “They’re an explosive-play team, a vertical-passing team. So, this will be a huge challenge for us as a defense. Obviously trying to be sticky in coverage, but also when we are playing zone, making sure we’re getting back in our zones, making sure we’re actually forcing those checkdowns. And sometimes I think in this game we’re going to have to accept the four- or five-yard checkdowns and not allowing the ball to get thrown over our head.” Through eight games this year, the Patriots defense has been uneven stopping the big passing play. In total, the unit has surrendered 25 of them — 10th-worst in the league. Patriots fans, join the game-day huddle! Follow every snap and discuss every decision with fellow fans on the SB Nation app. Connect through our live game chat Browse with fewer ads Seamlessly move between communities Enjoy faster commenting and posting Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Staying on the average so far could yield catastrophic results against a team like the Packers, that has specialized in taking the top off of defenses. Green Bay has been able to do so in large part due to its top wide receiver duo, Christian Watson and Matthew Golden. Watson is leading the team with 708 receiving yards and six touchdowns on 42 catches, an average of 16.9 yards per reception. Golden has caught 43 passes for 619 yards, four scores, and 14.4 yards per catch. Together, they have been responsible for 54 of Green Bay’s 97 passing first downs this year. “These receivers are explosive, especially Watson and Golden. That’s a nasty duo there about taking the top off,” said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr. “Christian Watson may be the fastest receiver in the league; he’s always a big play threat anytime he touches the ball,” added Byard. “But also Matthew Golden — he is a second-year player — has a lot of juice. He’s building a really good rapport. I know he’s dropped some passes and stuff like that, but he’s getting open. He’s creating separation.” Drops have indeed been a problem for the Packers, with Golden leading the league with nine of them this year. In total, Green Bay’s pass catchers have let 23 passes go through their hands. What this goes to show, however, is that the team’s potential for big plays has been even greater than the eventual statistics shows. A lot of that is not just due to the receiving talent, but the quarterback himself. “I think he’s one of the most underrated quarterbacks in this league,” said Byard about Jordan Love. “He doesn’t get put into the top-10 lists sometimes, but he’s very efficient. He’s leading the league in passing yards right now. He’s having a career year. A lot of it is because of those deep ball shots.” “He hunts explosives,” said Kuhr. “They can meticulously drive down the field and sometimes that’s what it’s got to be, but we have to try to limit those 20-plus-yard plays, and they are really good at it. He’s really good at it. He throws a great deep ball. … We have to do our best to try to defend that in more than just one way. We can’t just be, ‘Hey, we’re going to pressure him and make it get off quick, and we’re not covering as long.‘ And it’s also, ‘Hey, we can’t just sit back forever.‘ We have to be able to mix it up a little bit.” The Patriots’ defensive success on Sunday might depend on their ability to do just that.

title: Saints Hall of Fame Honors Mark Ingram, Terron Armstead and Sal La Rock
summary: On Friday, November 6, 2026, former New Orleans Saints left tackle Terron Armstead and running back Mark Ingram were inducted into the Saints Hall of Fame during a luncheon held at Chateau Country Club in Kenner. Sal La Rock, the Superdome’s press box security supervisor, received the Joe Gemelli “Fleur de Lis” Award, which recognizes […]
full_text: On Friday, November 6, 2026, former New Orleans Saints left tackle Terron Armstead and running back Mark Ingram were inducted into the Saints Hall of Fame during a luncheon held at Chateau Country Club in Kenner. Sal La Rock, the Superdome’s press box security supervisor, received the Joe Gemelli “Fleur de Lis” Award, which recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to the New Orleans Saints organization through their dedication, service and commitment to the franchise. Ingram was selected by the New Orleans Saints in the first round (28th overall) of the 2011 NFL Draft. Over 10 seasons in New Orleans (2011–2018 and 2021–2022), Ingram cemented his place in franchise history, becoming the Saints’ all-time leading rusher in 2021. However, his record was surpassed by Alvin Kamara just three years later. A three-time Pro Bowl selection, including two appearances as a Saint, Ingram retired following the 2022 season and currently serves as a college football analyst for FOX Sports. Due to his commitments with FOX Sports, Ingram was unable to attend the luncheon but will be in attendance at tonight’s gala and tomorrow’s game. In a prerecorded message, Ingram expressed his gratitude to his family, former teammates, the Saints organization and the fans for their unwavering support, encouragement and love throughout his career, fittingly closing his message with an enthusiastic “WHO DAT!” Armstead was selected by the Saints in the third round (75th overall) of the 2013 NFL Draft out of Arkansas-Pine Bluff. Over nine seasons in New Orleans (2013–2021), he established himself as one of the NFL’s premier offensive tackles and a cornerstone of the Saints’ offensive line. Armstead earned three consecutive Pro Bowl selections (2018–2020) and Associated Press second-team All-Pro honors in 2018. He played a key role in protecting quarterback Drew Brees and helping anchor one of the league’s most productive offenses during his tenure with the franchise. During his acceptance speech, Armstead expressed his gratitude to his family, who were in attendance, as well as Saints owner Gayle Benson, who was also present, and the entire Saints organization for their support throughout his career. He also shared that his only regret from his playing days was that he and his teammates were unable to bring another Super Bowl championship to the city of New Orleans. Sal La Rock has been a valued member of the Caesars Superdome staff since 1998, beginning his career in event services for public safety before being promoted to Press Box Supervisor just two years later. For nearly three decades, affectionately known as “Mr. Sal,” he has been a familiar face and a warm, welcoming presence for media members covering Saints games. His kindness, dedication and genuine hospitality have made him a beloved fixture in the press box, and game days at the Superdome simply wouldn’t be the same without him. All three honorees will be recognized by the Saints Hall of Fame during halftime of tomorrow’s game against the Cleveland Browns.

title: Saints vs. Browns: Key Matchups
summary: The New Orleans Saints are attempting to get back in the win column and step up in a weak NFC South with a win over the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. But it won’t be easy. The Browns are 5-3 on the season and have found ways to win the tough ones. If New Orleans comes […]
full_text: The New Orleans Saints are attempting to get back in the win column and step up in a weak NFC South with a win over the Cleveland Browns on Sunday. But it won’t be easy. The Browns are 5-3 on the season and have found ways to win the tough ones. If New Orleans comes out with a win, it will be due to taking advantage of these key matchups. Saints RBs vs. Browns run defense The Saints are coming off one of the worst rushing performances of all time. They rushed the ball 17 times against the Pittsburgh Steelers for a total of 18 yards. In the loss, Saints running backs ran 14 times for 11 yards, averaging 0.8 yards per carry. Fortunately for the Saints, they’ll be facing a Browns defense that has struggled against the run. Over the last two weeks, Cleveland is allowing an average of 170.5 rushing yards and three touchdowns per game. Although unlikely, reinforcements may be on the way for the Saints, with left tackle Kelvin Banks Jr. returning to practice. The run game is the biggest problem in New Orleans, and frankly, Kellen Moore’s career depends on correcting it. With a favorable matchup, the Saints should find success. Saints pass rush vs. QB Shedeur Sanders Browns quarterback Deshaun Watson has been placed in the concussion protocol and is unlikely to play. With it becoming more probable that second-year quarterback Shedeur Sanders will be starting, the Saints defense has a favorable matchup. Chase Young has been dominant to start the season, and despite an early bye, he remains top three in sacks. Alongside Young is Carl Granderson, who has logged 5.5 sacks himself. The Saints have been one of the better pass-rushing teams in the league in terms of sacks, and their standout tandem is looking to have a big game against a young, inexperienced quarterback. WR Jordyn Tyson vs. the Browns secondary Sunday will be a big game for the Saints. They are returning from the bye to a home crowd, still within a game’s reach of the top of the NFC South. Despite all the implications, the biggest headline for New Orleans against the Browns will be the return of eighth-overall pick Jordyn Tyson. Tyson will likely see his first NFL action on Sunday, and the Saints will be looking to get him started early. Tyson offers the catch-and-run ability the New Orleans offense has been missing, and he could be an immediate game changer. But if I know the Saints want to get Tyson the ball early, you could bet Cleveland knows it too. Getting Tyson back is big for the Saints, and he could be the difference in a win or a loss, but the Browns will zone in on the momentum New Orleans will be looking to gain out of the bye, and it starts with the rookie.

title: Saints Draft Position: NFL Week 9
summary: The New Orleans Saints did not play a game in Week 8, and maybe that was best for everyone involved. It was also great for the Saints’ draft position, because after their bye week, New Orleans is set to select at pick 8 Here are a couple of prospects the Saints could look at as […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - OCTOBER 31: Indiana Hoosiers wide receiver Charlie Becker (80) warms up prior to the start of a college football game between the Minnesota Golden Gophers vs the Indiana Hoosiers on October 31, 2026 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, IN. (Photo by Jeffrey Brown/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints did not play a game in Week 8, and maybe that was best for everyone involved. It was also great for the Saints’ draft position, because after their bye week, New Orleans is set to select at pick 8 Here are a couple of prospects the Saints could look at as an option in the first round. WR Charlie Becker Yes, the Saints just selected Jordyn Tyson in the first round, and although he hasn’t played yet, he should be the clear WR2 on this team. However, WR could become a need again. I know, that’s crazy to think about, but Devaughn Vele could get traded before the deadline, and he is turning 29 this year. So, the Saints may need another guy who complements Chris Olave and Tyson, and that’s Charlie Becker. With Indiana, Becker has single-handedly led the team to wins. He has a habit of completely taking over games, making some of the most clutch catches in college football, can speed past defenders, drop them with his route running, can make any impossible catch, and will take a hit and keep hold of the ball. He is an all-around WR. For the Saints, selecting another WR is greedy, even if they trade for Vele, but they have the cap space to fill most of the roster in free agency, and Becker could be incredible for this team. CB Kelley Jones On to the defensive side of the ball, the Saints must address this position in the offseason. Kool-Aid McKinstry has not shown the ability to be a consistent CB1 yet and the depth pieces around him are also not good enough right now to fill in at CB2. If the Saints can’t upgrade the pass rush enough, they need to focus on the CBs. Kelley Jones is a CB that a new defensive regime could fall in love with. At this moment, Kellen Moore has done nothing to make me feel like he’s staying past this year, so if that does happen, the defensive could go back to a man heavy scheme. That is where Jones shines, and his length is something front offices could fall in love with.

title: Interview with the Enemy: Cleveland Browns
summary: This week, the New Orleans Saints will return to action to face the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome in Week 9 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Chris Pokorny of Dawgs By Nature joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How would you evaluate Todd Monken’s first season as the Browns’ head […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 17: Taysom Hill #7 of the New Orleans Saints breaks a tackle attempt by Grant Delpit #9 of the Cleveland Browns on a touchdown run during the second half of a game at the Caesars Superdome on November 17, 2024 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick E. Hingle/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week, the New Orleans Saints will return to action to face the Cleveland Browns at Caesars Superdome in Week 9 of the 2026 regular season. To break it down, Chris Pokorny of Dawgs By Nature joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: How would you evaluate Todd Monken’s first season as the Browns’ head coach? What have been the biggest positives and negatives since his arrival in Cleveland? CP: It certainly got off to a rocky start after the Browns were blown out with no answers in Week 1 against the Jaguars. After that, though, things have been much better, to the point where he was getting coach of the year recognition (prior to the second blowout loss against Pittsburgh last week). I wouldn’t say he’s an amazing coach, but he’s gotten some good out of Deshaun Watson, which not many people thought was possible. As a team in general, and this extends to defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg too, the thing I’ve liked the most is that we’ve seen some week-to-week and in-game adjustments, which is something the previous coaching staff didn’t do well. In terms of negatives, there are a few things that Monken hasn’t been able to figure out: how to prevent Watson from getting sacked at a near-record pace, and how to cut out the high number of penalties. I don’t know if either of those is really an indictment on Monken, though, especially since the offensive line has played at what I would call a fair level this season. Cleveland has also had the benefit of an ‘easy schedule,’ so I’d give him like a B- so far in his first year as a head coach. NJ: Who are some notable names who will be sidelined for the Browns on Sunday against the Saints? Is there a particular area in which New Orleans could exploit? CP: Obviously, it’s looking like Deshaun Watson will be out as he is in the concussion protocol. All things considered, though, Cleveland has been relatively healthy this season. The player I might look at is second-year linebacker Carson Schwesinger. He is the type of player who could be a future All-Pro, and has had games where he lights it up. But, he also has a warrior mentality to where he’ll play through injuries. He’s been dealing with an ankle injury, and while it didn’t seem to hinder him previously, last week against the Steelers, he had an awful day in coverage, grading out as a 30.5 by Pro Football Focus. He had low marks across the board, grading poorly in run defense, tackling, pass rush, and coverage. It’s possible that was an anomaly, and that targeting Schwesinger might actually be a mistake, given his overall body of work. But it’s worth pointing out, given what happened last week. If we’re not talking about injuries, the area the Saints should try to explore is the Browns’ run defense. It has become a real liability lately, with the Titans and Steelers shredding it and the Browns not having any answers. Cleveland’s coaching staff talked about what went wrong this past week from a strategic standpoint against the run, so we’re hoping to see adjustments. But Cleveland’s pass defense is very sound, so the Saints — despite their struggles on the ground — are far better suited trying to capitalize on what’s worked for others lately via the ground game. NJ: With Shedeur Sanders in line to start on Sunday in New Orleans, how confident are you in his ability to operate the offense and rally his teammates? CP: Deshaun Watson has looked way better this season than he has in previous seasons with the Browns, and his knack for leading a game-winning drive — he’s done it in all five victories — can’t be denied. With that said, though, he’s still been a below average quarterback in my book because things are generally still a bit slow to process. At times, he seems timid to make a mistake downfield, which is both a good and bad thing. Worst of all is the inconsistency, though. Most weeks, it seems like the offense goes cold for three of the game’s four quarters, before finding a spark in one of the quarters. There isn’t a consistent rhythm. That’s not all on Watson, but I think a lot of it is. My point in mentioning all of that is that, despite Watson’s 5-3 record, I can’t really see it being ‘worse’ for Shedeur Sanders, per se. I mean, Watson hasn’t thrown a touchdown pass in three straight games. Last year, we saw a mix of good and bad for Sanders, but that also came behind a much worse offensive line in my opinion. I’m intrigued to see how Sanders plays with the Browns’ young weapons this year. One of Sanders’ biggest issues in the past has been backpedaling too much on third downs to try to avoid pressure, and it just leads to a bigger sack. He got better at it during the regular season last year, but because it’s been so long since he’s faced live game action, it’s possible that those tendencies will creep up again. Back in training camp, I thought he flashed some good chemistry with rookie WR KC Concepcion when they got reps together, which is a plus. Overall, I have like an average level of confidence that he’ll operate the offense fine. I don’t know about rallying his teammates. I’m not expecting a Gardner Minshew moment where he comes in and leads touchdown drives left and right, but I’m expecting him to keep us in the game at least as much as Watson would have. NJ: Who is one Browns player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Sunday—someone who may not receive much national attention but could have a strong performance? CP: I’ll go with tight end Harold Fannin. After a little lull where he only had 2 catches in 2 games, he’s had 16 catches for 245 yards in the last 2 games. He catches the ball well, and always has a knack for gaining an extra few yards after contact, no matter which defender is tackling him. In 7 games with Sanders last year at quarterback, Fannin had 4 touchdown receptions and a fair amount of targets week-to-week, so I’m expecting some of that hookup to continue this week. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Saints (-164) are currently 3.0-point favorites over the Browns (+138) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction and how do you see the game playing out? CP: It looks like the line shifted to +3, possibly with the news of Watson being in the concussion protocol. This is the end of a three-game road stretch for Cleveland, and they’re coming off of a bad loss. Also, in the Browns’ five victories this season, none of them have been by more than 4 points. On paper, I tell myself that Cleveland’s offense will find some success, since the Saints are allowing nearly 28 points per game. Although the Browns’ run defense has suffered lately, I think it’ll be a point of emphasis in the film room this week, and New Orleans has not had a lot of success in that area. If New Orleans stays one-dimensional, Cleveland is tough to pass the ball on consistently, so I see the potential for this week’s game being advantageous to the Browns. I’ll go with the Browns coming out on top 20-17. Thank you again to Chris Pokorny for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

full_text: November 27, 2022; Santa Clara, California, USA; New Orleans Saints team orthopedist Dr. W. Stephen Choate before the game against the San Francisco 49ers at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kyle Terada-USA TODAY Sports The New Orleans Saints have announced Dr. W. Stephen Choate as their nominee for the 2026 Salute to Service Award. The award is presented annually by USAA and the NFL and honors a league member who demonstrates an exemplary commitment to honoring and supporting the military community. Currently in his ninth season with the Saints, Dr. Choate is also an orthopedic surgeon and sports medicine specialist at Ochsner Sports Medicine Institute. Before joining the organization, he proudly served four years in the U.S. Air Force, attaining the rank of Major and deploying overseas in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. During his military service, Dr. Choate served as Chief of the Orthopedic Department and Medical Director of Surgical Services for the 56th Medical Group, earning the Air Force Commendation Medal for his meritorious service. Under his leadership, the medical group also received multiple awards for excellence in patient care and safety. Dr. Choate’s dedication to serving those he calls “warrior athletes” continues to shape his approach to sports medicine, bringing the same commitment, discipline and compassion to the professional athletes he cares for today. One of his favorite mottos comes from the U.S. Military Academy Cadet Prayer, “Make us to choose the harder right instead of the easier wrong and never to be content with a half-truth when the whole truth can be won.” Finalists for the 2026 Salute to Service Award will be announced in January with the recipient recognized at NFL Honors in February. Congratulations to Dr. Choate on this well-deserved recognition and thank you for your service.

title: Our Defense vs. Their Offense: Cleveland Browns
summary: As the New Orleans Saints’ offense has been the primary focus coming out of the bye week, the defense should not be ignored. Defensively, the Saints have had some obvious struggles, and this matchup against the Browns is a battle of weak against weak. The Browns enter this game with questions surrounding starting quarterback Deshaun […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 17: Taysom Hill #7 of the New Orleans Saints breaks a tackle attempt by Grant Delpit #9 of the Cleveland Browns on a touchdown run during the second half of a game at the Caesars Superdome on November 17, 2024 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick E. Hingle/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the New Orleans Saints’ offense has been the primary focus coming out of the bye week, the defense should not be ignored. Defensively, the Saints have had some obvious struggles, and this matchup against the Browns is a battle of weak against weak. The Browns enter this game with questions surrounding starting quarterback Deshaun Watson, as he entered concussion protocol earlier this week. That means, as of this moment, Shedeur Sanders is slated to make his first start of the 2026 campaign. The loss of Watson will be a significant challenge for the Browns to overcome, but they weren’t exactly setting the world on fire offensively with him. The Browns enter this week averaging 301 yards per game in total offense, which ranks 24th in the league. They rush for only 97 yards per game and throw for 204, ranking 24th and 22nd, respectively. They are also near the bottom of the league in scoring, averaging just 17 points per game, and rank dead last in pass protection, having allowed a league-worst 33 sacks in eight games. This is an offense that a defense should be able to take advantage of. The problem is that the Saints have a defense that an offense can take advantage of. This game feels like the Vikings game, when Minnesota’s offense wasn’t particularly good, but the Saints’ defense wasn’t either. The Vikings went on to have a very impressive day in the Dome. The Browns feature several players the Saints will have to keep their eyes on. Running back Quinshon Judkins is the primary rushing threat. So far this season, he is averaging only 3.4 yards per carry, but he has game-breaking talent. Matching up against a weak run defense like the Saints’ could be just what the young back needs to ignite a resurgence. Given the uncertainty surrounding Watson’s health, running the ball will likely be the focal point of the Browns’ offense. The Saints will have to stop Judkins. When the Browns look to pass, they will utilize a variety of weapons. Harold Fannin Jr. is a tight end, but he is also the team’s leading receiver. The Saints cannot allow Fannin to have a Brock Bowers-level impact against this defense. When it’s not Fannin, the Browns will look to KC Concepcion Jr., the rookie wide receiver from Texas A&M. Getting him the ball in space is a primary focus of Cleveland’s offense. Jerry Jeudy and Denzel Boston are the other primary receiving threats. Jeudy is a great route runner against zone coverage and knows how to find open space. He is complemented by Boston, who brings physical size, the ability to beat press-man coverage, and the talent to make contested catches. The Saints will have to generate pressure on the quarterback, regardless of who is under center. Playing against an offense that has allowed 33 sacks this season, while having Chase Young, one of the league’s sack leaders on your defensive unit, should make the coaching staff very excited. Stop the run and generate pressure. Doing those two things will help a secondary that has been looking to return to its top-10 form from a season ago. But stopping the run is a lot easier said than done for this squad. The Saints are currently allowing 139 rushing yards per game, ranking 29th in the league, and the answers to fixing this run defense may not be found in 2026. Hopefully, this game can ignite a renaissance of sorts for the Saints’ rushing defense. How do you think the Saints will match up against the Browns defensively? Do you expect the Saints to have an edge when their defense is playing against Cleveland’s backup quarterback?
author: Anthony Parker

title: Giants-Eagles ‘5 questions’: Even Bleeding Green Nation has given up
summary: The New York Giants are visiting Lincoln Financial Field, their own personal house of horrors, this Sunday when they face the Philadelphia Eagles. Things are upside-down in the NFC East, though, with the Giants on top and the wounded Eagles at the bottom. Let’s discuss that in our ‘5 questions’ segment with Brandon Lee Gowton […]
full_text: NIck Sirianni (left) and Howie Roseman. | Getty Images The New York Giants are visiting Lincoln Financial Field, their own personal house of horrors, this Sunday when they face the Philadelphia Eagles. Things are upside-down in the NFC East, though, with the Giants on top and the wounded Eagles at the bottom. Let’s discuss that in our ‘5 questions’ segment with Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation. Ed: How are Eagles fans processing what has happened to the team this year? It has been a shocking fall. Is there any light at the end of the tunnel? BLG: Back in the offseason, I talked about feeling less optimistic about the Eagles’ short-term outlook than their long-term outlook. Stand by what I said back in April. Optimistic about the Eagles in the long-term, less so in the short-term: pic.twitter.com/58vNJfo9M5 — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) October 12, 2026 There’s no denying that this season is a stinker. The Eagles are arguably the worst team in the NFL. There isn’t just one reason why that’s the case. When you’re this bad, it truly takes a team effort. The offense is bad and injured. New offensive coordinator Sean Mannion and new offensive line coach Chris Kuper (who replaced legendary two-time Super Bowl champion Jeff Stoutland) seem to be in over their heads. Nick Sirianni has no answers to help them. Jalen Hurts was a big reason why the Eagles won their first two games but he didn’t play as well after that and is now out for the season. Vic Fangio’s defense has way underperformed expectations. The veteran defensive coordinator is not having a good season. The Eagles paid big money to homegrown interior defensive linemen Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis … in addition to veteran edge rusher Jonathan Greenard … but the defensive line is getting pushed around. Howie Roseman didn’t have a very good offseason. You can’t point to many moves that are currently helping the team. (The A.J. Brown trade is looking pretty good, though. But the first-round pick they got for him doesn’t arrive until 2028.) Despite the current struggles, there is reason to be optimistic about this team’s future. Things previously looked bleak for the Eagles after they fired their head coach in 2012, 2015, and 2020. But Jeffrey Lurie and Roseman quickly righted the ship after each of those debacles. This isn’t to suggest that there’s a guarantee that the Eagles will get back on track as soon as next season. But there’s reason to give that duo some benefit of the doubt. I certainly won’t be surprised if they use this bad season to reset the franchise and focus on building a new championship contender. The Eagles probably won’t stay bad for very long. And even if they do … we’ve been able to witness two Super Bowl wins within the past nine years. It could be way worse! Ed: What are your thoughts on the Jalen Hurts situation? In my view, it is a really bad look for the Eagles. Does it look and feel as bad from where you sit? BLG: It certainly doesn’t look or feel great. And I know some people around him were not happy with how the situation was handled. Understandably so. Without knowing all the details, it’s difficult to speak definitively on the matter. I’ll just say that I hope the team truly did operate with Hurts’ health and safety in mind and this was just an unfortunate scenario. I also hope Hurts is getting better and can be cleared to play football again in the future. For many reasons, his standing with the team moving forward isn’t clear. But there’s plenty of time to figure that out down the road. Ed: If you could take one player off the Giants’ roster and put him in Philadelphia’s lineup, who would it be? Why? BLG: ’m not super interested in trying to salvage this season, which already seems lost. So, I’m not thinking about a short-term, win-now addition. Malik Nabers is tempting; he’s been good and the Eagles could use another stud receiver with Makai Lemon’s outlook uncertain. I’m interested in fortifying the Eagles’ offensive line with Lane Johnson retiring … maybe take Andrew Thomas and either move him or Jordan Mailata to right tackle? The Eagles could use help at tight end and I like Isaiah Likely. But he also got paid a lot of money. I’ve been hearing good things about Arvell Reese, though I haven’t had a ton of time to key in on him yet. But I’m ultimately going to go with Philly native Abdul Carter. I noticed he ranks top 20 in pressures generated. He seems to be having a better season than his sack numbers would indicate. The Eagles need edge rusher help in long term and it would be fun to have him return home to help his favorite NFL team. The Giants’ first-round pick. pic.twitter.com/31Tris2MVo — Brandon Lee Gowton (@BrandonGowton) April 25, 2025 Ed: How would you expect Howie Roseman to react to this? A seller in the short-term? What about the long-term? BLG: It seems like a no-brainer for Roseman to sell players who won’t be around next season. The likes of Riq Woolen (one-year contract), Hollywood Brown (one-year contract), and Moro Ojomo (playing on last year of his deal and the Eagles already paid Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis) should pretty much be gone for whatever the Eagles can fetch for them. The Eagles should be willing to take offers for more premium players, such as Saquon Barkley. It’s already been reported that they’re NOT going to deal him. And my guess is that report came to light because Roseman already sensed the market for him isn’t as lucrative as it would take for the Eagles to move him. That’s fine. But, again, they should be willing to sell almost every player on their roster as long as the price is right. Just like it was in the case of the Cam Jurgens trade. Absolutely no one in Philly thought the Eagles could get a second-round pick for a player who really struggled last season and wasn’t off to a great start this year. If there’s great value to be had, Roseman should take it. I doubt Roseman is of the mind the Eagles need to be in a multi-year rebuild. He’s built contenders in much shorter time-frames. Ed: How weird is it for you to look at the betting line and see the Giants as FAVORITES at the Linc? What do the Giants have to do to win this game? What, if anything, makes you think the Eagles can pull an upset? (And, yes, that sounds weird to me, too) BLG: It’s certainly not hard to believe given the current state of the Eagles. But it is wild in the historical context that they haven’t been in this home underdog position since 2009. The Eagles have mostly owned the Giants for a long time now; they are 21-6 in 27 meetings against the G-Men since I started covering the Birds for BGN in 2013. What do the Giants have to do to win? Pretty much just show up. The Eagles’ offense is abysmal. Their defense has had some moments but they’re bad, too. It doesn’t seem like this team stands much of a chance. I refuse to believe otherwise until they actually give us something to think otherwise. I think John Harbaugh will have his team ready and fired up to get a win in Philly. The Giants should also be well-rested coming off a bye while the Eagles are banged up and coming off a Sunday night road game. Eagles 7, Giants 28.
author: Ed Valentine

title: College football 2026: Draft Prospects for the Giants in a monster Week 10
summary: Good Morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 10 of the 2026 College Football season! I’m not going to beat around the bush today: We’re being treated to an absolutely monstrous slate of games that features seven matchups between ranked opponents. I’m not sure I’ve ever seen one day with this […]
full_text: Miami defensive tackle Ahmad Moten Sr. celebrates a fumble recovery﻿ | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Good Morning New York Giants fans! Happy Saturday and welcome to Week 10 of the 2026 College Football season! I’m not going to beat around the bush today: We’re being treated to an absolutely monstrous slate of games that features seven matchups between ranked opponents. I’m not sure I’ve ever seen one day with this many “good against good” match-ups, and not only will today’s action have a profound effect on the upcoming Draft Process, it will also have a seismic impact on the College Football Playoffs. With that in mind, we’re going about things a bit differently today, and I’ll be spotlighting a player who could appeal to the Giants, or fit their needs as we currently perceive them, on each team in these games. So grab your snacks of choice, buckle in, and let’s get to it. (3) Utah vs. (9) BYU ABC – noon (3) Utah player to watch – Wayshawn Parker (RB) Parker has solid, but unspectacular, size for an NFL back at 5-foot-10, 205 pounds. He might not be a big back, but he’s a physical runner who has great vision and patience running downhill and true home run speed when he sees daylight. Parker has averaged over 6.5 yards per carry in each of the last two seasons and is also a dangerous pass catcher out of the backfield. (9) BYU player to watch – Faletu Satuala (S) The Giants were reportedly very interested in Ohio State safety Caleb Downs, and the “Ravens” style defense loves to use versatile box safeties as pivot players to help dictate terms to the offense. Satuala is has a massive frame for a safety at 6-foot-4, 215 pounds, but is a versatile and dynamic athlete. He was a basketball and lacrosse star in high school, as well as a wide receiver, safety, and kick returner as a high school football player. He’s a comfortable zone defender with a nose for the ball, and knows how to use his rare length to close receiving windows. He also has the physical mentality to be a pseudo-linebacker and enforcer in the box. (18) Missouri vs. (7) Texas ESPN – noon (18) Missouri player to watch – Jamal Roberts (RB) Roberts stepped into the gaping hole left by the devastating injury to Ahmad Hardy and has absolutely thrived. Roberts has good size at 6-foot, 215 pounds, and a good balance of play strength, vision, and quickness. He had a dominant 211-yard, 3-touchdown performance against Florida and a 222-yard game against Texas A&M the next week. He currently leads the SEC in both rushing attempts and yards, and is a capable pass catcher as well as a true workhorse back. Roberts could be a fantastic value on the third day of the draft. (7) Texas player to watch – Maraad Watson (iDL) Watson has been below the national radar, but the New Jersey native is a massive young man at 6-foot-3, 333 pounds and has been quietly productive. He only has 19 tackles on the year, but also has 3.0 tackles for a loss, 3.0 sacks and a forced fumble. Watson is a projected 6th round pick at the moment, so he could be a hidden gem with long term upside for the Giants on the third day. (14) LSU vs. (5) Alabama ABC – 3:30 p.m. (14) LSU Player to watch – Princewill Umanmielen (EDGE) EDGE/OLB could be a sneaky need for the Giants in 2027. Fans might not want to see it, but the Giants would only have two starting caliber pass rushers on their team if they allow Kayvon Thibodeaux to leave in free agency. And while Thibodeaux’s stats haven’t been up to expectations, he’s emerged as a “Leonard Williams” style facilitator for the rest of the defensive front. Umanmielen is a long and fluid rusher with a great first step and the kind of motor that’ll brin a smile to Dennard Wilson’s face. He’s also fifth in all of college football for sacks at 8.5. (5) Alabama player to watch – Bray Hubbard (S) Hubbard is another industrial-sized safety who can play box safety or the STAR hybrid defender at the next level. He has great size at 6-foot-2, 215 pounds and isn’t afraid to be physical near the line of scrimmage. He’s a tone-setter coming downhill while also having the athleticism to be a real factor dropping into underneath coverage. Hubbard has 9 interceptions, 10 passes defensed, and 5 forced fumbles over the last three years while starting in Alabama’s sophisticated defense. (12) Ohio State vs. (23) Oregon CBS – 3:30 p.m. (12) Ohio State player to watch – Kenyatta Jackson (DE/EDGE) Jackson was supposed to be the next Ohio State defensive lineman. However, the fifth-year senior has yet to consistently play up to his athletic potential for the Buckeyes. He has an NFL-ready frame at 6-foot-6, 265 pounds, and Giants’ fans who want a return to a 4-3 front with “classic” 7-technique defensive ends will be intrigued. He does have the play strength to reduce inside to a 4i or 3-technique alignment, and that versatility could make him an intriguing option for Dennard Wilson’s defense as it’s being run today. He could be an option anywhere from the end of Round 1 into Day 2. (23) Oregon player to watch – A’Mauri Washington (iDL) Washington has been on our radar since the summer. Unfortunately, he’s been one of the (many) Oregon players who haven’t been able to consistently play up to their potential. However, if the Giants want to replace Dexter Lawrence, Washington might be worth a long look. He has a similar build at 6-foot-3, 330 pounds, with simply absurd lower-body power — he has a 35-inch vertical leap and a 765-pound squat. He’s also surprisingly fast for a big man and has topped 20 miles per hour in a sprint. He has the potential to be a game-wrecker if he can fully unlock his potential at the next level. (13) Tennessee vs. (6) Kentucky ESPN – 6:15 p.m. (13) Tennessee player to watch – Xavier Gilliam (iDL) We looked at Gilliam very recently, but he has been one of the biggest risers in all of college football. And if the Giants are as serious about adding to their defensive line as they seem to be, Gilliam has to be in consideration for their first round pick (if they have one, and he’s there). He has stormed onto the national stage after transferring from Penn State to the Tennessee and has been the best defensive tackle in the country. His leverage, power, and explosiveness has made him an absolute terror for interior offensive linemen. The 6-foot-2, 305-pound tackle currently has 6.0 sacks, 11.5 tackles for a loss, 2 forced fumbles, and 2 passes defensed. (4) Kentucky player to watch – Colton Price (OC) Bryan Hudson has played well at center over the last few weeks. However, the Giants may want to bring in some competition or depth for their pivot. Price has a good build for an NFL center at 6-foot-3, 308 pounds and is highly regarded for his football IQ as well as his competitive toughness. He transferred from Baylor to Kentucky after earning his degree at Baylor and is not only an excellent pass protector, but is proving to be a capable run blocker on Kentucky’s physical line. He might not have the athletic traits to be drafted early, but he could prove to be an excellent option as a Day 3 pick to battle for a starting center job. (11) Notre Dame vs. (1) Miami NBC – 7:30 p.m. (11) Notre Dame player to watch – Adon Shuler (S) Another New Jersey native, Shuler is a versatile piece in a very good Notre Dame secondary. He’ll likely be a strong safety or STAR nickel defender at the next level, with the ability to be a factor playing in space or coming downhill. He has solid size at 6-foot, 205 pounds, and has a reputation for toughness and intensity. He’s a two-time team captain (2025 and 2026) who’s well regarded for his football IQ as well as his propensity for making clutch plays. (1) Miami player to watch – Ahmad Moten Sr. (iDL) This is the third time around putting the spotlight on the Miami defensive line. The duo of Ahmad Moten Sr. and Justin Scott is among the best in the nation, and spotlighting one usually means spotlighting both. The Hurricanes will need both to play at their absolute…

title: NY Giants trade rumors: Ravens say Derrick Henry won’t be dealt
summary: Plan A for the New York Giants to upgrade at running back remains a mega-deal for Jonathan Taylor. Plan B, if there is a real Plan B, won’t be Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens. Per Adam Schefter, the Ravens have “informed Henry that they have no intention of trading him” to his former coach […]
full_text: Derrick Henry | Getty Images Plan A for the New York Giants to upgrade at running back remains a mega-deal for Jonathan Taylor . Plan B, if there is a real Plan B, won’t be Derrick Henry of the Baltimore Ravens. Per Adam Schefter, the Ravens have “informed Henry that they have no intention of trading him” to his former coach John Harbaugh and the Giants, or anywhere else. The understandable logic behind that, from a Ravens point of view, is that the Ravens are not a) giving up on this season, or b) giving up on the idea that they can retain star quarterback Lamar Jackson long term. Peter Schrager of ESPN added this on ‘GetUp’ , per Pro Football and Sports Network : “I don’t see it,” said Schrager. “My sense is this, talking to Baltimore’s sources: they have 12 draft picks in the upcoming draft, so draft capital doesn’t really do anything right now. They also play the Chargers, Panthers, Texans, Bucs the next four weeks. Those are winnable games. And they just traded for a quarterback; they traded for Cam Jurgens.” “They’re not already in this selloff, fire sale mode. They are not Tennessee, they are not Indianapolis. That said, if there are calls about some other players they would probably be listening to some. I’m talking about guys who might’ve put themselves as veterans on the trade market themselves by the way that they’ve been performing in recent weeks.” Justice Hill? Schefter mentioned in his report that the Giants had asked the Ravens about the availability of veteran running back Justice Hill . Hill was a 2019 fourth-round draft pick by the Ravens and has spent his entire career with Baltimore, so Harbaugh knows him well. The confusing thing about interest in the 28-year-old Hill is that in seven seasons he has never carried the ball more than 84 times, and has just 301 carries for his career. There is nothing on his resume to suggest he is better than Tyrone Tracy or Devin Singletary. Unless the Giants are concerned about the hamstring injuries Tryone Tracy (currently on IR) and Cam Skattebo (doubtful vs. the Eagles) are dealing with and see Hill as an emergency fill-in, I’m not sure what he adds to the backfield. Latest on Jonathan Taylor The Athletic’s Jonathan Jones believes that the Giants and Minnesota Vikings are the favorites to convince the Indianapolis Colts to trade their star running back. Jones said he was told the Colts have already rejected an offer of a second- and fifth-round pick. NFL.com also listed the Giants as one of the most likely landing spots for Taylor, and I believe the reasoning they offered is spot on: A splash move at the deadline could go a long way to ensuring the Giants keep their division lead into January — and provide them a chance to pull off a postseason upset. I believe that the Giants, with the investment they made in Harbaugh, would love to justify it with an NFC East title in Harbaugh’s first season. I also think they believe it would help set them up for the future, a future they believe Taylor can be part of for a couple of seasons. In regards’ to Jones’ reporting that the Colts rejected a second- and fifth-round pick, what if the Giants made this offer: A 2027 second-round pick, a 2028 fifth-round pick, and Tracy. If you are bringing in Taylor, and you have Skattebo, you don’t really have carries for Tracy. Why not include him in your offer in an effort to hold on to some of your draft capital? Vita Vea too pricey? We wrote Friday that Tampa Bay Buccaneers’ defensive tackle Vita Vea was reportedly on the Giants’ radar . Jones writes: Vea signed a one-year, $30 million contract extension in August after protracted negotiations. It would be unusual for the team to deal him less than three months later, even if he has a low base salary in 2026 that can fit under anyone’s cap. In the NFC South, furthermore, you’re always in it. The Bucs are a half-game behind Carolina for the division lead, and they hold the early tiebreakers over Carolina and Atlanta. A 3-5 record in Tampa looks radically different from a 3-5 record in Arizona. I don’t think Tampa Bay would turn down a first-round pick for Vea, but I also don’t think any team is going to offer one for a 31-year-old with one season left on his deal. Vea would help the Giants, but he also appears to be in decline: Giving up a first-round pick would seem like a massive overpayment.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Trade deadline, McCarthy vs. Dart, more questions
summary: Isaac L. Scharf asks: Hello, do you really believe that the Giants are contenders, or are they pretenders? We may be seeing a little bit of last year’s Patriots given the fact that we haven’t played a single team over .500. So do you think the Giants are contenders or pretenders? Ed says: Isaac, the […]
full_text: Isaac L. Scharf asks: Hello, do you really believe that the Giants are contenders, or are they pretenders? We may be seeing a little bit of last year’s Patriots given the fact that we haven’t played a single team over .500. So do you think the Giants are contenders or pretenders? Ed says: Isaac, the standings say they are contenders. The oddsmakers say they are the favorites to win the NFC East . The way everyone else in the division has played absolutely tells us that the Giants should be in the race for the division down to the wire. Pretenders? Well, yes, if you think of them as a team that will or should be a legitimate Super Bowl contender. I say just take the ride, enjoy it, and don’t try to label the Giants as anything. Chris Holland asks: I am wondering if the NFL has made any statements regarding the rampant use of the “peanut punch”. From a safety perspective this is an accident waiting to happen. Ball carriers are going to start suffering injuries to their hands and lower arm as the result of having very large and strong defenders throw full force punches at the ball. I have already seen a player get accidentally punched in the head by one of these “peanut punches”. I get the feeling that the league will continue to allow this practice despite obvious safety concerns because the punches can result in turnovers and looks good on Sportscenter. I also think it’s basically impossible for the ball carriers to truly secure the ball against these punches. Thoughts? Ed says: Chris, no, there have not been any statements about the Peanut Punch that I am aware of. The league did fine Dre Greenlaw for striking the helmet of Atlanta Falcons wide receiver on a missed punch. Maybe it comes up during the offseason when new rules are discussed. Until then, I don’t think anything changes. Darren Silver asks: Supposing JJ McCarthy continues to play well and the Giants make the playoffs as a result, does it really make sense to then trade him for draft picks? Since he’s on a manageable contract, I think having a starting caliber QB back-up is much more valuable than any extra draft picks he might attract. We know Dart (or any starting QB) can go down in a heartbeat. Why not have QB insurance to save us from losing a season due to another Dart injury? I don’t think even a first round pick is as valuable as that would be. Ed says: Darren, there is a line between having a good backup quarterback and having a full-blown quarterback controversy over who should be the starter. That can divide a locker room, a coaching staff, a fan base, and the media that pumps out content about the team every day. Nobody wants “who is playing quarterback this week?” to be a question that gets asked consistently. Or, for fans to start chanting the backup’s name the first time the starter plays poorly. If McCarthy plays well enough, that is is the risk you run. If he plays well enough the rest of the season to deserve to be a starting quarterback, you automatically set up a “who’s team is it?” situation if they are both on the 2027 roster. Those never work out well. Jameis Winston is the quarterback insurance, and he is fine for a few games. A lot of teams would love to have him. The only way I see McCarthy and Dart both being on the team next season is if McCarthy plays OK, but the overall body of work makes it clear that the ceiling is higher with Dart and there is zero question about who is No. 1. I still believe the ideal scenario is that McCarthy plays well enough to create a robust market for him this offseason, and that the Giants are able to turn that fifth-round pick they used to acquire him into multiple draft picks of higher value. Could McCarthy play so well that the Giants actually decide to put Dart on the market in the offseason? Sure. But, we are nowhere close to that yet. It has been five quarters of football. Tom Donlan asks: What is the biggest roster weakness that you think could prevent the Giants from winning the division, and how realistic can it (they) be upgraded via trade this year, and which parts of the Giants success look sustainable beyond this season so they challenge for the division with regularity? Also, when you look back at this deadline two years from now, what decision – or decision to stand pat – would tell us the Giants evaluated themselves correctly? Ed says: Tom, I think the biggest roster weakness the Giants need to address is defensive tackle. D.J. Reader is the only good, reliable interior defensive lineman they have. The run defense has been good at times, porous at other times. You can’t consistently defend the run if you can’t consistently hole the line of scrimmage. The sustainable part of the Giants is that they will have John Harbaugh for the next few years. Rosters change, and there are a lot of unforeseen things. I think we have to see what decisions ultimately get made before speculating on the last part of the question. The generic answer would simply be the tell-tale sign of whether or not the Giants did the right thing would be how much success they have beyond this year. Ronald Buchheim asks: Ed, have you talked with trainers or doctors about groin injuries in general or the one that Andrew Thomas has? Do you know whether it is wise to play through these injuries rather than resting completely? And whether playing through risks the injury becoming chronic and hampering the player’s subsequent career? Ed says: Ronald, I have not asked anyone. Players play through injuries all the time. I’m sure there is some risk of making the injury worse, but the Giants wouldn’t put him out there if he wasn’t capable of playing or was risking damaging his career. Michael Buscemi asks: Trying to understand the Colts philosophy — there’s four or five teams interested in Taylor. I don’t understand at this point the Colts demands if they want a number one and no one stepping up to the plate to pay a number one they have two choices — the first don’t do a trade, keep Taylor. By playing him this week they risked the factor of injury which removes any trade ability why take a chance if you really want to trade him trade him or do nothing? Again the risk of injury playing him could remove any possible trade. Ed says: Michael, the Colts, it seems, are going to play this out all the way to the trade deadline on Tuesday and see if anyone will get desperate and up their offer. There is risk, but if they hold him out and then don’t trade him that is not a good look for Indianapolis. Brennan Lyons asks: I was wondering if you guys have heard any solid rumors about us pursuing Brian Thomas of Jacksonville? I really liked him coming out of LSU, along with Nabers, a few years ago. I would love to see them paired up again on the Giants. I have seen reports that the Jaguars are looking for depth at Edge and are apparently intent on getting rid of Thomas. Do you think there would be any chance of trading Thibs for him? I doubt we will resign him after this year but I’m not so sure we would be willing to let him go now that we are in the midst of a legitimate playoff run. Do you think we can effectively replace Thibs for the rest of the season? Long term, we would have control of Thomas for two more years than Thibs. Do you think the Giants would make that move? Ed says: Brennan, I have not. The Giants, by all accounts, are focused on adding at defensive tackle or taking a big swing at a star running back. I understand the idea of trading Kayvon Thibodeaux. The issue with that is that the Giants have already lost Brian Burns, Tremaine Edmunds, and Chauncey Golston to injury. Thibodeaux is important to the defense right now. If the Giants were not in prime position to make a playoff run trading Thibodeaux would be an obvious move. Now? Love him or not, he is an important piece of the defense. Joseph LoBue asks: I found the Compensatory Free Agent chart that you put together last week quite informative (from a CFA process perspective) but even more interesting…

full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to as the first place Giants get ready to face off tomorrow against the Philadelphia Eagles. New York Giants ’ playoff fate will be heavily influenced by Eagles game | USAToday.com Based on the analytics and percentages, a Giants win would put them in prime position for a playoff spot. A loss would drop them back deep into the pack. A Giants win would give them a 68 percent chance to win the NFC East and a 71 percent shot at making the playoffs. A loss would lessen their division odds to 41 percent and their postseason odds to 43 percent. So, this is kind of a “must-win” for Big Blue (4-2-1) as their schedule gets dicey in the second half of the season. Coach Harbaugh breaking down Texans film Coach Harbaugh analyzes the last play of the game against Houston — New York Giants (@Giants) November 6, 2026 Harbs Weekly: Earn the right to play in memorable games | Giants.com Q: Getting into November football, is there a new skill that your team has to unlock? Harbaugh: Everything is new. Every step of the way is going to be new this year. I think it’s kind of what first years are a lot of times. Like we told them, this is November football. You’ve earned the right to play meaningful games in November. What does that mean? What are you playing for? I asked them, “What do they say about December football? Have you heard the old saying?” And someone got it. [Fullback Patrick] Ricard got it. “They remember what you do in December.” That’s right. I said that’s what they remember. I said they won’t really remember November too much. But without November you can’t get to the point where you’re playing games that are going to be memorable. That’s what we’re playing for right now. We’re playing for the opportunity to play in memorable games, and that’s why November is so important and we’ve earned the right to be to be playing in these games. So, it’s just another notch up of value and then I just talked to them a little bit about as the season goes along, it’s still one game but each game becomes worth more. It’s one game, that’s what this is about, but each game becomes even more valuable because there’s more payoff. Later, that’s why they remember what you do in December. There’s more payoff. So, that’s kind of cool. Giants not looking past Saquon Barkley and struggling Eagles | New York Post “Before Lane Johnson had a name, before Jason Kelce had a name, before Cam Jurgens had a name, they had to go earn it,” defensive tackle Shelby Harris said. “You can’t put down anybody just because they haven’t established themselves in the league. The idea is you don’t want them to establish themselves against you. They’re still physical, they’re humungous size-wise across the board, so it’s just go out there and don’t let them be the determining factor of the game.” “I’m expecting [Barkley] to be healthier than he has been so far,” Harris said. “They’ve done a good job trying to manage him on his way back from injury. If he’s going to play, I expect to get the best out of him — full-on star Saquon Barkley. And we’ll have to stop him in order to be successful.” NFL Week 9 preview: Picks, predictions, schedule, betting odds, fantasy tips | ESPN.com What we’re hearing on the Giants: The Giants believe the bye week should’ve helped QB J.J. McCarthy. He’s now fully caught up after being traded to New York in late September. McCarthy, who is making his second start for the Giants, expects Eagles DC Vic Fangio to make him “earn it.” It will be the latest test of whether the young QB can succeed while facing simulated pressures and getting through his progressions. How Skatt and the Giants are fed Dr. Matt Frakes is the head of nutrition for the New York Giants. Part of his job is to help the players understand the impact of their food choices. @charlottecrrll spoke with Cam Skattebo and Frakes on how nutrition has impacted the team's recent success, particularly with… pic.twitter.com/8elG7zg7gh — The Athletic (@TheAthletic) November 6, 2026 Ravens’ Derrick Henry is frustrated. Will Giants’ John Harbaugh try to trade for him? | NJ.com “I mean, we’ve lost four times [in a row],” Henry said. “It’s frustrating. I don’t have the magical answer. We’ve got to go back to work.” When asked about a potential trade, Henry said, “I have not mentioned me going anywhere else. I’m saying let’s go back to work.” Henry turns 33 in January. He is under contract through next season. Harbaugh doesn’t want a one-year rental, and Henry technically would not be that. His salary next year is $11 million — all of which is non-guaranteed. He has a $1 million roster bonus due in March. So the Ravens (or Giants) have a team option on him for 2027. The 10 best NFL player matchups to watch in Week 9 | PFF New York Giants WR Malik Nabers vs. Philadelphia Eagles CB Quinyon Mitchell. The Giants seek to widen their NFC East lead when they face the Eagles, losers of six in a row. While a battle of backup quarterbacks may be the top storyline, Nabers vs. Mitchell will be must-see television. Nabers has returned from his torn ACL with a vengeance. He’s earned an 82.8 PFF receiving grade with 2.54 yards per route run, numbers that have culminated despite a slower first three games. On top of that, the former sixth overall pick has dropped only two catchable targets all year. Philadelphia’s defense has regressed in 2026, but not because of Mitchell. He’s generated a 67.2 PFF coverage grade, letting up a 69.2 passer rating into his coverage while enabling just a 54.3% opponent completion percentage. Mitchell has had the advantage when these former 2024 first-round picks have squared off. Across 11 prior matchups, Nabers has gained just one catch for nine yards on two targets, being charted as open only three times. Giants look to snap losing streak in Philadelphia. If not now, when? | The Athletic The Giants have had heartbreakers at Lincoln Financial Field, but a loss Sunday would be the worst of the streak because they’re the better team with a far more promising outlook. The Giants are 3.5-point favorites Sunday and winning in Philadelphia would be another step in Harbaugh’s process of rebuilding the franchise. Harbaugh’s track record suggests the Giants are in a strong position to end the streak. His Ravens teams went 15-3 after the bye during his 18 seasons in Baltimore. “We’ve got everything to gain and we know how big this game is,” Harbaugh said. “We know who we’re going against. title: Giants-Eagles final injury report: Cam Skattebo misses practice, doubtful for Sunday
summary: Cam Skattebo missed a fourth straight practice on Friday due to his hamstring injury, but the New York Giants are not ruling their leading rusher out for Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Skattebo is officially considered doubtful. “Let’s see what happens” head coach John Harbaugh said of Skattebo’s status. Wide receiver Malik Nabers, who […]
full_text: Cam Skattebo missed a fourth straight practice on Friday due to his hamstring injury, but the New York Giants are not ruling their leading rusher out for Sunday’s game against the Philadelphia Eagles. Skattebo is officially considered doubtful. “Let’s see what happens” head coach John Harbaugh said of Skattebo’s status. Wide receiver Malik Nabers , who missed practice on Thursday, yelled to reporters that he practice on Friday . Harbaugh said that Nabers’ health is “not an issue” for Sunday. If Skattebo cannot play, Devin Singletary will be the Giants’ primary running back against the Eagles. Gregory Desrosiers is the other back on the 53-man roster, and Phil Mafah and Eric Gray are on the practice squad. The other injury of note for the Giants involves wide reciever/returner Charlie Jones . He turned up on the injury report this week with a hand injury, and is listed as questionable. “He’s managing it,” Harbaugh said. “He was out today catching and everything like that. Just want to make sure he could catch. I haven’t talked to him yet. We’ll see how he felt.” The Giants have an open roster spot after dropping quarterback Jake Haener from the 53-man roster on Thursday. Adding someone with running back, return experience, or both, might make sense before Sunday. Giants-Eagles final injury report Giants Doubtful RB Cam Skattebo | Hamstring Questionable WR Charlie Jones | Hand Eagles Running back Saquon Barkley (hamstring/back) was limited in practice on Friday, but does have an injury designation.
