title: Patience, professionalism paying off for NY Giants’ RB Devin Singletary
summary: New York Giants running back Devin Singletary was inactive from Weeks 3-5. In Weeks 1,2, and 6 — while the Giants were trying to figure out a workable backfield rotation — Singletary carried the ball only 13 times. Yet, there he was on the final play of overtime in Week 7 against the Houston Texans, […]
full_text: Devin Singletary | Getty Images New York Giants running back Devin Singletary was inactive from Weeks 3-5. In Weeks 1,2, and 6 — while the Giants were trying to figure out a workable backfield rotation — Singletary carried the ball only 13 times. Yet, there he was on the final play of overtime in Week 7 against the Houston Texans, the last man standing from what had been a four-man competition. An unhappy Najee Harris had been cut days before. Tyrone Tracy suffered a hamstring injury in the first half that would land him on IR. One play earlier, Cam Skattebo had injured his own hamstring on a career-best 42-yard run. So, it was Singletary left to take the handoff from J.J. McCarthy at the Texans’ 30-yard line in a tie game. Suddenly, he was in the secondary. Then, after a couple of nifty cuts, he was in the end zone and the Giants had won a game. In the post-game madness, a jubilant Singletary and head coach John Harbaugh landed in a heap on the ground. Harbaugh tackles Singletary after OT Win 🙌 Singletary gets tackled by his coach after game-winning TD pic.twitter.com/wHpduP4wOv — New York Post Sports (@nypostsports) October 25, 2026 Singletary said this week that “I still don’t know” if Harbaugh tackled him, or vice versa. “I think we just tripped,” Singletary said. “As Coach would say, it’s football joy. You go through a lot to be able to get to football joy. We were just so happy, so excited. He was telling me how much he loved me. I was telling him how much I loved him.” Singletary said there “was never no bad feelings” between himself and Harbaugh because of the eight-veteran’s lack of opportunities. Singletary, 29, understand that it was “business.” Of course Singletary, who has more than 1,100 carries and 5,000 NFL rushing yards, didn’t like not playing. He did appreciate Harbaugh’s honesty. “One thing I do respect about him, he kept it real with me. You don’t always see that in the league. That’s why I always got so much respect for him for that reason,” Singletary said. “It was just, this is what it is right now. I need you to stay patient and we’ll see how it plays out. Simple as that. “I was like, I appreciate that. Some people won’t even tell you that. They’ll just leave you there with no answers, with nothing.” It played out such that Singletary got to play the hero against the team he gained a career-high in rushing yards for in 2023. New York touchdown! Devin Singletary runs it in from 30 yards out with 7:25 left in overtime. NYG: 27 | HOU: 21 #NYGvsHOU #BigBlue #HTownMade pic.twitter.com/z8BoHAOp9m — NFL TD Bot (@nfltdbot) October 25, 2026 “I wouldn’t say frustrating,” Singletary said in reference to his lack of playing time. “It’s like, yes, part of it is how the game goes. It’s a lot of competition. It’s a deep backfield. But as far as being a pro, that’s me. That’s how I was brought up. “I’m going to always go about my business the right way. Stay ready, because when that opportunity comes, you want to be ready to seize the moment instead of being so mad or whatever it is, sad or whatever, and you can’t capture the moment when it’s here.” After the Texans game, Harbaugh said Singletary’s lack of playing time was “on me.” “We were looking for the formula, and Devin wasn’t — he was the odd man out for a number of weeks. Not because of anything he did or didn’t do, he just was the odd man out, and that’s exactly what I told him,” Harbaugh said. “He asked me, ‘what can I do?’ I said, ‘there’s nothing you can do, you’re doing everything you can do, and your time will come’. It was going to come. And look where it came, right there, and he came through.” Offensive coordinator Matt spoke this week about how appreciative he is of Singletary’s professionalism. “We went through the whole thing with the different running backs and four or five guys and he’s been here from day one, from OTA’s, and through training camp, through the season, wasn’t playing, wasn’t active. And he’d sit back in practice when he wasn’t playing and not say a word, but just be completely professional,” Nagy said. “And we talked, and we talked about great things happen to great people and I just think back to that Texans game, and when he scored that touchdown at the end, the discussions that we had in practice when he wasn’t playing, he never became negative, he never made it about him. He was as great of a professional player as there was, and look what happened. “And I think it’s a story for young kids, it’s a story for vets to be patient, to understand things happen for a reason and when he scored that touchdown, I couldn’t think but anything of how he handled himself the entire last five weeks. And we talked about it in the locker room, and I think for him, what a credit and we’re lucky to have him.” Baseball fans might recall the name Tommy Henrich, an outfielder/first baseman for the New York Yankees from 1937-1950. His nickname was ‘Old Reliable’. In a way, it is what Singletary has become for Harbaugh’s Giants. Now, with Tracy on IR and Skattebo perhaps unable to play Sunday against the Eagles, Singletary is likely to be the lead back. “I know what I can do. I want to be able to display that,” Singletary said. “We’ll see what this week brings, but yeah, I’m excited.”

title: NY Giants trade deadline 2026: Bucs’ DT reportedly on New York’s radar
summary: The New York Giants are one of the most interesting teams in the NFL as we approach the November 10th trade deadline. Few people would have predicted it, but the Giants are in sole possession of the NFC East and have a golden opportunity to seize control of the division and host a playoff game […]
full_text: Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea rushes against the Dallas Cowboys. | Getty Images The New York Giants are one of the most interesting teams in the NFL as we approach the November 10th trade deadline. Few people would have predicted it, but the Giants are in sole possession of the NFC East and have a golden opportunity to seize control of the division and host a playoff game for the first time since January 8th, 2012. By all reports, the Giants are eager to take advantage of that opportunity and want to use the trade market to a difference maker to their team before the trade deadline. Much of the focus has been on the running back position for the Giants, but the team has also been very interested in adding to their defensive line for the stretch run to the playoffs. And now, a new name has emerged as the Giants go big game hunting: Tampa Bay Buccaneers defensive tackle Vita Vea. Ralph Vacchiano of FOX Sports is reporting that the Giants “love” Vea and are willing to be aggressive in trying to pry the star nose tackle out of Tampa. I don’t believe the Tampa Bay Buccaneers will move him, but one player I’d keep an eye on is defensive tackle Vita Vea. I know the Giants love him. They were big-game hunting at that position, with John Harbaugh even calling Titans owner Amy Strunk to try and swing a deal for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons before he went to Chicago. The Giants called Washington about defensive tackle Daron Payne before he got hurt, too. I wouldn’t be shocked if they made an offer for Vea and were willing to deal a first-round pick. Both John Harbaugh and Joe Schoen courted the Tennessee Titans for Jeffery Simmons, but were rebuffed. The Giants were reportedly in on DeForest Buckner, however the Giants’ ability to trade for Buckner was complicated by the fact that they don’t have a fourth round pick or fifth round pick. It makes complete sense that the Giants would be enamored with Vea. Despite his age (31), Vea remains one of the top nose tackles in the NFL, and the 6-foot-4, 350-pounder has impressive power and rare movement skills for a man his size. He’s a big reason why the Buccs are 7th in run stop win rate and 8th in pass rush win rate. Even when Vea isn’t making the play himself, his ability to occupy blockers and collapse pockets creates opportunities for his teammates. But, as Vacchiano states up front, the Buccaneers seem unlikely to move Vea — or any defender — at this point. Tampa has a tough game against the Chicago Bears this week, but they’re only one game out of first place in a sagging NFC South and are on a 2-game win streak. Daniel Popper is covering the trade market for The Athletic and has removed all of the Buccaneers’ defenders from his Big Board 2.0 . He says: We also adjusted based on some movement in the standings. Several Tampa Bay Buccaneers were included in the 1.0 board. The Bucs have since won two straight and might be the best team in the NFC South. The New Orleans Saints, meanwhile, fell to 2-5. While the Giants may love to get Vea, they may have to move on to players like Grover Stewart (Indianapolis Colts), Roy Lopez (Arizona Cardinals), Dalvin Tomlinson (Los Angeles Chargers), or perhaps even DE/edge Tuli Tuipulotu (Chargers).
author: Chris Pflum

title: Giants’ offense vs. Eagles’ defense: The Vic Fangio factor
summary: The New York Giants emerge as winners from their Week 8 BYE. They’re (relatively) rested and still riding the emotional wave of a stunning overtime win in Week 7. They return to action this week as 3.5-point favorites (per FanDuel) on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles have been in a tailspin over […]
full_text: New York Giants quarterback J.J. McCarthy throws a pass against the Houston Texans. | Getty Images The New York Giants emerge as winners from their Week 8 BYE. They’re (relatively) rested and still riding the emotional wave of a stunning overtime win in Week 7. They return to action this week as 3.5-point favorites (per FanDuel) on the road against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Eagles have been in a tailspin over the last several weeks, losing the last six games. They’ve lost each of the last three games by at least 11 points, including a deflating 27-10 loss to the Washington Commanders last week. The Giants are looking to build on the momentum of their upset win over the Houston Texans, while the Eagles are just hoping to stop the skid. What can J.J. McCarthy and the Giants’ offense expect from the Eagles’ defense? Stats that matter Can J.J. McCarthy do it again? The last six (counting overtime) quarters of Giants’ football have turned former 10th overall pick J.J. McCarthy into a national story. Most had written McCarthy off after his rookie year was upended by injury, his sophomore year was a disappointment, and he fell to QB3 in his third year. Now? McCarthy has catapulted himself back into the “QB1” conversation with an electric 11 minutes against the New Orleans Saints and a game full of explosive plays against the Houston Texans. This of course, begs the question: Can he do it again? The Eagles now have about a game and a half worth of tape on the McCarthy-led Giants. That isn’t much to go on, but it may be enough to form a more effective gameplan. The good news is that McCarthy also has two more weeks in the Giants’ offense and more tme practicing with the Giants’ starters. Not to mention, McCarthy will get to enjoy the presence of a (hopefully) healthier Andrew Thomas and Jermaine Eluemunor. It seems likely that Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio will look to contain the explosive passing plays that defined his performance against the Texans. McCarthy excelled at throwing deep against Houston, delivering some legitimate “WOW” throws. He’ll need to capitalize on the opportunities to do so against the Eagles, but can’t count on them being regular occurrences. Instead, the Giants’ intermediate passing game will need to be more consistent on a down-to-down basis while they work to create opportunities for explosive plays. If there was a blemish on McCarthy’s game against the Texans, it’s that his passing success rate* was 25th out of 25 qualifying quarterbacks . * Success rate is defined as the rate at which a play that gains a percentage of the yards needed to convert a first down. A “successful” first down picks up 40 percent of the yards to convert, a successful second down picks up 60 percent of the yards to convert, and a successful third down picks up 100 percent of the yards to convert. Explosive plays are great and go a long way toward making it more likely that a team scores on a given drive. However, a team can’t rely on explosive plays to consistently move the ball down the field. While the Giants did an excellent job of scheming 1-on-1 opportunities and good receiving windows downfield for McCarthy, it’s not something they can live on. McCarthy will need to be more consistent in hitting underneath passes to keep the offense moving and on schedule. That will be particularly true if the Giants’ run game struggles with both Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy injured. Will the run game show up? The Giants finally got their run game going against the Texans. While the Texans’ defense isn’t what it was in 2025, they still filed one of the NFL’s best run defenses, which makes the Giants’ 180-yard, 3-touchdown performance all the more impressive. The Eagles’ run defense has decidedly mediocre this year. And their high Run Stop Win Rate but average YPC and high rushing EPA allowed (+11.45, 28th in the NFL) suggest that they’re prone to giving up explosive plays on the ground. That would be good news for the Giants in light of their performance against the Texans, but there are suddenly doubts about the Giants’ backfield. Tyrone Tracy landed on injured reserve with a hamstring injury suffered early in the game, while Cam Skattebo is currently not practicing with a hamstring injury of his own. Skattebo’s injury was suffered at the end of his final carry of the game, the 42-yard run which set up Devin Singletary’s 30-yard touchdown run to win the game. Skattebo ended that run early when he felt his hamstring tighten, and while he didn’t seem overly concerned after the game, he has yet to practice. That leaves Singletary and the newly-added Greg Desrosiers as the Giants’ healthy backfield, with practice squad backs Phil Mafah and Eric Gray as possible additions. The Giants offensive line will need to play well. While the Eagles’ defense has struggled this year, the trio of Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and Moro Ojomo remains dangerous. The Giants will also need to depend on McCarthy’s play to help unlock their running game. Not only will more consistent passing success help take the pressure off the run game, but the threat of McCarthy’s legs will help unlock the running game. The Giants used a slow mesh to simulate a read-option play on Tyrone Tracy’s touchdown, freezing a key Texans’ defender. The Giants could make (judicious) use of the read-option with McCarthy in this game — as they did with Jaxson Dart in Week 1 against Fangio acolyte Christian Parker — to help supplement their rushing attack. The Giants could also make use of Darnell Mooney as a pseudo-running back with sweeps and screen plays. Mooney has been disappointing as a receiver, but his athleticism and explosiveness have been apparent when he gets the ball in his hands. Doing so on schemed touches could be a way the Giants look to augment their rushing attack and adding an explosive element on the ground. Facing Fangio The Giants have spent most of the 2026 season facing defenses we’ve called “Fangio Adjacent”. That is, defenses designed and called by coaches who have either been inspired by Vic Fangio, or his acolytes. We’ve already been over the iterations enough to know the general shape of the “Fangio” defense. It’s based around a 4-2-5 nickel formation under a quarters coverage. He makes heavy use of pattern matching principles to add man coverage to his zone schemes, as well as using post-snap rotations to create ambiguity and doubt in quarterbacks’ reads. While his defenses frequently start out in a Cover-4 look, they often rotate to Cover 3, adding a defender to the box, or a hybrid coverage like Cover-6 or Cover-8* to give them a numbers advantage to the passing strength. * I go into more detail on Cover-6 and Cover-8 in our Week 1 preview of the Cowboys’ defense . Fangio doesn’t blitz all that often, just 22.5% of the time (26th in the NFL), instead trusting his defensive front to get home. While the details may shift with different coordinators and defensive rosters, the basic shape of the “Fangio” defense remains consistent and has become one of the most popular philosophies in the NFL. However, the biggest advantage that Fangio himself has always been that it’s his . More than any other coach, Fangio not only knows how is defense is able to attack offenses, but is also intimately aware of it’s weaknesses and how offenses go about attacking his scheme. We saw that first-hand last year when Fangio deviated from his scheme on Thursday Night Football. That game he opted to blitz Dart heavily in his second start. Fangio has typically eschewed the blitz, instead trusting his defensive front to get pressure while playing coverage behind them. While the decision to blitz a rookie is typically correct, it proved disastrous against Dart. The weaknesses were easily exploited by the athletic young quarterback, and it stressed the defense in ways that it wasn’t designed to sustain. Two weeks later, Fangio went back to his roots and played his usual coverages and didn’t blitz…

title: Previewing the Jets’ opposition: Kansas City Chiefs
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs have beaten the New York Jets in four of their five meetings since 2011, with the most recent being a controversial 23-20 win in 2023. That game saw Michael Carter II’s game-clinching interception negated by a phantom penalty on Sauce Gardner and wasted one of the best performances of Zach Wilson’s […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - NOVEMBER 1: Patrick Mahomes #15 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs with the football and looks to pass during the third quarter against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on November 1, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. The Broncos defeated the Chiefs 28-24. (Photo by Justin Edmonds/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs have beaten the New York Jets in four of their five meetings since 2011, with the most recent being a controversial 23-20 win in 2023. That game saw Michael Carter II’s game-clinching interception negated by a phantom penalty on Sauce Gardner and wasted one of the best performances of Zach Wilson’s career. In this matchup, the Chiefs will be heavy favorites despite having lost two in a row following a 5-0 start. Let’s break down the Chiefs’ roster going position by position: Quarterbacks The Jets have Patrick Mahomes to reckon with this week, and he’s having a solid season as he’s posting a quarterback rating of 99.7; his best since 2022. Mahomes has 12 touchdowns and four interceptions and is coming off a good game against the Broncos where he passed for 321 yards and three touchdowns with no interceptions. Behind Mahomes is a familiar face: Jets 2025 starter Justin Fields. Seventh round rookie Garrett Nussmeier is the number three. Offensive Line The Chiefs’ interior line is the same as last year led by pro bowlers Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith at center and right guard respectively. Smith has a team-high five offensive penalties. Kingsley Suamataia completes the interior trio at left guard, although he’s already been benched twice this year, including on Sunday where he was suddenly replaced before pre-game warmups by Mike Caliendo. That fuelled rumors that was was being disciplined by the coaching staff but Andy Reid denied this. Caliendo, who also started four games last year, has struggled in pass protection. Suamataia is expected to be back in the starting lineup for Sunday’s game. The tackle positions have seen some changes as last year’s starting right tackle, Jawaan Taylor, was released in March and the starting left tackle – 2025 first round pick Josh Simmons – is on injured reserve. Jaylon Moore, who started a handful of games last year, is currently starting at right tackle, while the left tackle is undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson, who is one of five undrafted rookies on the roster. Moore has given up a team-high three sacks, but Benson – while yet to surrender a sack – has given up the most pressure on the team. Moore missed week seven’s game, so former New York Giant Joshua Ezeudu started at right tackle in that one. The other backups are center Hunter Nourzad and another undrafted rookie; tackle Diego Pounds. Running Backs The Chiefs’ big offseason acquisition on offense was the reigning Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker. The move has been a resounding success as he rushed for 100 yards in four of his first five games as the Chiefs started 5-0. Since then, he’s averaged just three yards per carry, though. Even so, he’s just 10 yards off the league lead with 770 rushing yards. He has also caught 22 passes. There are two rookies backing up Walker – fifth round pick Emmett Johnson and the undrafted Jaydn Ott. Ott hasn’t played yet, though. The Chiefs also have a fullback – Ben VanSumeren – on the roster. However, they will also use defensive tackle Khyiris Tonga in short yardage situations. He has even carried the ball twice. Pass catchers The Chiefs’ top pass catching option has once again been tight end Travis Kelce, who has 410 receiving yards to lead the team. The leading pass catcher among the wide receivers is the speedy Xavier Worthy, who has 27 catches, albeit that he’s only averaging 8.5 yards per catch. Despite some injury concerns and legal issues, Rashee Rice is now back in the lineup for the Chiefs. He has 20 catches in five games this year. Tyquan Thornton was also starting at wide receiver, but he’s now on injured reserve. The backups are Jalen Royals, Andrew Armstrong, Nikko Remigio and fifth round rookie Cyrus Allen. Royals has seen the most action from this group. At tight end, Noah Gray is a solid contributor who gets plenty of playing time. Jake Briningstool and Jared Wiley round out this group. Defensive Line The Chiefs’ defensive line is anchored by pro bowler Chris Jones, although he is having a down year statistically with just half a sack, one tackle for loss and three quarterback hits. He had 7.5, 12 and 25 last year. George Karlaftis, who had six sacks last year, has a team-high two sacks and also leads the team with 16 quarterback hits (just one less than the rest of the team combined) and six tackles for loss. Karlaftis also has a team-high with eight passes defensed. In fact, these all eight of these came in the last five games. Prior to that, he had 17 in his first 67 NFL games. Tonga is the other starter at defensive tackle with Felix Anudike-Uzomah the other starting defensive end. Kansas City has been operating a three-man rotation inside with first round rookie Peter Woods getting plenty of playing time. However, Woods has been ruled out with a neck injury so Bryson Eason may need to step up. Last year’s second round pick Omarr Norman-Lott remains on the PUP list. The backups on the edge are second round rookie R Mason Thomas and Ashton Gillotte. Undrafted rookie Jack Pyburn is also on the roster. Linebackers Nick Bolton remains in a full-time role with Drue Tranquill on the field most of the time. Last year, Bolton had 154 tackles and Tranquill added 103. They’ve been productive this year, too, with Bolton on 68 tackles and Tranquill on 53 tackles, including five tackles for loss. Jack Cochrane gets playing time in three-linebacker sets, while Jeffrey Bassa has seen limited action. Cooper McDonald has yet to play any defensive snaps, though. Defensive Backs The Chiefs suffered a loss a few weeks ago when their top cornerback L’Jairus Sneed was placed on injured reserve. Sneed was also the team’s primary slot corner, so they’ve been using Christian Roland-Wallace in that role for the past few weeks. Nohl Williams and first round rookie Mansoor Delane are the current starters on the outside, although Kristian Fulton started in place of Delane on Sunday. Delane has a shoulder issue which is likely to limit him for the rest of the season but he was expected to return against the Jets. However, he has been ruled out, so Fulton will presumably start again. Melvin Smith and fourth round rookie Jadon Canady are also available to provide depth at cornerback. The starting safeties are Chamarri Conner, who had 117 tackles last season, and offseason signing Alohi Gilman. Jaden Hicks has also been getting playing time in three-safety sets. He also started the first three games with Conner out. Undrafted rookie safety Xavier Nwankpa has played five snaps so far this season. Special Teams Former pro bowl kicker Harrison Butker is having a rough year with six missed field goals already and Justin Tucker waiting in the wings on the practice squad in case he should falter again. Punter Matt Araiza is having his best year statistically in his third season with the Chiefs, though. Remigio is the team’s return specialist, although Johnson ends up sharing the work on kickoff returns. Remigio, who is yet to achieve a 50-yard return as he is halfway through his third season, is officially listed as questionable. Bassa and Nwankpa are the team’s most productive players in kick coverage this season, but last year they were led by McDonald and Cochrane. Canady and Nwankpa have been the primary gunners.

Hall gets 65+% of the snaps but does little with them, finishing with less than 50 yards from scrimmage. Hall and Allen combine for less than 90 yards from scrimmage. Taking advantage of Garrett Wilson’s absence, Omar Cooper, after being shutout last week, leads all Jets receivers with 80+ receiving yards and a touchdown. Geno Smith, forced to play from behind all game and without much of a ground game, is pressured into 2+ turnovers, including at least 1 interception for the fourth straight week. title: Eagles Film Review: Joe Milton is an easy player to get excited about
summary: This week got away from me. Life has been ridiculously busy, and I couldn’t put together my usual weekly preview article. But with the Eagles turning to Joe Milton at quarterback, I still wanted to give you something. So, let’s do this! Milton is an easy player to get excited about and a lot of […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 18: Joe Milton #14 of the Philadelphia Eagles reacts against the Carolina Panthers following an NFL football game at Lincoln Financial Field on October 18, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images This week got away from me. Life has been ridiculously busy, and I couldn’t put together my usual weekly preview article. But with the Eagles turning to Joe Milton at quarterback, I still wanted to give you something. So, let’s do this! Milton is an easy player to get excited about and a lot of fun to watch. I enjoyed this one. Strengths A rare arm The first thing you notice is the arm. Milton can rifle short and intermediate throws without needing a big wind-up or much of a step into the ball. It almost looks like a flick of the wrist, and the ball arrives with unusual zip. The release is quick, too. He does not need a long gathering motion to generate velocity, which matters when a defender is closing or when the offense wants the ball out before the underneath coverage can rally. That quick release could also make the Eagles’ RPO game more dangerous. A bubble or slant has to get out before the defender responsible for the receiver can drive downhill. Milton has the arm to deliver those throws quickly, and the ball can arrive before the defense has time to recover. The speed of the delivery gives the concept a chance to punish a defense for overcommitting to the run. Receivers may need to adjust, because the ball comes in hot, but this is a rare physical tool. It jumps out on film. The same velocity that makes an RPO throw difficult to defend can also make an ordinary catch harder if the ball is high or behind the receiver. Joe Milton thread… because why not! 1) He is a fun player to watch. If the Eagles can't be good, they can at least be a bit more fun. The most obvious thing that stands out is his arm strength. It is pretty absurd. He effortlessly rifles these short/intermediate throws. The… pic.twitter.com/5HHlW5Df4r — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 The arm also lets Milton challenge tight windows. On this rep, he sees the linebacker dropping underneath and trusts that he can beat him to the spot. The ball gets there with enough speed to take away the defender’s chance to close the space. That is the frustrating part of his film. His accuracy is not uniformly bad. He can put the ball exactly where it needs to go, then miss the next one by a mile. 2) He can throw into tight windows because of his arm talent. When he's accurate, it's very effective! He spots the LB dropping underneath here, but he knows he can beat him to the spot because of his arm talent. His ball placement is somewhat bizarre because it seems to be… pic.twitter.com/Q8rBcGZmBD — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 Milton can drive the ball downfield, too. The Eagles have been short on vertical passing lately, and this preseason throw shows why they should give him chances to attack deep. He drops the ball into the bucket with both velocity and placement. This isn’t just about throwing it far; he has to put enough air and location on it for the receiver to run onto the ball while keeping the defender from making a play. A strong arm can force a defense to respect the deep part of the field, but a deep passing game only works if the quarterback can pair range with precise ball location. Milton shows that combination here. The Eagles have not given us much vertical offense recently, and I need to see some of it. I’m hopeful Milton will throw some deep bombs this week! 3) I mean, phew. His arm talent includes throwing downfield. He had a couple of beautiful bucket throws this preseason, including this one. You can't throw it any better! The Eagles have had no vertical passing game at all the past two weeks, but expect them to take more deep… pic.twitter.com/n548HZd6Jb — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 Comfortable on the move and patient in the pocket I expect the Eagles to use more play-action bootlegs with Milton. He looked comfortable throwing on the move throughout the preseason, and this was supposed to be a bigger part of the offense already. Boot action can make the defense honor the run, change the quarterback’s launch point, and create a simpler picture outside the pocket. Milton can sell that action and still deliver the ball while moving, which gives the play a chance to stress the edge defender and the coverage behind him. If the Eagles want to lean on play action, Milton’s comfort on the move is a real reason to call it. Maybe we finally see more of it this week. If you can’t run play-action bootlegs with Joe Milton, I’m not sure you will be able to do it with anyone… 4) I expect the Eagles to run a lot more play-action bootlegs with Joe Milton at quarterback. He is very comfortable throwing on the move, and I saw a lot of bootlegs this preseason. This was supposed to be a big part of the offense, and it hasn't been, so maybe we will see a… pic.twitter.com/U4dEOTCyxR — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 Milton can run, but he does not seem eager to abandon the pocket at the first opportunity. Here, he eliminates the routes at the top of the screen, works back to the comeback, steps up to avoid the edge rusher, and keeps looking to throw. He could take off through the open lane, but he wants to win as a passer first. He is prepared to stay in the pocket, make space for the throw, and keep his eyes downfield. 5) Although he can run, he does want to win from the pocket first. This is a good example of him eliminating the routes at the top of the screen, getting back to the comeback route, stepping up in the pocket, and avoiding the edge rusher coming around the edge. He could run… pic.twitter.com/9TWQN6emS3 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 He is particularly comfortable rolling to his left. This is a 25-yard completion on the move, and he makes it look easy. A right-handed quarterback throwing across his body in that direction can make the ball sail, but Milton stays balanced enough to put it on the receiver without stopping and resetting. He gets the throw away while still moving rather than needing to gather himself and give the defense extra time to close. Throwing on the move while rolling to the left, for a right-handed quarterback, is one of the more difficult skills to execute. Milton can do it pretty easily. The Eagles can move him away from the original launch point without reducing the play to “run or throw it away.” The film shows that he can keep the play alive as a passer. 6) One of the other things that stood out from his film is his ability to throw when rolling to the left. The Eagles should definitely be able to use him on bootlegs to either side of the field. This is a 25-yard pass while rolling to the left, and it's effortless. pic.twitter.com/Gaci9JrN4s — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 A downfield weapon Then there is the deep ball. On this 50-yard throw, Milton looks off the safety, takes the one-on-one shot, and puts the ball in the back corner of the end zone. He may be a beat late, but the arm strength gives him enough margin to complete a throw that would be unavailable to many quarterbacks. He has to get it over the coverage and still keep it in a spot where only his receiver can make the play. 7) Remember what I said about the ability to drop it into a bucket downfield? Phew. 50 yards on a rope. He looks off the safety, takes the one-on-one shot, and puts it perfectly in the back corner of the end zone. I think he's actually a beat late throwing it, but he can still… pic.twitter.com/fbtMjVVHqF — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) November 6, 2026 Designed run threat The running ability is another obvious way to make this offense more interesting. Milton is a big, powerful quarterback who can move quickly in the open field. The 4.6 40 time is evident on film. The Eagles should design runs for him and use that threat to…

full_text: HOUSTON, TX - OCTOBER 25: J.J. McCarthy #18 of the New York Giants warms up before kickoff against the Houston Texans during an NFL football game at Reliant Stadium on October 25, 2026 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Eagles have been very consistent this season. Last Sunday, in their 27-10 at Washington, they were consistent across the board in all three phases of the game, special teams, offense and defense. They were terribly consistent in all three phases. Offensively, the Eagles are the worst team in the NFL, with 2,122 yards of total offense, which translates into a season-low 265.3 yards a game average. Staying consistent, the Eagles are the 27th-ranked defense in the NFL, giving up 367.3 yards a game, and not to be outdone, the Eagles are 30th in run defense, giving up 1,055 yards on the ground, for an average of 131.9 yards a game, which is 28th overall. Now, the Eagles face a hungry quarterback looking for his second chance to prove himself in the NFL in the New York Giants’ J.J. McCarthy, who is fresh off a bye week absorbing more of the Giants’ offense. The Eagles are in the throes of a six-game losing streak, their worst losing streak in 14 years, when they lost eight-straight in Andy Reid’s last season with the Eagles. The longest losing streak in Eagles’ history is 14 games, spanning back to their 1936 and 1937 seasons, when they lost 11-straight games in 1936 after winning their season opener, and losing the first three games of 1937. The longest losing streak in the Super Bowl era is 11-straight games, which goes to the infamous 1968 Eagles, who lost their first 11 games that season. The 2026 Eagles are in the running for records—just five more games to go to reach the magical mark of 12-straight losses, okay, four after the Eagles lose to the Giants at 1 p.m. on Sunday in a game and season no one really cares about anymore. Well, the Giants care. They’re looking to make the playoffs for the first time since 2022—and first NFC East title since 2011, when they went 9-7 and won the Super Bowl. The last time the Giants beat the Eagles in Philadelphia was on October 27, 2013, when the Giants won 15–7. McCarthy was 10, tossing touchdowns to fifth graders. When asked how different the Giants have looked with McCarthy, Eagles’ defensive coordinator Vic Fangio said this week, “Good. They’ve got a really good offense. They’ve got skill at the receiving position. They did a nice job raiding the Ravens, not only for [New York Giants Head Coach] John [Harbaugh], but for [New York Giants TE Isaiah] Likely and [New York Giants FB Patrick] Ricard. They’ve got a lot of the Ravens type offense that they had when [New York Giants Senior Offensive Assistant] Greg [Roman] was there, and they’ve intermixed Kansas City type passing in there with [New York Giants Offensive Coordinator] Matt [Nagy]. They’ve got it going right now. They’ve got good wideouts, good tight ends, two good backs. The quarterback has come in, in a short period of time and really done a nice job, for them to get him for a sixth-round pick is a steal.” Compounding the problem of stopping McCarthy is the challenge of stopping Giants’ wide receiver Malik Nabers, who is 9th in the NFL in receiving with 605 yards and 7th with 48 catches and 11th in receiving first downs (27). “He’s tough. He’s fast, he’s quick, he’s athletic, good hands,” Fangio said about Nabers. “I mean, he’s double tough.” If the Eagles continue their consistent path, the Giants’ 13-game losing streak at Lincoln Financial Field should end, while the Eagles lose their seventh-straight game, bringing them closer to that magic number of 12, with 8 games making the 2026 season a truly memorable, record-breaking year. The Eagles have been very consistent this season. Consistently bad.

summary: It’s hard to put into words just how important Jaylen Warren has been to the Steelers’ success this season. full_text: (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s hard to put into words just how important Jaylen Warren has been to the Steelers’ success this season. The running back’s 998 scrimmage yards through eight weeks of action is good for third in the league behind only Jahmyr Gibbs and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. There is no doubt that Warren is playing at an elite level, and people are starting to have some serious conversations about the way the back has been playing. Former Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger recently went as far as to say that Warren deserves MVP consideration for his play so far this season on his “Footbahlin with Ben Roethlisberger” podcast. “This guy needs to start to be talked about in some MVP stuff. Like league MVP or offensive MVP,” Roethlisberger said. “His numbers and some of the stuff he’s doing is pretty impressive. His yards after contact have to be some of the highest in the league. There’s a lot of things that don’t look good and then all of a sudden it’s like, oh, he fell forward for three.” Warren is averaging 4.89 yards per touch so far this season, the most by any running back with at least 100 touches. Despite his incredible efficiency and performance this season, there are still 16 players with higher odds to win the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award on FanDuel Sportsbook. Is Warren a value play? Possibly, but the clear reason for the lack of love for Warren comes from the fact that he only has three touchdowns this season. Despite being a workhouse and the best player on Pittsburgh’s offense, the touchdown output, coupled with the Steelers not being a flashy offense, hurts his chances significantly. All of this to say that Roethlisberger is absolutely correct in saying Warren deserves significantly more attention than he is getting for the unbelievable season he is in the midst of having for the Steelers. title: Reviewing Steelers narratives at the bye week: Elite defense? Top-5 O-line?
summary: As the Steelers enter a Week 9 bye, the midseason break from Pittsburgh football presents a perfect opportunity to look at the big picture of the team as the crucial second half of the season approaches. At 6-2 and currently on a four-game winning streak, it’s fair to say the Steelers might be overhyped in […]
full_text: Photo by Justin K. Aller/Getty Images | Getty Images As the Steelers enter a Week 9 bye, the midseason break from Pittsburgh football presents a perfect opportunity to look at the big picture of the team as the crucial second half of the season approaches. At 6-2 and currently on a four-game winning streak, it’s fair to say the Steelers might be overhyped in some areas. But every fanbase has its doubters, and there might be too much doom and gloom when it comes to some storylines, as well. As a result, this week Steelers Read & React will be taking a look at the 12 biggest Steelers narratives at midseason. Which ones are real? Which ones are stretching the truth? Is it just too early to tell with some? Find out our thoughts below, and let us know yours in the comments: Zach Frazier is an All-Pro RB: After a few seasons of always hovering near the top of NFL media’s top interior lineman rankings, Frazier has broken into “best center in the NFL” territory during the Steelers’ recent win streak. Frazier is an absolute dog on this run. Both guards are asked to get to the second level to engage the LBs, and they succeed in getting the job done. Washington almost inadvertently blows up the play by sending his man flying almost into the run, but the RB hurdles. 8 yd gain pic.twitter.com/1lkGZBuMNO — Ryan Parish (@ArmchairScout21) November 2, 2026 Film bros love Frazier. Analytics nerds do too, with Frazier ranking first in the NFL at his position in PFF grades, with 79.5 as of this writing. And the Steelers’ line as a whole has been mauling as of late, ranking top-10 in both run success rate and lowest quarterback pressure rate so far this season. Frazier’s combination of toughness, athleticism, strength, and football IQ has been quite literally in the center of all of Pittsburgh’s recent success on offense in 2026. Barring a big-time drop-off from Frazier and/or the Steelers’ offense in the second half of the season, a first- or second-team All-Pro seems almost guaranteed at this point for the Pittsburgh center. At the moment, he has all the media hype, and more importantly, the play to back it up. The verdict: Absolutely. The defense is elite RP: I don’t want to be a downer on what has been a better first half of the season than many expected, but I will be a stickler about how readily we throw the “E” word around. The Pittsburgh defense has been stellar over the past month. It’s been mostly healthy, save for the Derrick Harmon injury and Jalen Ramsey playing through a fractured wrist. Even DeShon Elliott is back. But I stop short of calling this unit “elite,” at least for now. For starters, just look at who they’ve played. Opponent QB (Rank in EPA/Dropback † ) Offensive EPA (Rank) Offensive Success Rate (Rank) PPG (Rank) Passing Yards Per Game (Rank) Falcons * Cooper Rush (54th) -62.53 (27th) 42.3% (17th) 21.4 (23rd) 188.4 (24th) Patriots Drake Maye (8th) 8.67 (9th) 44.8% (12th) 23.0 (16th) 244.1 (11th) Bengals Joe Burrow (6th) 31.46 (6th) 48.5% (4th) 29.4 (2nd) 288.4 (1st) Browns Deshaun Watson (24th) -63.63 (28th) 40.3% (25th) 17.4 (29th) 204.3 (22nd) Colts Daniel Jones (29th) -72.57 (30th) 40.9% (24th) 20.1 (26th) 174.6 (28th) Buccaneers * Jalon Daniels (40th) -70.33 (29th) 40.2% (26th) 22.3 (20th) 131.4 (32nd) Saints Tyler Shough (17th) -19.89 (18th) 41.8% (19th) 23.1 (14th) 229.7 (14th) * Team had an injury replacement at quarterback † Rush and Daniels haven’t played enough to be considered qualified passers; their ranks reflect where they rank when we expand that parameter, while all others are ranked among qualified passers With the clear exception of the Bengals, and a Patriots offense that requires a lot of context when discussing whether or not they’ve been “good” this year, the Steelers haven’t exactly been playing the NFL’s top offenses. Likewise, with the exception of Joe Burrow and Drake Maye — and again, Maye has significantly rebounded in his quality of play since facing the Steelers in Week 2 — the Steelers haven’t been facing the cream of the crop under center either. That doesn’t diminish what the Pittsburgh defense has been doing in recent weeks. Heading into the bye, the Steelers lead the NFL in sacks (26). They rank sixth in both EPA allowed per pass (-0.15) and per rush (-0.12), and are tied for the fifth-lowest average yards per carry allowed (3.6). They’ve allowed just 17 runs of 10 or more yards, tied for the eighth-fewest in the NFL. The 18 points per game they’re surrendering ranks third in the NFL, as do their 13 takeaways (seven interceptions, six fumble recoveries). The Steelers defense has given up 11 TDs through 8 games. They gave up 19 in the first 8 games last season. Of the 11 they've given up this year, only 1 is in the second half. 12 of the 19 through the first 8 games last year were in the second half. — Zachary Smith (@ZacharySmithPGH) November 2, 2026 "They want the ball, you kidding me?" The @Steelers defense took that personally 🤷 @InsideTheNFL pic.twitter.com/WfDmdsAdpE — NFL Films (@NFLFilms) November 4, 2026 Still, it’s hard for me to declare this an “elite” defense full-throatedly without seeing them face a great offense outside of the division. Unfortunately, a look at the Steelers’ remaining schedule likely won’t give many chances for them to be tested. Among the opponents left on Pittsburgh’s schedule, only Jacksonville (3rd), Cincinnati (6th), Houston (13th), and Carolina (14th) rank in the top half of the NFL in offensive EPA. Among those, only the Jaguars (+0.11) and the Bengals (+0.07) are generating positive EPA per play, and it should be noted that Carolina’s offense has been in free fall after a hot September. Similarly, among the quarterbacks the Steelers have left on the schedule, only Trevor Lawrence (4th), Burrow (6th), and C.J. Stroud (10th) rank inside the top-15 passers in EPA per dropback on the season. I’ll dive a little further into what the games against these passers might tell us about the AFC playoffs in the final question of this column. There’s also some nosiness with the Steelers current lead in sacks. While their raw total is enough to presently lead the NFL, some of the underlying metrics might indicate they’ve had some luck in that regard. The Steelers rank 26th in the NFL in pressure rate (32.6%) and just 16th in total pressures. This says to me that the Steelers might have had a knack for getting timely sacks, but they are not generating as much pressure against the pass as their sack totals might have us otherwise think. I could be overthinking things, certainly, but when paired with my nagging concern about the level of quarterback play this defense has faced, it does leave room to wonder how the defense might fare against some of the more skilled quarterbacks they’re certain to face in the playoffs. The verdict: Incomplete. The numbers are great, and Patrick Graham is accenting the strengths of his players while limiting exposure to their weaknesses — but we need to see them against better offenses first. T.J. Watt is back, baby RB: T.J. Watt is back atop the NFL sacks leaderboard (tied for first with the Texans’ Will Anderson with 7.5) after a two-sack performance against the Browns on Sunday. Sure, it took him one more game to reach that number than the Texans’ star, but considering Watt is 32 and was pronounced as “washed” by a number of fans last year after logging seven sacks in 14 games, it’s good to see him back in superstar territory. I’d argue the eye test and advanced stats still show that Watt isn’t quite the player he was in his prime. This year, his pressure rate is a very good 10.7% (that number hovered between 13.7% and 17.6% in all but one of his first six seasons) and his playing-time percentage has also dropped to what is by far a career low at 65.1% after being above 82% in all but one of his prior seasons. However, Watt’s sack percentage has jumped up to 3.5%, on track for the third-best mark of his career, while his get-off time is currently the…

title: Run game, not quarterback, is the offensive key to ‘Seahawks Football’
summary: This has been a challenging year for the Seattle Seahawks. Maybe we should’ve known it would be that way when Sam Darnold was injured just mere snaps into the season. Drew Lock stepped in admirably leading Seattle to victories in the first two weeks. When Darnold came back earlier than most expected, it looked like […]
full_text: This has been a challenging year for the Seattle Seahawks. Maybe we should’ve known it would be that way when Sam Darnold was injured just mere snaps into the season . Drew Lock stepped in admirably leading Seattle to victories in the first two weeks. When Darnold came back earlier than most expected, it looked like things were going to get back on track. Then, the maelstrom of turnovers and injuries hit, leaving Seattle looking rudderless at 4-4. Darnold is injured once again , and his long-term future with the Seahawks is (rightly) being questioned. John Schneider has done this before, pivoting from both Russell Wilson and Geno Smith. Regardless of who is taking snaps under center, Mike Macdonald wants to play “Seahawks Football.” He’s referenced that multiple times this year, and used it when discussing his hire of offensive coordinator Brian Fleury. The idea is to have a system that is replicable and not reliant on specific personnel. More specifically, “Seahawks Football” needs a strong run game as the backbone. Even just the threat of the run alleviates the pressure from the passing offense. Seattle hasn’t had the luxury of that in 2026 due to a litany of issues including poor blocking, fumbles, injuries, etc. The low hanging fruit is to bring up the defection of Ken Walker III. Yes, his departure is part of the reason for the struggling rushing attack, but I think even he would have a tough time running behind this offensive line. After a giant step forward with line play last season, expectations were extremely high for this year with all five starters returning. Anthony Bradford was injured early on, and the rest of the line seemed to regress and struggle. Quenton Nelson was brought in as part of the solution , but his addition created new problems that reared their ugly heads in the crapstorm against the Chicago Bears. Backup left tackle, new left guard Grey Zabel moving to the right side for the first time in the NFL, two running backs returning from injury. That kinda seems like a recipe for disaster, doesn’t it? And disaster ensued as the offense was ineffective in everything except the “throw it to JSN” play. When Nelson was acquired from the Indianapolis Colts, many were wondering why they traded him weeks before the trade deadline when they could’ve possibly gotten a bigger return down the line. I’m not going to say Seattle sacrificed the game against Chicago, but the three weeks following that are matchups against the Arizona Cardinals, Las Vegas Raiders, and the bye week with a huge rematch against the San Francisco 49ers looming. Having Quenton Nelson and Grey Zabel broken into their new teams/positions at that point for the stretch run is pivotal. Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet should also be rounding into form by then. The injury to Nelson throws a monkey wrench into things, but the theory would still be that the Seahawks run game should be improved coming out of the bye week. Mike Macdonald’s vision of “Seahawks Football” is not to throw the football 40 times a game. Control the game by moving the sticks on the ground, supplement with explosive passes, and play tough defense. That’s how the Seahawks were successful when they were on their Super Bowl run last season. Hell, that was the blueprint for Pete Carroll’s Seahawks as well. It’s a proven formula that works. The key to getting back on track starts with the OL and RB room, not who will be taking snaps be it Sam Darnold, Drew Lock, or Jalen Milroe. I still believe that Macdonald wants a QB who can be an asset in the run game. His time in Baltimore with Lamar Jackson showed him just how dangerous a dual threat QB can be. After Milroe was drafted, Macdonald spoke on that topic. “Quarterbacks who can extend the play are incredibly difficult to defend,” Macdonald said. “The worst thing in the world is you play the first (part) of the play perfectly on defense, and you’re like, ‘All right, sweet, we did it.’ And the guy still has the ball, and you’ve got to defend the next play, and then sometimes a third play. “He can kill you in the first play, he can kill you in the second play, he can kill you in the third play. It’s not a fun existence to live in consistently. He has that ability.” I swear that I read somewhere after that draft that Milroe was a Mike Macdonald pick, but I haven’t been able to find it. That would make a ton of sense, however, given Macdonald’s time playing against Baltimore and his history/respect for the armed forces, of which Milroe’s father was a part of just like Macdonald’s. Maybe Milroe isn’t the answer as the QB for Seattle, but I have a gut feeling that Macdonald wants a QB that can break the game open with his legs as well. Yeah, so does everyone else, I get it. A QB that can accentuate the run game makes the offense so much harder to defend. If it gives the defensive wunderkind Macdonald problems, you can bet it’s an issue for everyone else. That brings us back to the crux of the issue. Seattle’s run game just isn’t good enough right now to carry the team, and it needs to be. Forget worrying about a repeat. Don’t fret about playoffs. If the Seahawks can fix the run game everything will take care of itself. That’s the formula for replicable success that will bring Seattle back into championship contention no matter who the QB is. That’s “Seahawks Football” .

Brian Fleury had a unique background involving offense, defense, special teams and Kyle Shanahan mentorship. Most of the starters on the team remained. Darnold, who does well in the Shanahan style offense looked poised to continue his 2024-2025 success. Now, the team being 4-4 and while the defense has help up its end still being a top three unit, and special teams being top 15 or higher depending on the metric, the offense outside of Jaxon-Smith Njigba has been less stellar. This leaves fans wondering: How confident are we in this team? Will Darnold be the quarterback still in 2027? We asked you those very questions. Let’s see where you, the fans, landed. Just 33 percent of fans believe Sam Darnold will be the quarterback next season. This is understandable. He has struggled this season, and is now out with his second set of injuries this season . How much of his struggles are on him, and how much of it is due to Fleury, the scheme he has imposed on the offense, and his play calling, that is for fans to decide. We all have our opinions, and ultimately, only they know the truth. Sam Darnold was 30th out of 33 qualifying QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured, but he was also one of the least pressured QBs in the NFL last year. He's 31st out of 31 QBs in EPA/dropback when pressured in 2026, and he's top 12 in pressure rate. — Mookie Alexander (@mookiealexander) November 3, 2026 The fact is, Darnold has not looked comfortable in this offense, and it looks as thought the offensive players have been struggling with the new play calling and scheme. title: Seahawks release RB Velus Jones Jr., clear spot on active roster
summary: Although the Seattle Seahawks remain in the midst of an injury crisis ahead of their crucial Week 9 clash against their division rival Arizona Cardinals, they’ll have some some room to work with after Friday’s roster shuffle. The team announced they released running back Velus Jones Jr. and subsequently re-signed him to their practice squad, […]
full_text: Although the Seattle Seahawks remain in the midst of an injury crisis ahead of their crucial Week 9 clash against their division rival Arizona Cardinals, they’ll have some some room to work with after Friday’s roster shuffle. The team announced they released running back Velus Jones Jr. and subsequently re-signed him to their practice squad, where they had a vacant spot. As a vested veteran, he was not subject to waivers. With Jones Jr. reverting to the practice squad, Seattle now has an open spot on their 53-man roster. Through three games, Jones Jr. logged 28 yards on nine carries, but suffered a hamstring injury in the team’s Week 7 victory over the Kansas City Chiefs and was forced to miss Monday’s game against the Chicago Bears. Although he practiced in a limited capacity on both Wednesday and Thursday, the return of running backs Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet on top of the team already committed to Emanuel Wilson as well as George Holani likely would’ve made him odd man out even if he was deemed healthy enough to return. With DT Leonard Williams (stinger), OG Quenton Nelson (knee), WR Rashid Shaheed (knee), LB Uchenna Nwosu (ankle), QB Sam Darnold (quadriceps, ribs), Brandon Pili (back), and OT Charles Cross (ankle) already ruled out, the Seahawks appear poised to fill the vacant spot with a player of one of those seven positions and they’ll have plenty of options to choose from. While WR Montorie Foster Jr. was elevated against the Bears, Seattle signed QB Adrian Martinez and linebacker Jamie Sheriff to their practice squad on Wednesday, seemingly hinting one of them could take the final spot. Alongside Nwosu’s injury, LB Connor O’Toole (foot) is deemed questionable and if he’s ultimately ruled out, Sheriff fits the bill especially given his experience with the team. However, the Seahawks are currently poised to have just two quarterbacks (Drew Lock, Jalen Milroe) on the roster for Sunday’s game, so it wouldn’t be surprising if the opted to add a third, considering Milroe’s inexperience. The Seahawks are set to announce their game elevations on Saturday afternoon.

title: Seahawks All-22 storylines: Where the Bears found success against Seattle’s defense
summary: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest post by Ryan Woodall, assistant coach at Edmonds-Woodway High School in Edmonds, Washington) Football and life are games of living and learning, then improving. full_text: (Editor’s note: The following is a guest post by Ryan Woodall, assistant coach at Edmonds-Woodway High School in Edmonds, Washington) Football and life are games of living and learning, then improving. It’s hard to learn when you’re dominating. You need a couple punches in the mouth to truly ascend. Think of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers game last year. The Seattle Seahawks allowed 38 points, but after that, the Rams were truly the only team to score 20+ on Seattle. The Cardinals reached 20+ when down 41-15 in the 4th quarter, while the Titans scored a last-second TD to get over 20. This year the Commanders got Seattle early, but the 49ers and Chargers didn’t truly feel like their offense dominated. After watching the film, here are the storylines from Monday’s loss to the Chicago Bears: *Success = Positive EPA *All stats are from Sumer Sports Seahawks 1st down run defense dominance The Bears stayed committed to running the ball on 1st down. They did so 15 times with only 3 being successful (20%), averaging 1.6 yards on those carries. Overall the Seahawks had the Bears in 2nd & 8+ 12 times Monday. Across the NFL from ‘22-‘26 (regular season), series that have a 2nd & 8+ gain a first down 49% of the time. The Bears gained a 1st down 7/12 for a 58% conversion rate. Seahawks vs Bears On 1st & 10 the Bears rushed 15 times for 1.6 YPC. With only 3 successful runs. pic.twitter.com/TGLdiNjrjY — Ryan Woodall (@Egghand_FanDumb) November 6, 2026 Seahawks 2nd down let down Piggybacking off the 2nd & 8+ numbers, the Bears’ chances of reaching a 1st down go down significantly with another stop on 2nd down. Across the NFL from ‘22-‘26 (regular season), series with a 3rd & 8+ have a 26% conversion rate, while 3rd & 5+ has a 33% conversion rate. Bears 3rd down conversions on Monday 3rd & 8+ = 1/5 = 20% 3rd & 5+ = 2/7 = 29% 3rd/4th & <5 = 6/8 = 75% On 2nd down you don’t need it all; you just need to get half back. The Bears had quick route concepts to get what they needed without risking sacks. The quick throws beat some tight coverage. They had runs with combo blocks to move a DL and get up to a backer. Again not playing to get it all, just get to a manageable 3rd. The Seahawks also gave them a few with missed tackles, plus allowed Caleb Williams to escape when the Bears tried to throw deeper. Seahawks vs Bears. Here are the Bears on 2nd and long (couple 2nd & 5) – Good concepts to occupy Seahawks underneath defenders – Combo/Double team blocks to control the LOS – A couple missed reps by defenders – A screen that missed but could’ve gone for a lot Nothing… pic.twitter.com/3oKTM1kUhX — Ryan Woodall (@Egghand_FanDumb) November 5, 2026 Chicago Bears scheme Combo blocks/Bodies in the box The Bears know the challenge that comes with facing Seattle. 49% of the time the Seahawks only have 6 defenders in the box. Their light boxes allow the 10th most yards (4.1) while seeing the 6th most rush attempts (52). The Bears’ plan for the light box was to Combo (2 blockers are responsible for 1 DL & 1 LB together) where they could. But you can’t combo everyone, especially with only 5 OL, which prompted the Bears to bring in TEs or WRs to help combo with OL or seal off the edge rushers. The combos generally worked, but there’s still OL 1v1 blocking, which is where Seattle was able to fight off and help minimize the gains. LBs also did well hitting the OL first, to control the block and ricochet off to make tackles. Seahawks vs Bears Seahawks dare teams to run. By using a light box (6 or less) 49% of the time. Bears plan of attack was to bring in TEs and combo block wherever they could. Allowing Bears to stop DL penetration and get up to LBs. 2.69 YPC seems great, but it’s about timing.… pic.twitter.com/8tqBkbJeeE — Ryan Woodall (@Egghand_FanDumb) November 4, 2026 Attacking the Seahawks seam November just started, but Caleb Williams wasn’t waiting for Thanksgiving to feast. Williams had 17 throws between the numbers and hashes (known as the “seam”) for 170 yards , accounting for 69% of his yards with 11 successful . Williams had 7 throws 10+ yards downfield, tallying 99 yards ( 40% of total) with 5 being successful. On all Dig routes (deep in), Williams was 5/6 for 110 yards ( 45% of total). In weeks 1-7, the Seahawks allowed 72 yards/game between numbers and hash, with an average target depth (ADOT) of 3.9. This suggests check downs and quick throws were accumulating over the game. Williams finished with 7.6 ADOT. Seahawks vs Bears Caleb Williams feasting on Seahawks with In Breakers pic.twitter.com/EmPMEXIx0j — Ryan Woodall (@Egghand_FanDumb) November 6, 2026

title: Seahawks vs. Cardinals Week 9 preview: Can Drew Lock repeat his Week 2 success?
summary: A NFC West matchup always carries extra weight, and Sunday’s meeting between the Seattle Seahawks and Arizona Cardinals is no exception. Seattle enters Week 9 with a 4-4 record after a disappointing 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears, while Arizona arrives at 3-5 following an impressive 33-30 overtime victory over the Dallas Cowboys. The two […]
full_text: A NFC West matchup always carries extra weight, and Sunday’s meeting between the Seattle Seahawks and Arizona Cardinals is no exception. Seattle enters Week 9 with a 4-4 record after a disappointing 34-17 loss to the Chicago Bears, while Arizona arrives at 3-5 following an impressive 33-30 overtime victory over the Dallas Cowboys. The two teams already met in Week 2, when Seattle dominated Arizona 31-7 on the road. Drew Lock started that game in place of an injured Sam Darnold, completing 19 of 26 passes for 235 yards and three touchdowns. Now, with Darnold sidelined once again, Lock is expected to get another opportunity against the Cardinals. There is, however, a different challenge awaiting Seattle this time around. Arizona has made a quarterback change of its own, turning to Gardner Minshew after Jacoby Brissett struggled to close out the game against the Dallas Cowboys. The Cardinals are coming off their best offensive performance of the season Arizona’s comeback against Dallas was largely powered by two players: Gardner Minshew and Tyler Allgeier. After Jacoby Brissett struggled throughout the first half, completing just 10 of 23 passes for 119 yards and throwing an interception, head coach Mike LaFleur made the decision to turn to Minshew. The veteran quarterback immediately changed the complexion of the game. Minshew completed 17 of 23 passes for 188 yards and three touchdowns, leading four consecutive touchdown drives to bring Arizona back from a 17-3 deficit. His connection with Michael Wilson was particularly important, with the receiver finishing the afternoon with eight catches for 111 yards and a touchdown, including the game-tying score with six seconds remaining. However, the biggest surprise was the Cardinals’ running game. Tyler Allgeier (who would’ve been an amazing addition for the Seahawks in the last offseason…) exploded for 147 yards and a touchdown on just 11 carries, adding 44 receiving yards and another score. His performance was instrumental in Arizona’s 33-30 overtime victory. That is an important development for Seattle. The Seahawks have had their own difficulties defending the run in the edge, and allowing Allgeier to find the same kind of space he enjoyed against Dallas could make this a much more difficult afternoon for Mike Macdonald’s defense. There are still questions surrounding Arizona’s backfield. Jeremiyah Love suffered another ankle injury against Dallas, while Bam Knight entered concussion protocol. Their availability will be worth monitoring throughout the week. Trey McBride remains Arizona’s biggest receiving threat Even with the emergence of Michael Wilson, Trey McBride remains the centerpiece of Arizona’s passing game. The tight end has recorded 66 receptions for 544 yards and five touchdowns this season, making him one of the most productive players at his position. Seattle has historically had difficulties containing McBride. His ability to find space between linebackers and safeties, particularly in the middle of the field, presents a challenging matchup for the Seahawks’ defense. This becomes even more important considering some of Seattle’s recent defensive struggles. The linebackers have had difficulties consistently covering the space behind them, and McBride is exactly the kind of player who can exploit those situations. If Arizona can establish a rhythm with Minshew, expect the Cardinals to look for their tight end frequently. Michael Wilson also deserves attention. Despite playing through fractured ribs, he managed to produce a big performance against Dallas. His availability and effectiveness will be important, particularly with Arizona looking to build on the chemistry developed with Minshew. Can Seattle’s defensive line control the game again? The first meeting between these teams provided a pretty clear blueprint for Seattle. The Seahawks dominated the line of scrimmage, generated 18 quarterback pressures and limited Arizona to just 151 total yards. Jacoby Brissett struggled under pressure, completing only 4 of 11 attempts for 9 yards when pressured, while Seattle effectively shut down the Cardinals’ running game. However, Arizona’s offensive situation has changed since then. Minshew brings a different style of play, and the Cardinals are coming off a performance in which they accumulated 467 total yards against Dallas. Seattle will need to rediscover the defensive intensity it displayed in September. Getting pressure without consistently committing extra defenders will be particularly important against Minshew, who showed against Dallas that he can punish defenses when given time to find his receivers. The health of the defensive front is another concern. Leonard Williams left the game against Chicago with a stinger, while Uchenna Nwosu and other defensive contributors are also dealing with injuries. Their availability could have a significant impact on Seattle’s ability to control the line of scrimmage. The biggest question: Drew Lock For Seattle, the biggest storyline heading into Sunday is undoubtedly the quarterback position. Sam Darnold will miss the game after suffering a quadriceps injury against Chicago. Head coach Mike Macdonald also revealed that Darnold played through a cracked rib suffered early in that game. He will not be placed on injured reserve, but his return will depend on his recovery. Drew Lock is expected to start, although he has been dealing with an elbow injury that limited his participation over the previous two weeks. Seattle is also preparing Jalen Milroe to serve as the backup. There is some reason for optimism. Lock already faced Arizona in Week 2, when he threw for 235 yards and three touchdowns in Seattle’s 31-7 victory. He demonstrated that he can take advantage of opportunities against this defense, particularly when connecting with Jaxon Smith-Njigba downfield. Still, the circumstances are different. Lock will be coming off an injury of his own, and Seattle’s offense has struggled to find consistency in recent weeks. The offensive line also needs to provide better protection, especially against an Arizona defense featuring Josh Sweat and Budda Baker. If Lock is unable to play effectively, the Seahawks could be forced to lean more heavily on their running game and short passing concepts. That makes establishing the ground attack early even more important. Final Thoughts This is an important opportunity for both teams. Seattle needs to respond after its disappointing loss to Chicago, while Arizona has a chance to build momentum following an impressive comeback against Dallas. The first meeting was a one-sided affair, but the Cardinals are a different team offensively with Minshew under center. Their passing game has a new spark, Allgeier is coming off a tremendous performance, and McBride remains a difficult matchup for any defense. For the Seahawks, the key will be controlling the line of scrimmage, limiting explosive plays and giving Drew Lock a manageable situation. Seattle has already shown that it can dominate this opponent, but doing so again will require a much more complete performance. Playing at Lumen Field should help, but the absence of Darnold makes this a far more intriguing divisional matchup than the first meeting suggested.

title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from an ugly loss to the Bears
summary: Losing to the Chicago Bears isn’t exactly a shocking outcome. Ben Johnson has built a competitive team, and Chicago has shown it can hang with anyone. But the way the Seattle Seahawks lost is what should frustrate Seattle fans. The offense struggled to sustain drives, the defense failed to make enough plays, and several issues […]
full_text: Losing to the Chicago Bears isn’t exactly a shocking outcome. Ben Johnson has built a competitive team, and Chicago has shown it can hang with anyone. But the way the Seattle Seahawks lost is what should frustrate Seattle fans. The offense struggled to sustain drives, the defense failed to make enough plays, and several issues that have followed this team throughout the season resurfaced at the worst possible time. Seattle had opportunities to make this a competitive game, but too many mistakes on both sides of the ball made that difficult. The loss also carries significant weight in the standings. The Seahawks are now further behind the 49ers and have dropped an important head-to-head matchup against a team that could be competing with them for a Wild Card spot down the stretch. These are the kinds of games Seattle needed to win. The Bad Third-down struggles come back to haunt the Seahawks Seattle’s third-down problems returned in a big way against Chicago. The Seahawks converted just 1 of 11 attempts, a dismal 9.1% conversion rate. That’s particularly frustrating considering how well the offense had handled some difficult third-down situations against the Chiefs. Seattle had been finding ways to convert third-and-long situations at an impressive rate, but there’s a difference between being good at converting those situations and constantly putting yourself in them. Converting third-and-long is a valuable skill, but it shouldn’t be mistaken for a sustainable offensive strategy. When an offense consistently finds itself facing long third downs, it usually means something has already gone wrong on first and second down. Whether it’s ineffective runs, poor play sequencing, or a lack of answers against the defensive front, the offense is making life harder for itself. Eventually, a good defense is going to make you pay for that. Chicago did exactly that. The Bears consistently put Seattle in difficult situations, and the Seahawks had no answers when it mattered. Brian Fleury and Sam Darnold share the blame There’s been plenty of debate among Seahawks fans about who’s more responsible for the offensive struggles. Is it Brian Fleury and his play-calling, or is it Sam Darnold and his decision-making? The answer is pretty simple: both are to blame. Fleury has struggled to put together a consistent offensive plan. The route concepts don’t always complement each other, the play sequencing can feel disconnected, and there are too many situations in which the offense appears to have no answer for what the defense is doing. Until the run game comes around — or even when it does, I guess — the Seahawks gotta hit on play-action explosives. Keeps em out of 3rd down, flips the field, scores points, etc. It's not hitting the same as last year and that makes it hard for the offense to function. pic.twitter.com/ErAQtizS2d — Dugar, Michael-Shawn (@MikeDugar) November 3, 2026 One example is how defenses have been sending blitzes on early downs, anticipating an under-center play-action pass. Fleury hasn’t found a way to counter those looks, repeatedly leaving Darnold under pressure. It’s not just about individual play calls. Good offensive design should create opportunities from one play to the next, manipulate defensive reactions, and give the quarterback answers against different coverages. Too often, Seattle’s offense looks like a collection of unrelated plays rather than a cohesive system. In other words, even some creative play designs struggle to work because they aren’t connected to a larger plan. The red zone offered another example. In this play, Darnold finishes the play without a dropback, and the routes essentially just run toward the defenders. There’s no real attempt to create space or take advantage of the double coverage on JSN. It’s discouraging to watch. Having him call two running plays with ten minutes left in the fourth quarter, while trailing by more than one possession, was one of the strangest decisions I’ve seen in a long time. Even if it looks like Darnold changed the play the second time around, the decision itself was bizarre. Darnold’s performance is concerning, too. He held onto the ball too long on several occasions, missed throws he should have made, and made questionable decisions throughout the game. There were also instances in which he abandoned progressions that appeared to offer better options. His pre-snap recognition was particularly concerning on the play that resulted in his rib injury. On the second snap of the game, Kyler Gordon lined up in an obvious blitz position. Yet Darnold didn’t appear to make any meaningful adjustment to the protection or prepare for the pressure coming from that side. Gordon wasn’t exactly hiding his intentions. The alignment itself should have been enough to trigger an adjustment, whether that meant changing the protection or preparing to get the ball out quickly. Instead, Darnold appeared caught off guard by a pressure that should have been anticipated. Darnold hesitates too much and abandons his reads. It’s not necessarily that he’s missing throws to completely uncovered receivers; he’s failing to hit windows that an NFL quarterback should be able to recognize and attack. Here, at the end of his dropback, he has JSN, who has confused the defensive back. With better anticipation and timing, the ball should already be on its way. On several occasions, Darnold failed to anticipate his receivers’ routes. Here, he tries to read JSN’s release, but Kyler Gordon does a good job covering him. Darnold moves to his next read and finds Horton. However, he hesitates for a moment and puts the receiver directly in harm’s way, throwing toward the safety. It’s an exact example of what a hospital ball looks like. Here’s a rare good play call from Fleury. Horton’s route creates separation with the cut in JSN’s route. Darnold sees it, but once again hesitates, doesn’t throw the ball, and decides to run. I’m not saying this is an easy throw, but it’s an NFL throw. Darnold was intercepted for the ninth time, but that’s not the play I want to focus on. Instead, there’s an interception that was wiped out by a penalty. Darnold recognizes that JSN has drawn the safety’s double coverage and, once again, just as he did on his second interception against the Broncos, puts the ball where it shouldn’t go. The throw to Kupp should have been placed toward the back of the end zone, away from the defender and out of harm’s way. Instead, it goes right into the defender’s hands. The defense wasn’t the reason Seattle lost, but it certainly didn’t help The Bears finished with 34 points, and Caleb Williams became the first quarterback to in awhile against this Seattle defense to surpass 200 passing yards. Chicago found success through the air and on the ground, while also creating problems for the Seahawks in the red zone. The Seahawks defense had been excellent against Kenneth Walker in its previous outing, particularly when it came to tackling. Against Chicago, that discipline disappeared. Missed tackles repeatedly turned what should have been negative plays into significant gains. There were also opportunities to bring down the quarterback or finish plays behind the line of scrimmage that Seattle couldn’t capitalize on. The edges remain a problem Seattle continues to be relatively solid against the run between the tackles, but the edges have become a concerning weakness. The defensive ends haven’t consistently generated pressure, and their run fits have also created opportunities for opposing offenses. Three of the Bears four red-zone touchdowns Monday night were on the ground, and two were to Lawrence's side. pic.twitter.com/WDzzL0KSqC — Brady Henderson (@BradyHenderson) November 5, 2026 Take DeMarcus Lawrence, for example. At times, he attacks an interior gap that is already occupied by Ernest Jones, leaving the outside vulnerable and forcing someone like Julian Love or a cornerback to make the replacement. That alignment issue led…

summary: Brett Favre never got this kind of coverage.
